title: Support variable-length hard negatives in CrossEncoder ranking losses
body:
## Summary

Addresses #3581: support `(anchor, positive, [negative_1, ..., negative_n])` in CrossEncoder `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss` and `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss`, including empty and unequal-length negative lists. The baseline failure was reproduced by code analysis and an offline local-Bert example, not reported as a production incident.

Each anchor-positive row contributes one cross-entropy term, avoiding the changed weighting caused by expanding it into repeated triples. All explicit negatives participate; `num_negatives` caps additional candidates sampled without replacement from other rows. Only real text pairs are scored. Row activations run before score padding, and cached backward replays the same sampled pair plan.

Existing fixed-column sampling/call order is retained; `num_negatives=0` also now avoids an invalid zero-sample multinomial call. Adds opt-in `NoDuplicatesBatchSampler(flatten_list_values=True)` for individual-text duplicate checks, including the hashed sampler, while preserving default whole-list comparisons. The docs show an end-to-end Trainer recipe. This does not add multi-positive supervision or cross-device gathering.

## Validation

```sh
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest \
  tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_ragged_multiple_negatives_ranking.py \
  tests/cross_encoder/test_data_collator.py tests/base/samplers -q
```

**147 passed, 3 skipped** (unavailable torchcodec audio tests). Coverage includes per-anchor loss/gradient oracles, sampled ownership, empty/singleton cases, cached replay/dropout/scaled gradients, activation masking, unchanged sampler defaults, and real locally initialized Bert Trainer train/evaluation with incomplete batches in both sampler modes. No model downloads. Ten existing cached-loss regression cases also pass with their downloaded fixture explicitly replaced by local Bert. Ruff 0.15.6 lint/format and `pip check` pass.

Fixed-format seeded outputs and model gradients match the pinned baseline exactly. A small CPU toy benchmark (batch 32; one thread; seven repeats of 30 forward/backward steps) measured essentially unchanged fixed-path medians: 1.0834→1.0837 ms uncached, 2.6486→2.6213 ms cached. Ragged processing incurs per-row Python/activation overhead; no speedup or retrieval-accuracy improvement is claimed.

CPU validation only: the full upstream suite, GPU/DDP behavior, and retrieval-quality benchmarks were not run. Full Sphinx HTML builds succeed for both this patch and pristine main with the same 80 warnings (no new warnings after path normalization); the new section, both API backlinks, and loss-table targets were checked in generated HTML.

## AI assistance

AI agents substantially assisted with implementation, tests, documentation, and technical review. Review found and corrected padding-induced activation NaNs, helper-override compatibility, unnecessary zero-sampling RNG consumption, and positional-ownership coverage gaps. The validation scope and remaining limitations are stated above.

title: [fix] Make SparseAutoEncoder picklable so CSR models work with multi-process encoding and DataLoader workers
body:
CSR models can't be pickled, so multi-process and multi-GPU encoding fail for all of them. `SparseAutoEncoder.__init__` stores a local function on the module (`self.auxk_mask_fn = auxk_mask_fn`), and pickle can't serialize a local function. Every CSR model has this module: published ones such as `tomaarsen/csr-mxbai-embed-large-v1-nq`, and any dense model loaded with `SparseEncoder(...)`, which gets a `SparseAutoEncoder` on top by default (the CSR shortcut in the training overview). `encode(..., device=[...])` and `start_multi_process_pool()` always start their workers with `spawn`, which pickles the model, so this fails on every OS:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SparseEncoder

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = SparseEncoder("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
    print([type(module).__name__ for module in model])  # ['Transformer', 'Pooling', 'SparseAutoEncoder']

    texts = ["The weather is lovely today.", "It's so sunny outside!", "He drove to the stadium."] * 4
    embeddings = model.encode(texts, device=["cpu", "cpu"])
    # main:    AttributeError: Can't get local object 'SparseAutoEncoder.__init__.<locals>.auxk_mask_fn'
    #          (raised by p.start() in start_multi_process_pool(); on Windows the started worker then exits with EOFError: Ran out of input)
    # this PR: the same embeddings as model.encode(texts), up to float rounding (about 1e-6)
```

`pickle.dumps(model)` and `model.start_multi_process_pool(["cpu", "cpu"])` raise the same error. The closure has three more effects:

- **DataLoader workers:** the data collator holds `model.preprocess`, so the model is pickled for every DataLoader worker that is spawned, which is how workers start on Windows and macOS. Here, `SparseEncoderTrainer` with `CSRLoss(model, loss=SparseMultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model))` and `dataloader_num_workers=1` raises the same `AttributeError`, after torch's warning "Got pickle error when attempting to start a worker Process"; with `dataloader_num_workers=0` it trains. The warning adds that Python 3.14+ starts workers with `forkserver` on Linux, which also needs picklable arguments; I couldn't test that.
- **Copies:** `copy.deepcopy` copies functions by reference, so a copy's `auxk_mask_fn` keeps reading the original module's `stats_last_nonzero`, and when the copy is trained, its AuxK loss never sees the copy's own dead latents. I deep-copied a fresh `SparseAutoEncoder` (64 latents, `dead_threshold=2`) and trained the copy for 6 steps with `CSRReconstructionLoss`: on main, some of the copy's latents were dead from the second step on, but its auxiliary latents stayed all zero; with this change, they come from the copy's own dead latents. `test_csr_copy_masks_with_its_own_dead_feature_stats` below shows the same thing directly. `merge_models` and the test fixtures deep-copy models.
- **`dead_threshold`:** the closure uses the value passed to `__init__`, but `save()` writes the `dead_threshold` attribute to the config, so setting `model[-1].dead_threshold` only takes effect after saving and loading the model.

This has been the case since CSR models were added in v5.0.0. On main, CSR is the only one of these model types that can't be pickled: SPLADE, inference-free SPLADE (`Router`), `SentenceTransformer`, `CrossEncoder` and `MultiVectorEncoder` models built from tiny test models all round-trip through `pickle`.

**Cause:** the mask that keeps only the dead latents for the auxiliary (AuxK) loss is a closure over `self` and the `dead_threshold` argument, created in `__init__` and stored as an instance attribute.

**Fix:** `auxk_mask_fn` is now a regular method that builds the same mask from `self.stats_last_nonzero` and `self.dead_threshold`. `module.auxk_mask_fn(x)` works as before, and the saved config, the weights and the outputs don't change: training a `SparseAutoEncoder` for 6 steps, with 4 to 8 dead latents from the second step on, gives bitwise-identical auxiliary latents, auxiliary reconstructions, losses and `stats_last_nonzero` on main and with this change. The open draft #3796 also calls `self.auxk_mask_fn`, which works the same with the method.

**Tests:**
- In `tests/sparse_encoder/modules/test_csr.py`, next to the other `SparseAutoEncoder` tests (not marked slow, so CI runs them):
  - `test_csr_pickle_roundtrip`: after `pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(module))`, the state dict, the inference output and the mask are unchanged.
  - `test_csr_copy_masks_with_its_own_dead_feature_stats`: a deep copy and the original each build the mask from their own `stats_last_nonzero`.
  - `test_csr_auxk_mask_uses_the_current_dead_threshold`: changing `dead_threshold` after init changes the mask.
- `test_multi_process_encode_csr_model` in `tests/sparse_encoder/test_multi_process.py`, marked slow like the other multi-process tests: multi-process encoding of the `csr_bert_tiny_model` fixture gives the same embeddings as `encode()`.

On main, `test_csr_pickle_roundtrip` and the multi-process test fail with the `AttributeError` above, and the other two with `assert False` (the copy's mask comes out all zeros, and the mask ignores the new threshold). All four pass with this change. The snippet above, `start_multi_process_pool()` and the training run with `dataloader_num_workers=1` work as well; both multi-process paths match `model.encode(texts)` up to float rounding (about 1e-6; the `SparseAutoEncoder` is randomly initialized on load, so the exact difference varies from run to run).

```
python -m pytest -m "slow or not slow" tests/sparse_encoder/modules/test_csr.py tests/sparse_encoder/test_multi_process.py \
  -k "pickle_roundtrip or own_dead_feature_stats or current_dead_threshold or csr_model"
  main + new tests: 4 failed
  this PR:          4 passed

python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/modules/test_csr.py tests/sparse_encoder/losses/test_csr.py
  main:    23 passed, 8 skipped
  this PR: 26 passed, 8 skipped

# other suites that use CSR models
python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/test_model.py        # main and this PR: 359 passed, 1 failed (test_detect_mlm)
python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/test_model_card.py   # main and this PR: 11 passed
python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/test_trainer.py      # main and this PR: 6 passed, 160 deselected
python -m pytest -m "slow or not slow" tests/sparse_encoder/test_multi_process.py
  main:    14 passed, 1 skipped
  this PR: 15 passed, 1 skipped

pre-commit run --files <the 3 changed files>   # ruff check, ruff format, typos: Passed
```

`test_detect_mlm` needs the full-size `distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased` model, which I didn't download, and fails the same way on both sides; compared test by test, the new tests are the only difference. The skipped tests need CUDA (the multi-process one needs two CUDA devices).

title: [fix] Wait for Qdrant upload before searching
body:
### Problem
`semantic_search_qdrant` builds the index with `client.upload_collection(...)`, which defaults to `wait=False`. Qdrant then acknowledges each batch before the points are searchable. The function starts querying straight after the upload, so on a freshly built index it can intermittently return incomplete top-k results that are missing documents, with no error.

Reproduced locally against a Qdrant server (v1.20.0, qdrant-client 1.16.1)

### Reproducer
```python
import random
from uuid import uuid4
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models

client = QdrantClient(url="http://127.0.0.1:6333")
for wait in (False, True):
    misses = 0
    for _ in range(40):
        name = f"race_{uuid4().hex}"
        client.create_collection(name, vectors_config={}, sparse_vectors_config={"text": models.SparseVectorParams()})
        vecs = [
            {"text": models.SparseVector(indices=random.sample(range(30000), 256), values=[random.random() for _ in range(256)])}
            for _ in range(2000)
        ]
        client.upload_collection(name, vectors=vecs, ids=range(2000), wait=wait)  # same call as semantic_search_qdrant
        misses += client.count(name, exact=True).count < 2000
        client.delete_collection(name)
    print(f"wait={wait}: {misses}/40 fresh indexes missing points on immediate read")
```

Output:
```
wait=False: 1/40 fresh indexes missing points on immediate read
wait=True: 0/40 fresh indexes missing points on immediate read
```
With larger upload batches (1000 points per request) the gap is much bigger: 30 of 30 trials had points that weren't visible yet on the immediate read.

### Fix
Pass `wait=True` to `upload_collection`, so indexing finishes before any query runs.

### Tests
Added `test_qdrant_waits_for_upload_before_searching`. The Qdrant stub now records the `wait` argument of each upload. The test fails without the fix and passes with it.

```
$ pytest tests/sparse_encoder/test_search_engines.py
12 passed
$ ruff check / ruff format --check (changed files)
All checks passed!
```

### Related
- #3909, #4217: earlier `semantic_search_qdrant` fixes
- No open issue or PR covers this.

title: [fix] Keep adapters trainable when loading a saved PEFT/LoRA model
body:
Fixes #3434

A model trained with a LoRA adapter (`model.add_adapter(LoraConfig(...))`) and saved can't be trained further after loading it again: `SentenceTransformer(path)` returns it with the adapter frozen, so a second round of training fails on the first step, as #3434 reports. Adapter models from the Hub load the same way (`sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-lora` loads with 0 trainable parameters). It still reproduces on main:

```python
from datasets import Dataset
from peft import LoraConfig, TaskType

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer, SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import MultipleNegativesRankingLoss

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
model.add_adapter(LoraConfig(task_type=TaskType.FEATURE_EXTRACTION, r=4, lora_alpha=8, target_modules=["query", "value"]))
print(sum(param.requires_grad for param in model.parameters()))  # 8
model.save_pretrained("st-lora")

reloaded = SentenceTransformer("st-lora")
print(sum(param.requires_grad for param in reloaded.parameters()))  # main: 0, this PR: 8

train_dataset = Dataset.from_dict({"anchor": [f"query {i}" for i in range(8)], "positive": [f"document {i}" for i in range(8)]})
args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(
    output_dir="st-run", per_device_train_batch_size=4, num_train_epochs=1, save_strategy="no", report_to="none"
)
trainer = SentenceTransformerTrainer(
    model=reloaded, args=args, train_dataset=train_dataset, loss=MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(reloaded)
)
trainer.train()
# main:    RuntimeError: element 0 of tensors does not require grad and does not have a grad_fn
# this PR: trains, and only the 8 LoRA tensors change
```

`CrossEncoder`, `SparseEncoder` and `MultiVectorEncoder` load adapter checkpoints through the same `Transformer` module, and their adapters come back frozen too. For example, `CrossEncoder("cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce")` with a `TaskType.SEQ_CLS` LoRA has 8 trainable tensors before saving and 0 after loading, and `CrossEncoderTrainer.train()` then raises the same `RuntimeError`.

**Cause:** for an adapter checkpoint, `Transformer._load_model` calls `from_pretrained`, which loads the adapter with transformers' `load_adapter()` and its default `is_trainable=False`. That sets `inference_mode=True` on the adapter config and freezes the adapter layers, while PEFT keeps the base model frozen as after `add_adapter`, so nothing is left to train. `from_pretrained` has no option to load the adapter as trainable (transformers 5.21.0 and main).

**Fix:** when the loaded model carries adapters, `Transformer.__init__` sets the active adapter(s) again with `self.model.set_adapter(self.model.active_adapters())`, the call that `add_adapter` ends with. This makes the adapter weights (and `modules_to_save`, if any) trainable and leaves the base model frozen. Nothing else changes: the weights and outputs are the same as on main (bit-identical embeddings for a reloaded adapter with random weights), the transformers model stays in eval mode, as on main, and `model.load_adapter(path)` still loads a frozen adapter unless `is_trainable=True` is passed, as in transformers.

After loading, the trainable parameters are now the same as after `add_adapter` for the default LoRA config with all four model classes, and for DoRA, `target_modules="all-linear"` and a `CrossEncoder` with `modules_to_save=["classifier"]`. That's also what `load_adapter(path, is_trainable=True)` gives. On main, calling `model.set_adapter("default")` after loading works around it.

**Tests:** `test_peft_roundtrip_keeps_adapter_trainable` in `tests/base/modules/test_transformer.py`, next to the existing PEFT round-trip test, for `transformer_task="feature-extraction"` (`SentenceTransformer`) and `"sequence-classification"` (`CrossEncoder`). It checks that the reloaded module has the same trainable parameters as after `add_adapter`, and that a backward pass gives gradients to exactly those. Both cases fail on main with `assert set() == {...}` and pass with this change. The snippet above now trains and changes only the 8 LoRA tensors (of 47); the `CrossEncoder` variant also trains and changes only its 8 LoRA tensors.

```
python -m pytest tests/base/modules/test_transformer.py -k peft
  main + new test: 2 failed, 3 passed
  this PR:         5 passed

python -m pytest tests/base/modules/test_transformer.py
  main + new test: 16 failed, 195 passed, 4 skipped
  this PR:         14 failed, 197 passed, 4 skipped

# other suites that load or add adapters
python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_model.py          # main and this PR: 107 passed, 14 skipped
python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py   # main and this PR: 8 failed, 504 passed, 13 skipped
python -m pytest tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_model.py   # main and this PR: 4 failed, 82 passed, 6 skipped, 60 errors

pre-commit run --files <the 2 changed files>   # ruff check, ruff format, typos: Passed
```

I ran the tests offline. The failures and errors on both sides are tests whose Hub models or revisions aren't in my local cache (e.g. `hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-LlamaForCausalLM`, `multi-vector-encoder-testing/bert-tiny-multi-vector`); compared test by test, the 2 new cases are the only difference. `test_load_adapter_with_revision`, which CI skips, loads `sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-lora` through the changed code and passes.

Run on Windows 11 (CPU), Python 3.12.15, torch 2.14.1+cpu, transformers 5.21.0, peft 0.21.2, on main at 5017dedc; the snippet's main output is from main at 7bfaf1cc, which has the same `transformer.py`. I didn't run into this in my own use: #3434 reported it, and I reproduced it with the snippet above. I didn't run the minimum-versions setup (transformers 5.0.0), where `set_adapter` also accepts a list of adapter names.

**Notes:**
- With `bias="all"` or `bias="lora_only"` in the `LoraConfig`, the biases of the adapted layers (e.g. `query.base_layer.bias`) still load frozen, as on main, since `set_adapter` only covers the adapter weights. `load_adapter(path, is_trainable=True)` on the base model makes those trainable too.
- A loaded adapter model is now trainable, like a loaded full model. Code that loads one to train only other modules, and relies on the adapter staying frozen, would now train the adapter too unless it freezes it.
- The trainer's `_load_from_checkpoint` (`load_best_model_at_end`, `resume_from_checkpoint`) copies the checkpoint's weights into the model being trained, so it isn't affected.

Related: #3405 (loading adapters through the transformers integration), #3978 (the base model's config for adapter checkpoints), #3701 (saved LoRA weights not loaded, fixed in transformers 5.6.0; a different problem), #3980 (restoring a trained `modules_to_save` head; also different, this PR only changes `requires_grad`). I searched open and recently closed issues and PRs and found no other report or fix for this.

title: Speed up BinaryClassificationEvaluator threshold search ~10x with NumPy, using 3x less memory
body:
`BinaryClassificationEvaluator.find_best_acc_and_threshold` and `find_best_f1_and_threshold` build a Python list of `(score, label)` tuples, sort it with a `lambda` key, and walk it pair by pair. They run once per similarity function on every evaluation, and `CrossEncoderClassificationEvaluator` calls them too. On 1M pairs the two take 1.7 s and add 164 MB of peak memory, mostly the tuples of NumPy scalars.

This PR keeps the algorithm and does it with NumPy: one stable `argsort`, a `cumsum` of positives, and the ends of each group of tied scores (the only valid cuts, as #4023 made explicit). Accuracy and F1 are computed for all cuts at once with the same formulas, and `argmax` picks the first best one, like the strict `>` in the loop. The chosen threshold is still computed with the same scalar expression, including the rounded-midpoint guard from #4023, so it has the same value and type. Both functions share that sorting through a small `_sorted_score_groups` helper.

The outputs are identical. I compared main and this branch on 338 cases: empty, single pair, all positive, all negative, the adjacent float32 values from #4023, and random scores from 2 to 5000 pairs in float16/32/64, rounded to create ties, with int and bool labels, as NumPy arrays and as Python lists, in both directions. Values and types match for NumPy arrays, which is what both evaluators pass. For other inputs, `find_best_acc_and_threshold` now converts the scores with `np.asarray`, as `find_best_f1_and_threshold` already did, so its threshold gets the same type and precision as the F1 threshold:

- a Python list of floats gives `np.float64` instead of `float`, with the same value;
- a torch tensor gives a NumPy scalar (`np.float32(-0.65)`) instead of a 0-d tensor (`tensor(-0.6500)`);
- a float32 pandas Series computes the midpoint in float32 instead of float64 (`-0.65` instead of `-0.6500000059604645`), so the threshold can differ in the last bits, still between the same two score groups.

Integer and float labels, lists of NumPy scalars and bfloat16 tensors give identical results.

Fresh process per run, `float32` random scores and labels, accuracy + F1 together (Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, main at 0531feb0):

| pairs | main | this PR | speedup | peak RSS, main | peak RSS, this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100,000 | 0.10 s | 0.01 s | 10x | +15 MB | +4 MB |
| 1,000,000 | 1.71 s | 0.17 s | 10x | +164 MB | +57 MB |
| 5,000,000 | 9.70 s | 1.05 s | 9x | +856 MB | +291 MB |

(Median of 3 runs. At 100,000 pairs the new times are 0.01 to 0.02 s, too short to give a precise ratio.)

New test: `test_BinaryClassificationEvaluator_best_thresholds_match_brute_force` rounds random scores to one decimal to get many tied groups, tries every cut between groups with scikit-learn, and checks that none beats the returned accuracy or F1, and that the returned thresholds reproduce them. It passes on main too, so it guards the behaviour rather than reproducing a bug.

`pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_binary_classification_evaluator.py` gives 45 passed, and the CrossEncoder classification evaluator tests pass. ruff check and ruff format pass on the changed files.

I found this while profiling the evaluators after #4290, and I found no existing issue or PR. I used AI assistance for the profiling, the benchmark scripts and this text, and I reviewed everything it produced.

Versions: sentence-transformers main (0531feb0), torch 2.15.0, numpy 2.5.4, scikit-learn 1.9.1, Python 3.12.13.

title: Speed up paraphrase_mining_embeddings up to 3.3x by replacing the per-pair heap loop with tensor ops
body:
`paraphrase_mining_embeddings` spends most of its time outside the score computation: after each query chunk it moves the top-k scores and indices to Python lists and pushes every candidate pair through a `heapq` + `set` loop, one pair at a time. With the defaults (`top_k=100`) that is about 100 Python iterations per sentence. On 50k sentences the profile shows about 3.6 s of the 4.9 s in that loop on CPU.

This PR keeps the search exactly as it is (same chunked scoring, same top-k merge across corpus chunks) and replaces the heap loop with tensor ops on the embeddings' device:

- Each unordered pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` is keyed as `i * n + j`. Self matches are skipped and each sentence keeps its first `top_k` other neighbours with a mask instead of a list comprehension.
- After each query chunk, the new candidates are appended to the kept pairs, duplicates are removed keeping the first occurrence (a stable sort of the keys), and `topk` caps them at `max_pairs`. So the memory bound stays `max_pairs` plus one chunk of candidates, as before.
- Once `max_pairs` pairs are kept, candidates below the lowest kept score are dropped before that step, the same role `min_score` played in the heap loop.
- Scores and indices go to Python once, at the end.

The result is the same contract #3979 and #4131 settled on: the top `max_pairs` unique pairs among each sentence's `top_k` neighbours, highest score first. I compared main and this branch on about 16,700 random configurations (n from 0 to 40, `top_k` 0 to 100, `max_pairs` 0 to 1000, chunk sizes 1 and non-divisors, float16/32/64, cos, dot, Euclidean and Manhattan), on the Quora reproducer below, and on CPU and MPS. The score lists are identical. Two things can differ, both only on exactly tied scores:

- The order among tied pairs. Before, it came from the heap's internal layout; now ties stay in the order they were found.
- Which pair survives when the `max_pairs` cut falls inside a group of tied scores. With duplicated sentences this happens: 66 sentences repeated 3 times with `max_pairs=1000` keep the same 1000 scores, but 2 of the tied pairs at the cut differ.

With an asymmetric `score_function`, which the docstring already rules out, the kept orientation can differ too: with one query chunk, this branch keeps the first orientation found, as the brute-force top-k does, and main could re-add a pair it had evicted with its other orientation's score.

Reproducer (downloads `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` and `quora-duplicates`, 95,524 unique questions):

```python
import time

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.util import paraphrase_mining_embeddings

pairs = load_dataset("sentence-transformers/quora-duplicates", "pair", split="train[:80000]")
questions = list(dict.fromkeys(q for row in pairs for q in (row["anchor"], row["positive"])))[:100000]
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # picks MPS on a Mac
embeddings = model.encode(questions, batch_size=256, convert_to_tensor=True)

start = time.perf_counter()
mined = paraphrase_mining_embeddings(embeddings)
print(f"{len(mined)} pairs in {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")
```

Median of 5 interleaved runs after warm-up, defaults (`top_k=100`, `max_pairs=500000`), on the embeddings above (Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, main at 0531feb0):

| device | sentences | main | this PR | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | 20,000 | 2.10 s | 0.88 s | 2.4x |
| CPU | 50,000 | 4.38 s | 2.18 s | 2.0x |
| CPU | 95,524 | 7.81 s | 5.42 s | 1.4x |
| MPS | 20,000 | 2.21 s | 0.59 s | 3.7x |
| MPS | 50,000 | 5.25 s | 2.49 s | 2.1x |
| MPS | 95,524 | 15.12 s | 10.08 s | 1.5x |

The speedup shrinks with more sentences because the remaining time is the score matrix and its `topk`, which this PR doesn't touch. Memory doesn't grow: peak RSS added by the call, each in a fresh process, goes from +4221 MB to +4206 MB on CPU with 95,524 sentences (the chunk score matrix dominates both) and from +224 MB to +106 MB on MPS with 50,000 sentences, with the same MPS driver memory.

New tests: `test_paraphrase_mining_embeddings_duplicate_sentences` uses three copies of each sentence, so every top-k neighbour is a tie, and checks each pair comes back once across several chunk sizes. It passes on main too, so it guards the dedup rather than reproducing a bug; it fails with the dedup removed. `test_paraphrase_mining_embeddings_input_formats` checks that NumPy arrays and lists of tensors or arrays give the same pairs as a tensor; the lists failed on the first version of this PR, which read the device from the input instead of from the scores. I also added `max_pairs=-1` to `test_paraphrase_mining_embeddings_respects_max_pairs_capacity`, which keeps returning `[]`.

`pytest tests/util/test_retrieval.py` gives 185 passed, 5 skipped, and `tests/util/test_import.py` passes. ruff check and ruff format pass on the changed files. On torch 2.2.2 (the minimum) the new function matches a brute-force top-k over the full score matrix. I didn't measure CUDA.

I found this by profiling the retrieval utilities after #4290, and I found no existing issue or PR. I used AI assistance for the profiling, the benchmark scripts and this text, and I reviewed everything it produced.

Versions: sentence-transformers main (0531feb0), transformers 5.21.0, torch 2.15.0, datasets 5.1.0, Python 3.12.13.

title: [fix] Fix CrossEncoder.fit() crash with a DataLoader batch_sampler
body:
`CrossEncoder.fit()` crashes before training when the `DataLoader` was built with `batch_sampler=...`. This is the CrossEncoder counterpart of #4227, which #4228 fixed for `SentenceTransformer.fit()` only. `CrossEncoder.old_fit()` handles this case because it counts steps with `len(train_dataloader)`.

```python
from torch.utils.data import BatchSampler, DataLoader, RandomSampler
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder, InputExample

model = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce")
examples = [InputExample(texts=[f"q {i}", f"d {i}"], label=float(i % 2)) for i in range(16)]
loader = DataLoader(examples, batch_sampler=BatchSampler(RandomSampler(examples), batch_size=4, drop_last=False))
model.fit(train_dataloader=loader, epochs=1, warmup_steps=0)
# main:    TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for //: 'int' and 'NoneType'
#          (cross_encoder/fit_mixin.py, `steps_per_epoch = len(train_dataset) // batch_size`)
# this PR: logs the warning below and trains
```

**Root cause:** PyTorch sets `DataLoader.batch_size` to `None` when a `batch_sampler` is passed. `CrossEncoder.fit()` reads `getattr(train_dataloader, "batch_size", 8)`, so `None` reaches the scheduler step count and `per_device_train_batch_size`.

**Fix:** the same as #4228. When the loader's `batch_size` is `None`, use `train_dataloader.batch_sampler.batch_size` (falling back to the existing default of 8), and log that `fit()` does not keep the custom batch grouping, pointing to `CrossEncoderTrainer` or `old_fit()`. The warning text matches the `SentenceTransformer.fit()` one. Loaders built with `batch_size=...` and `NoDuplicatesDataLoader` go through the same path as before.

**Test:** `tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py::test_fit_with_custom_batch_sampler`, modeled on the `SentenceTransformer` test from #4228. It patches out `CrossEncoderTrainer.train`, then checks that `per_device_train_batch_size == 4` and that the warning is logged. It fails on main with the `TypeError` above and passes with this change.

```
pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py -k custom_batch_sampler   # main: 1 failed (TypeError), this PR: 1 passed
pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py                           # 37 passed
```

title: [fix] Save the best model and call `callback` after each epoch in CrossEncoder.fit()
body:
Since `CrossEncoder.fit()` moved onto the `CrossEncoderTrainer` in v4.0, the evaluation it runs after each epoch never reaches its other callbacks. With the default `evaluation_steps=0`, `fit(..., evaluator=..., output_path=...)` never saves the best model (`output_path` only gets `eval/`), and the `callback` passed to `fit()` is never called:

```python
import os

from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder, InputExample
from sentence_transformers.cross_encoder.evaluation import CrossEncoderCorrelationEvaluator

model = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce")
train = [InputExample(texts=[f"query {i}", f"passage {i}"], label=float(i % 2)) for i in range(16)]
dev = [InputExample(texts=[f"dev query {i}", f"dev passage {i}"], label=float(i % 2)) for i in range(8)]
evaluator = CrossEncoderCorrelationEvaluator.from_input_examples(dev, name="dev")
model.fit(
    train_dataloader=DataLoader(train, shuffle=True, batch_size=4),
    evaluator=evaluator,
    epochs=2,
    warmup_steps=0,
    output_path="ce-fit-output",
    callback=lambda score, epoch, steps: print("callback:", epoch, steps),
)
print(sorted(os.listdir("ce-fit-output")))
# main:    no "callback:" lines, then ['eval']
# this PR: callback: 1.0 4
#          callback: 2.0 8
#          ['README.md', 'config.json', 'config_sentence_transformers.json', 'eval', 'model.safetensors', 'modules.json', ...]
```

The evaluator does run on main (`ce-fit-output/eval/CrossEncoderCorrelationEvaluator_dev_results.csv` has rows for epochs 1.0 and 2.0), but nothing else sees its results. Loading the trained model from `output_path`, as v3.4.1's `examples/training/cross-encoder/training_stsbenchmark.py` does right after `fit()`, then fails on main with ``ValueError: Unrecognized model in ce-fit-output. Should have a `model_type` key in its config.json.`` In v3, `fit()` called `_eval_during_training(..., epoch, -1, callback)` after every epoch, which called `callback` and saved the model whenever the score improved (`old_fit()` still does), and the `fit()` docstring says it should give the same results as before v4.0.

**Cause:** `EvaluatorCallback.on_epoch_end` runs the evaluator and then passes the metrics to the other callbacks (`SaveModelCallback`, `OriginalCallback`) with `self.trainer.callback_handler.on_evaluate(...)`, but only if `self.trainer` is set. Its docstring says "The `.trainer` must be provided after the trainer has been created". `SentenceTransformer.fit()` does that right after creating its trainer, but `CrossEncoder.fit()` never has: from v4.0.0 to v6.2.0 and on main, the only assignment is `self.trainer = None` in `__init__`. The same run through `SentenceTransformer.fit()` (with `EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator` and `CosineSimilarityLoss`) calls `callback` twice and saves the model on main.

**Fix:**
- `CrossEncoder.fit()` sets the trainer on its `EvaluatorCallback`, like `SentenceTransformer.fit()`.
- `SaveModelCallback` and `OriginalCallback` in both `fit()` mixins now look up the metric with `getattr(evaluator, "primary_metric", None) or "evaluator"`. The old `getattr(evaluator, "primary_metric", "evaluator")` gives `None` for an evaluator that returns a single float and keeps the `BaseEvaluator` default `primary_metric = None` (only evaluators that return a dict must set it), so `key.endswith(None)` raises a `TypeError`. Both `EvaluatorCallback` and the trainer's evaluation loop store a float score as `eval_evaluator`, so `"evaluator"` is the right fallback. Without this change, the first one would turn the missing save in `CrossEncoder.fit()` into this crash for such evaluators. `SentenceTransformer.fit()` already crashes this way when given `output_path` or `callback`:

```python
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from sentence_transformers import InputExample, SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.base.evaluation import BaseEvaluator
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import MultipleNegativesRankingLoss

class MyEvaluator(BaseEvaluator):
    def __call__(self, model, output_path=None, epoch=-1, steps=-1):
        return 0.5

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
train = [InputExample(texts=[f"query {i}", f"passage {i}"]) for i in range(16)]
model.fit(
    train_objectives=[(DataLoader(train, batch_size=4), MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model))],
    evaluator=MyEvaluator(),
    epochs=1,
    warmup_steps=0,
    output_path="st-fit-output",
)
# main:    TypeError: endswith first arg must be str or a tuple of str, not NoneType
#          (in SaveModelCallback.on_evaluate, sentence_transformer/fit_mixin.py line 74)
# this PR: trains and saves the model to st-fit-output
```

Nothing else changes. Evaluators that return a dict have `primary_metric` set by the time these callbacks run, so they match the same keys as before. One that returns a dict but leaves `primary_metric` unset (the `BaseEvaluator` docstring requires it) now gets no save or `callback`, where `SentenceTransformer.fit()`, and `CrossEncoder.fit()` with `evaluation_steps > 0`, raised the `TypeError` on main. With `evaluation_steps > 0`, the trainer's own evaluations already reached these callbacks, so only the evaluations after each epoch were missing: with `evaluation_steps=3` in the first snippet, `callback` now runs at steps 3, 4, 6, 8 and 8 instead of 3, 6 and 8, the same as `SentenceTransformer.fit()` with those settings on main. `fit()` without an evaluator still doesn't save a `CrossEncoder`, as in v3, and `old_fit()` and the trainers are untouched.

**Tests:**
- `test_fit_saves_best_model_and_calls_callback_after_each_epoch` in `tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py`, with a `CrossEncoderCorrelationEvaluator` and with a `BaseEvaluator` subclass that returns a float. It checks that `callback` is called after epochs 1 and 2, that the model is saved to `output_path`, and that the saved model loads and predicts.
- `test_fit_with_float_evaluator_saves_best_model_and_calls_callback` in `tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py`: the float evaluator with `output_path` and `callback`.

On main, both `CrossEncoder` cases fail with `assert [] == [1.0, 2.0]` and the `SentenceTransformer` test fails with the `TypeError`. With only the first change, the float `CrossEncoder` case fails with the `TypeError`.

```
python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py -q
  main:    86 passed, 320 deselected
  this PR: 89 passed, 320 deselected

# other suites that use CrossEncoder, the trainers and the evaluators
python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_model.py tests/base/test_trainer.py tests/cross_encoder/test_model_card.py \
  tests/cross_encoder/evaluation tests/base/evaluation -q
  main:    167 passed, 15 skipped
  this PR: 167 passed, 15 skipped

pre-commit run --files <the 4 changed files>   # ruff check, ruff format, typos: Passed
```

Run on Windows 11 (CPU), Python 3.12.15, torch 2.14.1+cpu, transformers 5.21.0, on main at 5017dedc. This was found through code analysis (comparing `CrossEncoder.fit()` with `SentenceTransformer.fit()` and the v3 `fit()`), not in actual use; the snippets above reproduce it.

Related: #3062 (the evaluator in the backwards-compatible `fit()`), #4285 (another `CrossEncoder.fit()` fix), #2324 (`fit()` without an evaluator doesn't save a `CrossEncoder`; unchanged here, as in v3). I searched open and recently closed issues and PRs and found nothing else about this.

AI assistance: Claude Code found this issue while comparing `CrossEncoder.fit()` with `SentenceTransformer.fit()` and wrote the fix, the regression tests and this description.

title: [core] Add native AWS Neuron inference support
body:
Adds native torch_neuronx support through the existing PyTorch backend. Models can use `device="neuron"`, `.to("neuron")`, inference-time device overrides, and automatic device selection.

Multiprocessing assigns each worker a separate Neuron core. Because Neuron reserves cores per process, the parent must start fresh with the model loaded on CPU; this requirement is documented and enforced.

Validation extends existing tests:

- Verified inference and multiprocessing across four physical Trainium2 devices, comparing embeddings against CPU results.
- Covered model placement, tensor/NumPy outputs, normalization, and variable-length inputs.
- Passed 116 CPU regression tests and lint/format checks.

title: Fix division by zero when mining filters exclude all negatives
body:
Combining a margin filter with `min_score` can crash `mine_hard_negatives` with `ZeroDivisionError` when the margin removes every retrieved candidate. The minimum-score filter counts already excluded `-inf` scores again, then divides by the remaining candidate count of zero. With some candidates left, it instead overstates how many candidates the minimum-score filter removed.

Exclude scores already marked as removed from the minimum-score mask. The added tests use the existing deterministic model helper and exercise the public mining function without downloading model weights: absolute and relative margins, verbose on/off, and a partially retained candidate pool.

Discovered through code analysis, then reproduced locally; this is not a report of a production training incident. Affected workflow: mining from a separate corpus where retrieved candidates score above a relatively weak labeled positive, with both margin and minimum-score constraints configured.

Validation:
- Before the change, all 5 added test cases failed (4 division-by-zero failures, 1 exclusion-count mismatch).
- After the change, the focused suite passed: 19 passed, 4 skipped (FAISS unavailable), 140 deselected. Command: `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py -k 'min_score_after_margin_removes_all_candidates or min_score_counts_only_remaining_candidates or relative_margin_with_negative_positive_score or anchor_exclusion_preserves_candidate_window or cross_encoder_rescores_without_score_filters or default_column_selection_allows_extra_columns' -q --tb=short`.
- Ruff 0.15.6 check/format and git diff --check passed.
- Existing standard-deviation warnings occur when verbose statistics process zero/one sample. Full-suite, GPU, FAISS and pretrained-model validation were not run.

AI assistance: OpenAI Codex helped identify the issue, implement the fix and regression tests, and prepare this description.

title: Speed up mine_hard_negatives up to 10x on MPS by vectorizing the per-query loops
body:
`mine_hard_negatives` spends most of its non-search time in Python loops over queries: the positive mask runs one `torch.isin` per query, and the triplet, n-tuple and labeled-list outputs build their repeated rows with one `repeat` + `cat` per query. On MPS each of those per-query ops is a small kernel launch, so on 50k pairs the mining step takes about 70 s on MPS against 5 s on CPU.

This PR replaces those loops with batched tensor ops and leaves the search, filtering and sampling untouched:

- The positive mask encodes each (query, corpus index) pair as one integer key and looks up all candidates in the sorted positive keys with a single `searchsorted`. The `+1` in the key keeps the FAISS `-1` padding from matching a real index.
- The per-query `repeat` + `cat` becomes `repeat_interleave` over the number of positives per query, and the triplet anchor/positive index matrices are built the same way instead of filling them row by row.
- Index tensors are converted with `.tolist()` before the loops that build the output dataset, instead of indexing Python lists with 0-d tensors and calling `.item()` per score.
- The anchor and positive columns are read with `dataset[column][:]` instead of `list(dataset[column])`.

The output is identical. I compared main and this branch byte for byte on 49 synthetic configurations (all four output formats, with and without scores, margins, `range_min`, random sampling, a separate corpus, score bounds, `include_positives`, 1 to 3 positives per query) on CPU and MPS, and on the reproducer below for `triplet` and `n-tuple` with `output_scores=True`, on CPU and MPS.

Reproducer (downloads `static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1` and the `natural-questions` train split):

```python
import time

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.util import mine_hard_negatives

device = "mps"
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1", device=device)
dataset = load_dataset("sentence-transformers/natural-questions", split="train").select(range(50_000))

start = time.perf_counter()
mined = mine_hard_negatives(dataset, model, batch_size=1024, verbose=False)
if device == "mps":
    torch.mps.synchronize()
print(f"{len(mined)} rows in {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")
```

Median of 3 runs, each a fresh process, main and this PR alternated (Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, main at 298ce58a):

| device | main | this PR | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| MPS | 70.30 s | 6.76 s | 10.4x |
| CPU | 4.91 s | 3.58 s | 1.37x |

With precomputed random embeddings (so the timing excludes encoding), median of 5 alternated fresh processes, 384 dims, `num_negatives=3`:

| device | pairs | format | main | this PR | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MPS | 10k | triplet | 13.16 s | 0.29 s | 45x |
| MPS | 50k | triplet | 70.15 s | 4.67 s | 15x |
| CPU | 10k | triplet | 0.37 s | 0.11 s | 3.5x |
| CPU | 50k | triplet | 2.80 s | 1.41 s | 2.0x |
| CPU | 50k | n-tuple | 2.13 s | 1.35 s | 1.6x |
| CPU | 50k | labeled-pair | 2.19 s | 1.66 s | 1.3x |

I didn't measure CUDA.

New test: `test_multiple_positives_are_never_mined_as_negatives`, for `triplet` and `n-tuple`, uses queries with 3, 2 and 1 positives and a candidate window that reaches every non-positive passage, then checks that no positive comes back as a negative. It passes on main and on this branch, and fails on this branch with the positive mask disabled.

`pytest tests/util/` gives 1357 passed, 57 skipped, 1 deselected, and `tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py` gives 160 passed. pre-commit (ruff check, ruff format, typos) passes on the changed files. I ran the tests with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`: without it, `test_faiss` hangs inside `faiss` `index.search` on my machine, on main as well, which looks like the usual faiss + torch OpenMP conflict on macOS.

I found this by profiling `mine_hard_negatives` on MPS, where it was much slower than on CPU. It is not from a user report, and I found no existing issue or PR.

Versions: sentence-transformers main (298ce58a), transformers 5.21.0, torch 2.15.0, datasets 5.1.0, Python 3.12.13.

I used AI assistance (Claude) to profile, write the benchmark and comparison scripts, and draft this description. I reviewed the change and the numbers myself.

title: [fix] Warn when saving a Dense or CrossEncoder activation that is a plain function
body:
Saving a `Dense` module or a `CrossEncoder` whose activation is a plain function (`torch.nn.functional.gelu`, `torch.relu`, `lambda x: x`, a `functools.partial`, ...) writes a config that can't restore it. The reloaded model uses Tanh (`Dense`) or the default activation (`CrossEncoder`: Sigmoid for `num_labels=1`) instead, so it gives different outputs whenever the function differs from that default. Both arguments accept any `Callable`, so this is easy to hit, e.g. when a reranker should return raw logits or an embedding model gets a GELU projection head:

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder, SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.base.modules import Dense

pairs = [("how tall is everest", "Mount Everest is 8,849 m tall."), ("how tall is everest", "Bananas are yellow.")]
model = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce", activation_fn=lambda x: x)
print(model.predict(pairs))  # [ 2.6783125 -2.6769624]
model.save_pretrained("reranker-logits")
print(CrossEncoder("reranker-logits").predict(pairs))  # main: [0.9357347  0.06434652], i.e. Sigmoid

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
model.append(Dense(model.get_embedding_dimension(), 8, activation_function=torch.nn.functional.gelu))
before = model.encode(["hello world"], convert_to_tensor=True)
model.save("embedder-gelu-head")
after = SentenceTransformer("embedder-gelu-head").encode(["hello world"], convert_to_tensor=True)
print((before - after).abs().max())  # main: tensor(0.6733), the reloaded Dense uses Tanh
```

On main the only signal is a warning while loading: `Activation function path 'builtin_function_or_method' is not trusted, falling back to the default activation function (Tanh)` (the CrossEncoder logs a similar warning for `'function'`). The warning suggests `trust_remote_code=True`, but that raises `ImportError: builtin_function_or_method doesn't look like a module path` (`function doesn't look like a module path` for the CrossEncoder), so these saves can't be restored from the saved configuration. With this PR, both `save` calls log a warning that says so:

```
Saving activation function <function <lambda> at 0x...>: plain functions can't be restored from the configuration, so loading with default settings will use the default activation function. Please use a `torch.nn.Module` instead, e.g. `torch.nn.Identity()` instead of `lambda x: x`.
```

**Cause:** `Dense.get_config_dict()` and `CrossEncoder._get_model_config()` store the activation with `util.fullname()`, which records the class of the object. For a function that class is `function` or `builtin_function_or_method`, so the config names the type rather than the function, and loading treats it as an untrusted path. Before #3714 the `Dense` case failed on load instead (#1470 used `lambda x: x`; the answer was `nn.Identity()`). Since then it falls back to Tanh.

**Fix:** log a warning on save when the activation is a plain function (`inspect.isroutine`) or a `functools.partial`, pointing to the `torch.nn.Module` equivalent. The save itself goes through, so checkpointing during training isn't interrupted, and a `CrossEncoder` loaded with `activation_fn=...` passed again keeps working. (The first version raised a `ValueError`; tomaarsen changed it to a warning in 4281c3a8.)
- `Dense`: the check is in `save()` rather than `get_config_dict()`, because `Module.__repr__` calls `get_config_dict()` and printing the model has to keep working.
- `CrossEncoder`: the check is in `_get_model_config()`, which `BaseModel.save()` calls before it writes any file.

Nothing else changes. Models in memory still run, and loading is untouched: existing saves, including ones that contain `function`, load exactly as before, and `CrossEncoder(path, activation_fn=...)` still overrides them. Instances of other callable classes are still saved by class path, which `trust_remote_code=True` can restore when the class can be built without arguments. Both docstrings now say to use a `torch.nn.Module` if the model will be saved.

**Tests:** `test_dense_save_warns_for_plain_function_activation` (builtin, Python function, lambda, `functools.partial`, and the default `torch.tanh`) in `tests/base/modules/test_dense.py` and `test_save_warns_for_plain_function_activation_fn` (builtin, lambda, `functools.partial`, and the default `torch.sigmoid`) in `tests/cross_encoder/test_model.py`. They check the warning and that the saved model still loads; the `CrossEncoder` test passes the activation again on load and gets the same scores.

```
python -m pytest tests/base/modules/test_dense.py tests/cross_encoder/test_model.py -q
  this PR (4281c3a8): 120 passed, 14 skipped

# other suites that save Dense or CrossEncoder models
python -m pytest tests/base/modules/test_router.py tests/base/test_model.py tests/base/test_trainer.py \
  tests/base/test_distributed_evaluation.py tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py tests/cross_encoder/test_model_card.py \
  tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_model.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py \
  tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gradcache.py tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_matryoshka.py \
  tests/test_merging.py tests/util/test_file_io.py tests/util/test_decorators.py -q
  main:    1262 passed, 75 skipped, 4 deselected
  this PR: 1262 passed, 75 skipped, 4 deselected

pre-commit run --files <the 4 changed files>   # ruff check, ruff format, typos: Passed
```

Run on Windows 11 (CPU), Python 3.12.15, torch 2.14.1+cpu, transformers 5.21.0, on main at 298ce58 (the two-file run above is on 4281c3a8; the wider run was on the first version). This was found through code analysis (reading how activations are saved and loaded), not in actual use; the snippet above reproduces it.

**Notes:**
- A plain function that matches the default (`torch.sigmoid` on a 1-label `CrossEncoder`, `torch.tanh` on a `Dense`) reloads with the same outputs, and now also gets the warning on save.
- A training run that writes checkpoints keeps going; each checkpoint save logs the warning.
- Out of scope: `nn.Module` activations with constructor arguments (e.g. `nn.LeakyReLU(0.2)`) still reload with default arguments.

Related: #1470, #3714, #4175, #4006. I searched open and recently closed issues and PRs and found nothing else about saving these activations.

title: Fix NaN KL for excluded multi-vector teacher candidates
body:
## Problem

A teacher score of `-inf` intentionally excludes a candidate, as recognized by `check_teacher_targets`. Both multi-vector KL consumers use `log_target=True`, where that zero-probability target contributes `exp(-inf) * (-inf - student_log_prob)`, producing a NaN loss/evaluator metric instead of zero.

Discovered through code analysis, not a claimed production incident. This affects distillation batches with excluded teacher candidates and evaluation of the same candidate sets. The existing student gradients can remain finite despite the NaN scalar; this is not a claim that model weights become NaN.

## Change

Replace only negative-infinite teacher log-probabilities with the finite dtype minimum before log-target KL in the loss and evaluator. That value still exponentiates to zero. Finite log-targets, detachment, temperatures, reductions and the log-target objective stay unchanged. No new API or normalization strategy.

#4083 proposes score-normalization parameters and has a dense-path exclusion test. This fixes the two multi-vector log-target consumers without adding those parameters. #4133's tensor-target/device fix remains intact.

## Reproducer and validation

From the repository root after installing the project and test dependencies:

```sh
pytest tests/multi_vector_encoder/losses/test_excluded_teacher_candidates.py -q
pytest tests/multi_vector_encoder/losses tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_evaluators.py -q
```

The new file includes a deterministic MaxSim/expected-KL reproducer, flat and nested evaluation, finite-target compatibility, NaN-teacher rejection, and a real pretrained `MultiVectorEncoder` workflow comparing training loss/backward with evaluation.

Independently verified on main `145ef47d5a4bcb9c88ab5e0684e14a4222ef408f`, Python 3.10.12, PyTorch 2.14.1+cpu, Transformers 5.20.2, Sentence Transformers 6.3.0.dev0:

- New tests: baseline 4 failed / 5 passed; fixed 9 passed.
- Exact published tree, nearby loss/evaluator modules: 83 passed, 2 existing CUDA-only skips (6.74s), plus the existing constant-input Spearman warning.
- Repository-pinned Ruff 0.15.6 lint/format and `git diff --check` pass on changed files.

Full repository tests, GPU execution and typos were not run. All-excluded rows, positive-infinite teacher scores and non-finite student scores remain undefined and are not repaired here. This does not claim bit-exact equivalence to the probability-target implementation in low precision.

AI assistance was used for investigation, implementation, tests and this description. Every changed line was reviewed and the reported checks were independently run against the final published files.

title: fix: preserve caller options during CrossEncoder initialization
body:
## Problem
CrossEncoder's top-level `num_labels` and `max_length` overrides write into caller-owned `config_kwargs` and `processor_kwargs`. Reusing a shared processor configuration therefore silently gives the next model the previous model's shorter maximum length. The deprecated `classifier_dropout` adapter similarly mutates the supplied dictionary (including `config_args`) and crashes when `config_kwargs=None` is explicitly supplied.

Discovered through code inspection and reproduced against main at 145ef47. For example:
```python
processor_kwargs = {"model_max_length": 64}
short = CrossEncoder(local_checkpoint, max_length=32, processor_kwargs=processor_kwargs)
normal = CrossEncoder(local_checkpoint, processor_kwargs=processor_kwargs)
# before: processor_kwargs was rewritten to 32, and normal.max_seq_length is 32
# expected: short.max_seq_length == 32 and normal.max_seq_length == 64
```
`local_checkpoint` in the regression fixture is a locally generated one-layer BERT sequence classifier and tokenizer; no Hub downloads are required.

## Change
Copy the two option dictionaries before applying CrossEncoder-specific overrides. The classifier-dropout compatibility adapter also makes a local copy, treating explicit None the same way as omission. Existing override values and deprecated argument precedence are preserved; no weights or inference algorithms change.

## Validation
- New public-constructor regressions on unchanged main: **5 failed**.
- `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_init_kwargs.py tests/util/test_decorators.py -q`: **69 passed**, Python 3.13.7.
- The new tests instantiate actual CrossEncoder models from a small temporary BERT checkpoint; they check effective settings, caller dictionaries, reuse across two models, old `config_args` compatibility and explicit None.
- Repository pre-commit hooks on all three changed files: Ruff check, Ruff format, and typos **passed**.
- Full pretrained-model/training suite and GPU tests were not run. This fix makes no performance or model-quality claims.

Searched existing issues/PRs for classifier_dropout, config_kwargs mutation/caller/None, and num_labels/max_length mutation, without a matching fix. No production-incident claim.

AI assistance: Codex helped inspect the code, prepare the patch and local-model regression tests, and draft this description. The changed lines and the reported test outcomes were reviewed before submission.

title: Add token pooling-aware and Matryoshka training for MultiVectorEncoder
body:
Hello!

Heads up, I developed this PR with AI assistance and reviewed the changes before opening it.

## Pull Request overview

* Token pooling-aware and multi-vector Matryoshka loss modifiers
* Document vector budgets, adaptive pooling, and token embedding truncation
* Training and evaluation examples with matched baselines and published models

## Details

Multi-vector indexes can require substantial storage because each document is represented by many token vectors. Pooling them into fewer vectors or reducing their dimensionality makes the index smaller, but ordinary retrieval training does not explicitly teach the model to preserve quality under those transformations. I've added two loss modifiers to train for these deployment settings.

`MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss` applies an existing retrieval objective using a list of pooling configurations, including `None` for the original embeddings. `MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss` applies it at several truncated, normalized embedding widths. Both support cached losses and reuse embeddings across variants. For example, the token pooling example averages ordinary retrieval and retrieval with approximately one quarter of each document's vectors:

```python
from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.losses import (
    CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss,
    MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss,
)
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling

model = MultiVectorEncoder("answerdotai/ModernBERT-base")
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor=4)
loss = CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model, mini_batch_size=64)
loss = MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss(
    model,
    loss,
    token_poolings=[None, pooling],
    weights=[0.5, 0.5],
)
```

I've extended `HierarchicalTokenPooling` with `max_tokens` for a per-document cap and `distance_threshold` for adaptive pooling, alongside the existing `pool_factor`. `calibrate_distance_threshold` selects a threshold from representative document embeddings for a target average vector count. Hierarchical pooling uses straight-through gradients during training.

`MultiVectorEncoder` now accepts `token_pooling` in its constructor as a runtime default for encoding, alongside the per-call option. It also accepts `truncate_dim` in its constructor and encode methods, truncating and normalizing token embeddings after pooling. The evaluators support both compression options and retain the full pooling configuration in their metadata. NanoBEIR keeps short pooling labels and accepts an explicit `name` for comparisons that would otherwise share metric keys.

The loss modifiers can be combined with token pooling wrapping Matryoshka, matching the pooling-before-truncation order used at inference. The reversed order raises an explanatory error. I've also shared the cached-loss resolution utility with dense Matryoshka so it can find the underlying cached loss through wrappers.

The new examples include educational READMEs, concise training scripts with a `--baseline` option, and separate evaluation scripts for larger post-training comparisons. I trained matched pairs from `answerdotai/ModernBERT-base` with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection. The token pooling pair uses 120,000 MS MARCO triplets and the Matryoshka pair uses 30,000. Within each pair, initialization, data, and optimization settings are identical, with only the loss changing. The results below use seed 42 and mean nDCG@10 (%) across all 13 NanoBEIR datasets.

| Experiment | Inference setting | Ordinary model | Compression-aware model | Gain (points) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Token pooling | Unpooled | 51.84 | 52.39 | +0.55 |
| Token pooling | `pool_factor=2` | 50.10 | 51.74 | +1.64 |
| Token pooling | `pool_factor=4` | 49.03 | 51.23 | +2.20 |
| Token pooling | `pool_factor=6` | 47.07 | 49.85 | +2.78 |
| Token pooling | `max_tokens=16` | 46.61 | 49.26 | +2.65 |
| Token pooling | Adaptive (29.58 mean vectors) | 48.38 | 50.96 | +2.58 |
| Matryoshka | 128 dimensions | 48.45 | 48.95 | +0.50 |
| Matryoshka | 96 dimensions | 47.00 | 47.69 | +0.68 |
| Matryoshka | 64 dimensions | 45.46 | 47.11 | +1.66 |
| Matryoshka | 32 dimensions | 37.38 | 43.44 | +6.06 |
| Matryoshka | 16 dimensions | 18.76 | 28.48 | +9.71 |

With `pool_factor=4`, mean document vector count falls from 193.22 to 48.68, approximately a 4x reduction at unchanged dimensionality and precision. Pooling-aware training increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, measured against each model's own unpooled mean nDCG@10. At 32 dimensions, token vector storage is also 4x smaller than at 128 dimensions.

The adaptive row uses a separate threshold for each model and NanoBEIR corpus, calibrated to match that corpus's average vector count under `max_tokens=32`. These are exploratory measurements, with NanoBEIR used during development. The READMEs include the full comparisons and figures.

The four example models are available on the Hub:

* https://huggingface.co/tomaarsen/mve-ModernBERT-base-token-pooling-baseline
* https://huggingface.co/tomaarsen/mve-ModernBERT-base-token-pooling
* https://huggingface.co/tomaarsen/mve-ModernBERT-base-matryoshka-baseline
* https://huggingface.co/tomaarsen/mve-ModernBERT-base-matryoshka

Validation passed with 308 focused tests and 1 skipped, covering pooling, both loss modifiers, evaluators, encoding and save/load, dense Matryoshka, and the shared gradient cache. Ruff, formatting, diff checks, and README snippet and local-link checks also passed.

- Tom Aarsen

title: [fix] Restore CrossEncoder.fit() with a custom loss_fct
body:
`CrossEncoder.fit()` crashes as soon as you pass a `loss_fct`. That is the v3-style call the migration guide shows under "CrossEncoder.fit(loss_fct)" (e.g. `loss_fct=torch.nn.MSELoss()` for score distillation), and the guide says the softly deprecated `fit()` still works.

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder, InputExample

model = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce")
examples = [InputExample(texts=[f"query {i}", f"passage {i}"], label=float(i % 2)) for i in range(8)]
model.fit(train_dataloader=DataLoader(examples, batch_size=4), loss_fct=torch.nn.MSELoss(), epochs=1, warmup_steps=0)
# main:    TypeError: BaseModel.forward() missing 1 required positional argument: 'input'
# this PR: trains
```

**Root cause:** `FitMixinLoss.forward` (`cross_encoder/fit_mixin.py`) tokenizes with `self.model.tokenizer(...)` and calls `self.model(**tokens)[0]`. That worked while `CrossEncoder.forward(*args, **kwargs)` passed everything on to the Hugging Face model (up to v5.3). Since v5.4 the CrossEncoder is a `BaseModel` whose `forward` takes a single features dict, so the keyword call fails on the first training step. `fit()` without `loss_fct` is not affected because it uses `BinaryCrossEntropyLoss` / `CrossEntropyLoss`, and no test covered a custom `loss_fct`.

**Fix:** preprocess the pairs with `self.model.preprocess` and read `self.model(tokens)["scores"]`, the same way the CrossEncoder losses do. For a regular sequence-classification model this gives the same logits as the old path (checked against `model.model(**model.tokenizer(pairs, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors="pt")).logits`). It also uses `self.model.num_labels`, which follows the scoring head, instead of `config.num_labels`, and accepts the `prompt` / `task` arguments that `CrossEncoderTrainer.compute_loss` passes to every loss, so the call no longer goes through the trainer's `TypeError` fallback.

**Test:** `tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py::test_fit_with_loss_fct` fits the tiny reranker for two steps with a recording `MSELoss` and checks that it received the flattened logits and float labels. It fails on main with the `TypeError` above and passes with this change.

```
pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py    # 35 passed
ruff check + ruff format (0.15.6), typos     # clean
```

Tested with Python 3.13, torch 2.7.1 (CPU), transformers 5.14.1. I found this by reading the `fit()` code rather than in actual use.

**AI assistance:** I used Claude Code for this PR. It found the bug while auditing the `fit()` code, wrote the fix and the test, and drafted this description. The fail-before and pass-after runs above were done locally.

title: Exclude self-pairs when GIST guide scores tie
body:
GIST's anchor-anchor and positive-positive blocks rely on guide false-negative filtering to remove self-pairs. With the default zero margin, its strict comparison leaves an example as its own negative when the guide's positive score ties its self-score.

Explicitly exclude only known self positions. Keep the strict guide comparison and tied off-diagonal candidates unchanged. Cached indices include the mini-batch position; positive-positive indices also include the gathered rank offset.

Found through code analysis and reproduced entirely offline with a tiny randomly initialized BERT, a local vocabulary, and real SentenceTransformer tokenization/retokenization. Two distinct texts (`the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog` / `the quick brown fox jumps over the sleeping cat`) differ for the training-mode student (context 32), but become identical for the eval-mode guide (context 8). A singleton pair has no eligible negatives, so its loss should be zero. On current main the losses are 2.928710 (GIST) / 3.547449 (cached); with this fix both are zero, with backward executed. These are local random weights, not a pretrained-model or learning-quality claim.

Fresh validation on `1492e43a9f07ab0b082cb815ea33ce05a4a0a37c` (Python 3.12.14, torch 2.8.0+cpu, transformers 5.20.2):
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gist_self_contrast.py -q`: **10 failed, 2 passed on upstream; 12 passed with the fix**. Both public loss classes and parameter gradients are checked, including isolated AA/PP terms, a singleton, simulated rank 1, explicit negatives, and a partial final cached mini-batch.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gist_self_contrast.py tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gist_embed.py tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_cached_gist_embed.py -q -k 'not two_forwards and not matches_gist and not replays_dropout and not rejects_static and not matryoshka and not token_budget'`: **28 passed, 10 deselected** (model-fixture cases).
- 64 additional non-tied comparisons against current main: bit-exact loss and gradient preservation, including positive margins.
- Changed-file Ruff 0.15.6 check/format, typos 1.45.0 and `git diff --check`: passed.

Limitations: an initial run of all three files had 28 passes and 10 setup errors because the model fixture's HTTP client requires unavailable `socksio` under the cloud proxy. No model downloads were enabled for this bounded offline validation. Full repository, GPU and actual multi-process distributed tests were not run; rank tests use a deterministic gather stub.

Related: #3817 protects AP positives; #3260 attempted duplicate-input detection. This patch does neither and does not claim to fix #2756. Open #4223 adds global AA gathering and is complementary; if it lands first, the AA self-column indices here need the rank offset on rebase.

OpenAI Codex assisted with investigation, implementation, tests and this description. A separate Codex agent reviewed the code and validation evidence; no human review is claimed.

title: [feat] Export a Router route as a standalone SentenceTransformer
body:
Add `SentenceTransformer.save_route(path, route=...)` to deploy a Router's query and document encoders separately. Each exported directory is a normal SentenceTransformer checkpoint containing the selected route and all modules before and after the Router, without the other route's weights or a Router wrapper.

```python
model.save_route("query_encoder", route="query")
model.save_route("document_encoder", route="document")

query_encoder = SentenceTransformer("query_encoder")
document_encoder = SentenceTransformer("document_encoder")
query_embeddings = query_encoder.encode_query(queries)
document_embeddings = document_encoder.encode_document(documents)
```

Refs #3696. Preserve prompts, default prompt name, similarity function, truncation dimension, and surrounding modules' explicit forward kwargs. Use a temporary shallow model view for serialization so weights are not duplicated and constructing another model does not move shared modules or rerun readiness hooks. Copy model-card metadata separately and generate a card for the selected architecture.

Scope: exactly one top-level Router and an exact `sub_modules` route key. Unknown routes, multiple top-level Routers, and nested Routers in the selected pipeline fail before writing. Use the same encoding method after export: `encode_query`/`encode_document` still control task-specific preprocessing and prompts; exporting does not change plain `encode` defaults.

Validation:

- `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_save_route.py tests/base/modules/test_router.py -k 'save_route or save_load_preserves_shared_modules' -q` — 20 passed, 74 deselected. One existing deprecated-import warning.

title: [feat] Add an evaluator for exporting sentence embeddings
body:
Add `EmbeddingExportEvaluator` for inspecting how dense sentence embeddings change across training checkpoints. Each evaluation writes an `.npz` containing embeddings and the original sentences in matching row order, with epoch and step in the filename. The archive loads with `allow_pickle=False`.

```python
from sentence_transformers.base.evaluation import SequentialEvaluator
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.evaluation import EmbeddingExportEvaluator

export = EmbeddingExportEvaluator(
    ["A cat sits outside.", "A dog plays in the park."],
    name="dev",
    encode_kwargs={"normalize_embeddings": True},
)
# Pass a scoring evaluator first; export contributes no metric of its own.
evaluator = SequentialEvaluator([scoring_evaluator, export])
evaluator(model, output_path="evaluation", epoch=1, steps=100)
# evaluation/dev_embeddings_epoch_1_steps_100.npz
```

Refs #3517. This follows the suggestion to add a dedicated exporter rather than extend every existing evaluator. `SequentialEvaluator` skips score aggregation for empty metric dictionaries, so exporting does not replace the scoring evaluator's checkpoint-selection metric. Existing evaluators retain their behavior. A repeated evaluation at the same name/epoch/step overwrites that archive.

Scope: dense `SentenceTransformer.encode()` outputs. Sparse and variable-length multi-vector outputs are outside this proposal. Other encoding options, including prompt selection, can be passed via `encode_kwargs`.

Validation:

- `python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_embedding_export_evaluator.py tests/base/evaluation/test_sequential.py -q` — 25 passed.
- Tests use a local, deterministic StaticEmbedding model: archive round trips, Unicode and repeated inputs, prompt/normalization options, checkpoint filenames, validation errors, metric aggregation, and nonzero-rank participation without writing.
- A two-step CPU `SentenceTransformerTrainer` training test exports both checkpoints and verifies the final archive and evaluation score. Actual multi-process/sharded training was not run.
- `make docs` — passed with the same 76 warnings as unchanged `main`, no new warnings.
- Pre-commit Ruff lint/format and typos checks passed on all changed files.

title: [fix] Pin documentation source links to the build commit
body:
API reference `[source]` links combine line numbers from the documentation build with a moving `main` URL. After `main` changes, the links can highlight unrelated code. This was verified by code analysis and by invoking the current resolver; it was not discovered in an application workload.

Resolve the source ref from the documentation checkout's Git HEAD and use it for API source links, GitHub page links, and repository download links. For source archives without Git metadata, fall back to the release tag, or `main` for development versions. Resolve source paths relative to `conf.py` so invoking Sphinx outside `docs/` also works.

Fixes #4074. This revisits the withdrawn, unmerged #4201: using the build commit also prevents development documentation from drifting, rather than only pinning release builds. The version fallback follows the earlier proposal.

To reproduce the original problem with the documentation dependencies installed, run from the repository root:

```python
import runpy

config = runpy.run_path("docs/conf.py")
print(config["linkcode_resolve"]("py", {
    "module": "sentence_transformers.util.quantization",
    "fullname": "quantize_embeddings",
}))
```

Before this change the URL contains `/blob/main/`; afterwards a Git checkout uses its build commit and the inspected function's line range.

Validation:

- `python -m pytest tests/docs/test_linkcode.py -q` — 5 passed, covering the build commit, working-directory independence, and release/development archive fallbacks with unavailable Git or missing metadata.
- `make docs` — passed. All 76 warnings also occur on unchanged `main`; no new warnings. Checked the generated quantization page's source URLs against the build commit.
- Pre-commit Ruff lint/format and typos checks passed on both changed files.

Environment: Python 3.12.11, Sentence Transformers 6.3.0.dev0, Sphinx 8.1.3, PyTorch 2.14.1, Transformers 5.20.2.

title: 🚨 [fix] Strip left padding from token embeddings in encode()
body:
`encode(..., output_value="token_embeddings")` only strips trailing padding. With a left-padding tokenizer, the shorter inputs in a batch keep their padding rows, so anything computed from the returned token embeddings (mean pooling, late chunking, ...) includes padding.

The Qwen3-Embedding model cards recommend `tokenizer_kwargs={"padding_side": "left"}`, so following the card hits this. `Pooling` already handles left padding (#3767, #4104), but this path in `SentenceTransformer._inference` was missed. I found it while reading the code and then confirmed it with Qwen3-Embedding.

### Reproducer
```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

texts = ["hello", "a much longer sentence with many more tokens in it"]
model = SentenceTransformer("Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B", tokenizer_kwargs={"padding_side": "left"})
print("batched:", [tuple(x.shape) for x in model.encode(texts, output_value="token_embeddings")])
print("alone:  ", [tuple(model.encode(t, output_value="token_embeddings").shape) for t in texts])
```
```
# before
batched: [(11, 1024), (11, 1024)]
alone:   [(2, 1024), (11, 1024)]
# after
batched: [(2, 1024), (11, 1024)]
alone:   [(2, 1024), (11, 1024)]
```
The same happens with any model once `model.tokenizer.padding_side = "left"`, e.g. `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`.

Versions: sentence-transformers 6.3.0.dev0 (`main` @ 1ecc8bb8), transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1+cpu, Python 3.12, Windows 11.

### Change
Slice each row from its first to its last attended token instead of only trimming the end. Right-padded outputs are unchanged, and an all-zero mask still returns the first row as before.

### Tests
Parametrized the existing `test_encode_token_embeddings` over `padding_side`. It already encodes sentences of different lengths with `batch_size=2` and checks each output length against the tokenized input.

```
pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_compute_embeddings.py
# before: test_encode_token_embeddings[left] fails, 5 passed; after: 6 passed

pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_compute_embeddings.py tests/sentence_transformer/modules -n 4
# 798 passed, 172 skipped, 2 failed: test_clip and test_unsupported_modality fail the same way on main here (Pillow/torchvision not installed)

pre-commit run --files sentence_transformers/sentence_transformer/model.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_compute_embeddings.py
# Passed
```

### Related
- #4080 adds a re-padding step right before this loop. `model.py` merges cleanly; the only conflict is the import block of the test file (keep both).
- No existing issue, and not in the #4206 list.
