title: Docs: deployment guidance for cold starts and offline model loading
body:
## Summary

Closes #3923.

The docs did not cover what happens to model loading when Sentence Transformers
runs on a scale-to-zero platform (Cloud Run, Lambda-style containers, KEDA-scaled
pods): searching `docs/` found no mention of `HF_HUB_OFFLINE`, `local_files_only`,
cold starts, or container warmup.

This adds a new Sentence Transformer usage page, **"Deployment, Cold Starts and
Offline Loading"** (`docs/sentence_transformer/usage/deployment.rst`), linked from
`index.rst` and the usage toctree, covering:

1. **What a cold start is made of** — container start, model load, and first
   inference, with a short snippet for timing model load and first inference
   separately, and why an aggregate number hides which lever to pull.
2. **Making model loading deterministic** — pre-downloading the model into the
   image at build time, `local_files_only=True`, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`, and cache-dir
   placement, framed as removing a variable network dependency (reliability and
   restricted environments) rather than as a latency fix.
3. **Warmup** — a dummy `encode()` at startup, ordered before the readiness probe
   so traffic is not routed to an instance that has not finished loading.
4. **What did not help** — the measurement reported in #3923: local-only loading
   moved model load from 24.24s to 23.09s (median) but end-to-end cold latency was
   unchanged (37.68s vs 37.78s), because instance startup and transport dominated.
5. **Trade-offs** — image size vs cold start, and minimum-instances cost vs latency.

Two notes for maintainers, raised in #3923 and still open there:

- I placed this under Sentence Transformer usage, next to "Speeding up Inference",
  since that is where the loading arguments are most discoverable, and the page
  notes the same arguments apply to Cross Encoder, Sparse Encoder, and
  Multi-Vector Encoder models. Happy to move or split it if you prefer another home.
- The `local_files_only` / `HF_HUB_OFFLINE` material is limited to how those
  settings affect Sentence Transformers model loading, with the mechanism owned
  by `huggingface_hub`. Happy to trim it if you consider it out of scope here.

Also cc'ing the discussion in #3923: @jgjoe proposed this page and offered to
draft it, and @Bhoomi-jain offered to help — I checked that no PR existed yet
before writing this, and I am glad to hand over, split, or co-author if either
of you would prefer.

## Validation

- All Python code blocks in the new page were extracted and verified with
  `ast.parse`; every constructor argument and environment variable used
  (`local_files_only`, `cache_folder`, `SENTENCE_TRANSFORMERS_HOME`,
  `HF_HUB_OFFLINE`) was checked against the current source.
- Docs-only change; no library code or tests are affected.
- I could not run the full Sphinx build (`make docs`) in my environment, so
  the docs CI check is the first full build of this page.

CONTRIBUTING.md. I reviewed every line, verified all API names, environment
variables, and the quoted measurement against the source code and issue #3923,

title: Fix concurrent HTTP downloads sharing a temporary file
body:
## Problem

`http_get()` always stages a download at `<path>_part`. Two callers downloading to the same destination therefore share the staging file: one can truncate the other's bytes, move its open file, or remove it during error cleanup. The other call then fails with `FileNotFoundError` at `os.replace()`.

This can affect callers sharing a download destination, such as simultaneous `WordEmbeddings.from_text_file()` initialization for a missing embeddings file. Found through code analysis; reproduced against main at `33f9bd81610560e48ff5eac80e910496b49ae193`, rather than encountered in a production workload.

## Change

Stage each call in a unique temporary directory beside the destination. The file is still closed before `os.replace()`, the replacement remains on the same filesystem, and cleanup is limited to that call's temporary directory.

The original destination remains intact until a download completes. This does not deduplicate downloads or choose a winner: the last successful replacement wins.

## Validation

The two controlled concurrency regressions fail on the original implementation, for both successful concurrent downloads and one interrupted download. The tests use HTTPX mock transport, real filesystem writes, and events to coordinate threads without sleeps or external requests.

After the fix:

```sh
pytest tests/util/test_http_get.py tests/util/test_file_io.py -q
# 93 passed
ruff check sentence_transformers/util/file_io.py tests/util/test_http_get.py
ruff format --check sentence_transformers/util/file_io.py tests/util/test_http_get.py
git diff --check
```

Coverage includes relative paths, missing parent directories, replacing an existing destination, stream failure, replacement failure, and removal of temporary files.

Environment: Python 3.12.15, macOS arm64. The full suite and Windows were not run.

## AI assistance

Codex assisted with code analysis, implementation, regression tests, and this description.

title: [fix] Restore loss-owned weights when resuming from a checkpoint
body:
Resuming training from a checkpoint silently resets weights that belong to the loss instead of the model, such as the `SoftmaxLoss` classifier (the NLI setup from the SBERT paper) and the `MSELoss`/`EmbedDistillLoss` projection (`projection_dim`). The Trainer's optimizer trains these weights (#2881, and #4066 for `fit()`), but `_save` only writes the model. On resume, `optimizer.pt` brings back their Adam moments while the weights themselves restart from a fresh random init. So training continues against a random head with stale optimizer state, and everything those weights learned before the interruption is lost. The same applies to the copied model in `ContrastiveTensionLoss`. Nothing warns about it.

This affects any interrupted long run (preemption, OOM, time limits) that uses one of these losses. Losses without weights of their own are not affected.

Minimal reproducer:

```python
import torch
from datasets import Dataset
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer, SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import SoftmaxLoss

dataset = Dataset.from_dict({
    "premise": [f"premise {i}" for i in range(32)],
    "hypothesis": [f"hypothesis {i}" for i in range(32)],
    "label": [i % 3 for i in range(32)],
})

def train(max_steps, resume_from_checkpoint=None):
    model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
    loss = SoftmaxLoss(model, model.get_embedding_dimension(), num_labels=3)
    args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(
        output_dir="out", max_steps=max_steps, save_steps=2, per_device_train_batch_size=8, report_to=[]
    )
    trainer = SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=dataset, loss=loss)
    trainer.train(resume_from_checkpoint=resume_from_checkpoint)
    return loss.classifier.weight.detach().clone()

trained = train(max_steps=2)  # writes out/checkpoint-2
resumed = train(max_steps=2, resume_from_checkpoint="out/checkpoint-2")  # nothing left to train
print(torch.equal(trained, resumed))
# main:    False (the classifier is back at its random init)
# this PR: True
```

I found this through code analysis while reading how the trainer handles weights owned by the loss, not in actual use. I searched issues and PRs for resuming with loss weights and found nothing. #3756 reports a higher loss after resuming, but with `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss` + `MatryoshkaLoss`, which have no weights of their own, so this PR does not fix that issue.

### Change

`BaseTrainer` now overrides `_save_optimizer_and_scheduler` and `_load_optimizer_and_scheduler`, so it applies to all four trainers:

- On save, the loss state is written to `loss.safetensors` in the checkpoint, next to `optimizer.pt`. This only covers parameters and buffers that are not part of the model, matched by identity so that a model behind a DDP or `torch.compile` wrapper is still excluded. Losses with no weights of their own (most of them) write no file, so their checkpoints don't change.
- On resume, `loss.safetensors` is loaded back into the loss (or the dict of losses) before the optimizer state.
- `loss.safetensors` is added to the training-state files that `_push_from_checkpoint` doesn't copy into the output directory.

It is saved with the optimizer rather than in `_save`, so the final `save_model()` output does not change, and `save_only_model=True` checkpoints (which can't be resumed) stay model-only.

### Tests

`tests/base/test_trainer.py::test_resume_from_checkpoint_restores_loss_weights` trains 2 steps with `SoftmaxLoss`, `MSELoss(projection_dim=12)` and `CosineSimilarityLoss`, then resumes from `checkpoint-2` with a freshly built model and loss, and checks that the loss state matches the trained one. It also checks that only the losses with their own weights write `loss.safetensors`. The model is the small local `StaticEmbedding` fixture, so nothing is downloaded.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/base/test_trainer.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py tests/sparse_encoder/test_trainer.py -q
```

| Environment: macOS arm64, CPU, Python 3.12, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.2, accelerate 1.15.0 | Result |
| --- | --- |
| New test on main | 2 failed (`SoftmaxLoss`, `MSELoss`), 1 passed (`CosineSimilarityLoss`) |
| Command above with this PR | 116 passed, 1 skipped |

`ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` pass on the changed files. I did not run multi-GPU (DDP/FSDP/DeepSpeed) resumes. Under DeepSpeed the optimizer state is handled by DeepSpeed itself, and I did not change that path.

### AI assistance

I used Claude Code to help find the issue, write the fix, the test and this description. I reviewed every change and ran the reproducer and tests above myself.

title: [fix] Accept a plain dict as duplicates_dict in ParaphraseMiningEvaluator
body:
`ParaphraseMiningEvaluator` crashes with a `KeyError` when `duplicates_dict` is a plain `dict`, e.g. labels loaded from JSON:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.evaluation import ParaphraseMiningEvaluator

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
sentences = {"a": "The cat sits outside", "b": "A cat is sitting outside", "c": "The new movie is awesome", "d": "Stocks fell today"}
evaluator = ParaphraseMiningEvaluator(sentences, duplicates_dict={"a": {"b": True}, "b": {"a": True}})
evaluator(model)
# KeyError: 'c'
```

The evaluator used the given dict directly and then looked up `self.duplicates[id1][id2]` for every mined pair, which only works for a nested `defaultdict`. The parameter is typed as `dict[str, dict[str, bool]]`; only the docstring mentions a "default dictionary". The same lookups also fail in `add_transitive_closure` and in `__init__` (for a pair marked `False`). Because the dict was used as-is, `duplicates_list` pairs and the transitive closure were also written into the caller's `duplicates_dict`.

The fix copies `duplicates_dict` into the evaluator's own nested `defaultdict(bool)`. A `defaultdict` input gives the same results as before, and the caller's dict is no longer modified. I also changed "A default dictionary" to "A dictionary" in the docstring.

I found this by reading and testing the code, not in a real training run.

Tests:
- Added `test_plain_duplicates_dict` (with and without `add_transitive_closure`). It checks that a plain dict gives the same metrics as the equivalent `duplicates_list` and that the input dict is left unchanged. It fails on `main` and passes with this change.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation`: 97 passed, 1 skipped.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` (0.15.6) and `typos` pass on the changed files.

AI disclosure: Claude Code was used to find this bug, write the fix and tests, and draft this description.

title: [fix] Score RerankingEvaluator with the model's similarity function
body:
`RerankingEvaluator` defaults to `similarity_fct=cos_sim` ([reranking.py#L97](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/33f9bd8/sentence_transformers/sentence_transformer/evaluation/reranking.py#L97)), so with default arguments it ranks documents with cosine similarity even when the model is configured to score with something else. The retrieval and pair evaluators already follow the model: `InformationRetrievalEvaluator` and `NanoBEIREvaluator` default to `model.similarity`, and `TripletEvaluator`, `EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator` and `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` to `[model.similarity_fn_name]`. #4252 made the same change for `SparseRerankingEvaluator` and noted it left the dense default unchanged, and `MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator` already used `model.similarity`. For a model with `similarity_fn_name="dot"` (for example `sentence-transformers/multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-dot-v1`), the reranking numbers that reach the trainer's evaluation metrics, the model card, and `load_best_model_at_end` when a reranking metric is the `metric_for_best_model`, come from a function the model is not used with. I found this by reading the code after #4252, which fixed the same default for SparseRerankingEvaluator, and then confirmed it on a real dot-product model (results below).

Measured on the docstring example data (first 1000 rows of MS MARCO v1.1 validation):

| Model | Metric | main (cosine) | this PR (model's dot product) |
|---|---|---|---|
| sentence-transformers/multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-dot-v1 | MAP | 47.89 | 57.57 |
| | MRR@10 | 48.59 | 58.24 |
| | NDCG@10 | 60.81 | 68.22 |

Models configured for cosine similarity, and models that don't set `similarity_fn_name` (it falls back to cosine), are unaffected because `model.similarity` is `cos_sim` for them. On the same data, `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (the docstring example model) gives bit-for-bit identical MAP, MRR@10 and NDCG@10 with the new default and with `similarity_fct=cos_sim`, in both batched and per-sample encoding. Passing `similarity_fct=cos_sim` keeps the old scores for any model.

`TranslationEvaluator` (hardcoded `pytorch_cos_sim`) and `ParaphraseMiningEvaluator` (`paraphrase_mining` without a `score_function`) still use cosine regardless of the model. I left them out to keep this to the reranking evaluators that #4252 started on, since `SparseRerankingEvaluator` inherits this class. I can include them here or in a follow-up if you'd prefer.

## Changes

- `RerankingEvaluator(similarity_fct=None)` is now the default, and `compute_metrics_batched` / `compute_metrics_individual` use `self.similarity_fct` if it was given and `model.similarity` otherwise. This is the same fallback `MultiVectorDistillationEvaluator` uses, and it is resolved where the scores are computed, so calling `compute_metrics(model)` directly also works and a reused evaluator follows each model it is called with.
- `SparseRerankingEvaluator` no longer needs the `_user_similarity_fct` override from #4252 (not yet released), because the parent now does the same thing, so I removed it. `MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator` keeps its override, since it adapts the query shape for MaxSim. I updated its class docstring, which described resolving the scoring at call time as the difference from the parent.
- Updated the `similarity_fct` docstring. The docstring example uses `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, which is cosine, so its numbers stay the same.

## Reproducer

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.evaluation import RerankingEvaluator

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-dot-v1")
print("similarity_fn_name:", model.similarity_fn_name)

# Same data as the RerankingEvaluator docstring example, first 1000 rows
eval_dataset = load_dataset("microsoft/ms_marco", "v1.1", split="validation").select(range(1000))
samples = [
    {
        "query": sample["query"],
        "positive": [t for s, t in zip(sample["passages"]["is_selected"], sample["passages"]["passage_text"]) if s],
        "negative": [t for s, t in zip(sample["passages"]["is_selected"], sample["passages"]["passage_text"]) if not s],
    }
    for sample in eval_dataset
]

for label, kwargs in [("default", {}), ("similarity_fct=model.similarity", {"similarity_fct": model.similarity})]:
    results = RerankingEvaluator(samples=samples, batch_size=32, write_csv=False, **kwargs)(model)
    print(label, {key: round(float(results[key]), 4) for key in ("map", "mrr@10", "ndcg@10")})
```

| Run | main (33f9bd8) | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| default | map 0.4789, mrr@10 0.4859, ndcg@10 0.6081 | map 0.5757, mrr@10 0.5824, ndcg@10 0.6822 |
| `similarity_fct=model.similarity` | map 0.5757, mrr@10 0.5824, ndcg@10 0.6822 | map 0.5757, mrr@10 0.5824, ndcg@10 0.6822 |

`model.similarity_fn_name` is `dot` in both runs. On main the default disagrees with the model's own similarity, and with this change they match.

## Tests

The new `test_reranking_evaluator_similarity` in `tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_reranking_evaluator.py` follows the sparse test from #4252, using a two-dimensional `StaticEmbedding` model where the positive document ranks first on dot product, euclidean and manhattan but second on cosine similarity. It covers the default for dot, euclidean, manhattan and cosine models, plus an explicit `similarity_fct=cos_sim` on a dot model, with batched and per-sample encoding. Euclidean and manhattan are included because they are the only functions with negative scores.

On main (33f9bd8), with `similarity_fct` left out, the dot, euclidean and manhattan cases fail with `assert 0.0 == 1.0` in both encoding modes, and passing `similarity_fct=None` raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable`. With this change all ten cases pass.

- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_reranking_evaluator.py`: 16 passed
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_evaluators.py -n 4`: 149 passed, 5 skipped
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer tests/sparse_encoder -n 4`: 1921 passed, 236 skipped
- ruff check, ruff format and typos at the versions pinned in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` (ruff 0.15.6, typos 1.45.0): pass on the changed files

I ran these on Windows with CPU only, so the CUDA-only tests were skipped. Versions: sentence-transformers main (33f9bd8), transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1+cpu, Python 3.12.

title: [fix] Skip the anchor itself when mining hard negatives
body:
`mine_hard_negatives` builds its candidate corpus from the positive column (plus `corpus`, if given). Before filtering and sampling, it only masks padding and each anchor's own positives ([hard_negatives.py#L628-L641](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/33f9bd81610560e48ff5eac80e910496b49ae193/sentence_transformers/util/hard_negatives.py#L628-L641)). So when an anchor's text is also in the corpus, its own entry is the closest candidate and comes back as a hard negative. This is common in symmetric pair data, where an anchor is often another row's positive. In the full `sentence-transformers/quora-duplicates` `pair` split, 63,188 of 149,263 rows (42.3%) have an anchor that is also some row's positive.

I ran `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` with default settings on the first 10,000 quora rows. Each of the 927 rows whose anchor is in the corpus got itself as its top negative, for example:

```
{'anchor': 'How I can speak English fluently?', 'positive': 'How can I learn to speak English fluently?', 'negative': 'How I can speak English fluently?'}
```

Training on that triplet asks the model to score the anchor lower against itself than against its positive. The `labeled-pair` and `labeled-list` outputs also label `(anchor, anchor)` as 0.

The change masks the anchor's own corpus entry next to the padding mask, unless that entry is one of the anchor's positives. That way `include_positives=True` still keeps a positive that is the same text as its anchor in the ranking. To do this, the positive mask is now built before the `include_positives` check.

Reproducer (CPU; downloads the 91 MB model and the 11 MB quora `pair` parquet file):

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.util import mine_hard_negatives

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
dataset = load_dataset("sentence-transformers/quora-duplicates", "pair", split="train").select(range(10_000))

mined = mine_hard_negatives(dataset, model, batch_size=64, verbose=False)
self_negatives = [row for row in mined if row["negative"] == row["anchor"]]
print(f"{len(self_negatives)} of {len(mined)} triplets have the anchor as the negative")
print(self_negatives[:1])
```

| | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| first line printed | `927 of 30000 triplets have the anchor as the negative` | `0 of 30000 triplets have the anchor as the negative` |

The table below counts rows that contain the anchor as a negative. Each run used `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` on the first 10,000 rows of the `train` split:

| Dataset | Settings | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| quora-duplicates `pair` | defaults | 927 of 30,000 | 0 of 30,000 |
| | `include_positives=True` | 927 of 10,000 | 0 of 10,000 |
| | `min_score=0.5` | 927 of 24,987 | 0 of 24,945 |
| | docstring example settings | 0 of 49,290 | 0 of 49,290 |
| stackexchange-duplicates `title-title-pair` | defaults | 15 of 30,000 | 0 of 30,000 |
| | `include_positives=True` | 28 of 10,000 | 13 of 10,000 |
| | docstring example settings | 0 of 43,565 | 0 of 43,565 |
| natural-questions `pair` | defaults | 0 of 30,000 | 0 of 30,000 |
| | docstring example settings | 0 of 49,740 | 0 of 49,740 |

- The docstring example settings already skip the self-match: `range_min=10`, `range_max=50`, `max_score=0.8`, `relative_margin=0.05`, `num_negatives=5`, `sampling_strategy="random"`, with the same seed before each run. Their output is identical before and after on all three datasets. The natural-questions output with defaults is identical too, since no anchor there is in the corpus.
- With defaults, only rows of affected anchors change: 2,777 of 30,000 quora triplets.
- The 13 stackexchange rows left with `include_positives=True` have a positive that is the same text as the anchor. They keep it, as on main.
- With `min_score=0.5`, the self-match no longer fills one of the 3 negatives. For some anchors the next candidate is below 0.5, which gives 42 fewer triplets.

Tests: the new parametrized `test_anchor_is_not_mined_as_its_own_negative` covers three cases:
- defaults and `include_positives=True`: both fail on main (`Column(['q', 'p'])` instead of `['n_more_similar', 'n_more_similar']`) and pass with this change.
- an anchor that is its own positive, with `include_positives=True`: passes on both.

title: [`fix`] flaky rendezvous in distributed tests
body:
The distributed tests picked an available TCP port, released it, and then started the worker processes. That leaves a small timing window where another process can claim the port, causing the workers to fail while setting up their process group.

This updates the distributed-inference and Trainer tests to use a unique temporary FileStore rendezvous instead. The Trainer tests now initialize Gloo explicitly and check whether the process group is still active before destroying it, since Trainer may already have shut it down.

This only changes test setup, it does not affect the library’s runtime behavior.

title: Speed up community_detection ~64x on MPS by using the batched path
body:
`community_detection` takes the slow per-row loop on MPS. This sends MPS to the batched path that CUDA and NPU already use: 20k embeddings go from 3.9 s to 0.06 s on an M5 Max, with the same communities.

On a Mac, `SentenceTransformer` defaults to MPS, so `examples/sentence_transformer/applications/clustering/fast_clustering.py` passes MPS tensors to `community_detection`. They hit the per-row loop, where `top_k_values[i][-1] >= threshold` syncs with the GPU once per embedding (about 0.2 ms per row), slower than CPU (3.9 s vs 0.31 s for 20k). The CUDA/NPU branch gives the same communities in a few batched ops, so this adds `mps` to the device check, the same way #2466 added `npu`. No API change; same centers and members as before and as on CPU (the order inside a community can differ on ties).

I found it by timing the retrieval functions in `sentence_transformers.util` on MPS against CPU; this was the one much slower on MPS. It is not from a user report, and I found no existing issue or PR.

Reproducer (the example's `threshold` and `min_community_size`, on 20k questions from `sentence-transformers/quora-duplicates`):

```python
import time

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

pairs = load_dataset("sentence-transformers/quora-duplicates", "pair", split="train[:30000]")
questions = list(dict.fromkeys(q for row in pairs for q in (row["anchor"], row["positive"])))[:20000]

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # picks MPS on a Mac
embeddings = model.encode(questions, batch_size=256, convert_to_tensor=True)

start = time.perf_counter()
communities = util.community_detection(embeddings, threshold=0.75, min_community_size=25)
torch.mps.synchronize()
print(f"{len(communities)} communities in {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")
```

It takes about 4 s on main and 0.1 s here (first call, with MPS warm-up). Median of 5 interleaved runs after warm-up (M5 Max, macOS 26.6.2, torch 2.14.1, main at 33f9bd8):

| n | main, MPS | this PR, MPS | speedup | main, CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 0.172 s | 0.0008 s | 220x | 0.003 s |
| 6,000 | 1.058 s | 0.0126 s | 84x | 0.035 s |
| 20,000 | 3.892 s | 0.0608 s | 64x | 0.313 s |

CPU is unchanged. The output matches CPU for fp32, fp16 and bf16, an 8,000-member community, and fp32 on torch 2.2.2 (the minimum).

Tests: `pytest tests/util/test_retrieval.py` gives 178 passed, 5 skipped (CUDA, no GPU here); `test_import.py`, `test_similarity.py`, `test_tensor.py` and `pre-commit` pass too. I added `mps` to the device cases of `test_community_detection_preserves_centers`; they also pass on the old loop, so they guard the batched output, not the speed.

I used AI assistance for the profiling, the benchmark scripts and this text, and I reviewed everything it produced. Measured on one M5 Max; the CUDA and NPU paths are unchanged.

title: Handle empty retrieval results in cross-encoder reranking evaluation
body:
`CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator` treats `documents=[]` as though the alternative `negative` schema was supplied, then evaluates `positive + None`. One zero-hit query therefore aborts the whole evaluation with `TypeError: can only concatenate list (not "NoneType") to list`.

Found through code analysis, then reproduced through the public evaluator. Thresholded or filtered first-stage retrieval can legitimately return no candidates.

### Reproducer

No model download is needed because an empty retrieval should not invoke prediction when positive injection is disabled:

```python
from unittest.mock import Mock
from sentence_transformers.cross_encoder.evaluation import CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator

model = Mock()
evaluator = CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator(
    [{"query": "no hits", "positive": ["relevant"], "documents": []}],
    always_rerank_positives=False,
)
results = evaluator(model)
assert all(value == 0.0 for value in results.values())
model.predict.assert_not_called()
```

### Change

Distinguish an empty documents list from an absent one with `documents is not None`. The existing zero-relevance path gives zero base and reranked metrics, keeps zero-hit queries in macro averages, and preserves prediction alignment in mixed batches. Positive injection still applies when enabled; no metric formulas change.

### Validation

Against base `33f9bd81610560e48ff5eac80e910496b49ae193`, using Python 3.12.14, Sentence Transformers 6.3.0.dev0, PyTorch 2.14.1+cpu, Transformers 5.20.2 and scikit-learn 1.9.1:

- `python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/evaluation/test_reranking.py -k empty_documents -q`: all 12 new cases fail with the wrong-branch TypeError on the base; all 12 pass with this patch.
- `python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/evaluation/test_reranking.py -q`: 18 passed, including the five unchanged real-model fixtures using `cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce`.
- Ruff 0.15.6: `ruff check --no-fix .` and `ruff format --check .` passed. `git diff --check` passed.
- The full repository test suite and full pre-commit hooks were not run.

The tests cover positive-injection modes, zero/one/multiple known positives without injection, interleaved empty queries, cutoffs, primary-metric naming, and unchanged duplicate-candidate scoring.

Known separate limitation: with `always_rerank_positives=True` (the default) and exactly one positive, this reaches the existing singleton NDCG error addressed by #4244. This PR fixes schema selection, not singleton metrics or the nonempty missing-positive scoring discussed in #4054.

title: Honor CrossEncoder rescoring without mining score filters
body:
`mine_hard_negatives(..., cross_encoder=teacher, output_scores=True)` silently ignores `teacher` when no score filters are set. Candidate ordering and exported scores still come from the bi-encoder. This matters when using the returned scores as distillation targets or selecting negatives with a reranker: the requested scoring model is never called.

Found through code analysis. The public API describes CrossEncoder rescoring without requiring a threshold, but the implementation gates it on `absolute_margin`, `relative_margin`, `max_score`, or `min_score`. #4073 fixed the min-score-only case; this handles the remaining no-filter case.

The change runs the existing rescoring path whenever a CrossEncoder is supplied and clarifies that contract in the docstring. Candidate retrieval and its automatic range remain unchanged; calls without a CrossEncoder are unchanged.

Validation (Linux, Python 3.12.14, CPU PyTorch 2.14.1, Transformers 5.20.2):
- Runnable regression: `python -m pytest tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py -k cross_encoder_rescores_without_score_filters -q`. All 8 cases fail before and pass after. A deterministic teacher reverses the bi-encoder's negative ranking; tests check ranking and exported scores across all four output formats, with score export enabled and disabled. No model downloads needed for these cases.
- `CI=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py -q`: 146 passed, 1 skipped. This includes existing real-model/FAISS tests. The existing multi-process integration test stalled in this environment and is skipped by the repository's CI guard; its five mocked pool-cleanup tests passed. No GPU validation.
- Ruff check and format check pass for both changed files.

title: Document adaptive-layer evaluation during training
body:
In #3329, the suggested way to evaluate an Adaptive Layer model at a reduced layer count during training was a small evaluator subclass. The Adaptive Layers guide only shows permanent truncation for inference, so this adds that subclass as a short section.

title: Infer ContrastiveTensionLoss labels for flattened inputs
body:
`ContrastiveTensionLoss` infers its labels by comparing the paired `input_ids`. A text-only model loaded with `attn_implementation="flash_attention_2"` flattens its inputs by default: each column becomes one packed `input_ids` row with `cu_seq_lens_q` offsets and no `attention_mask`. The fallback comparison then works on the packed rows, so every batch with more than one pair fails:

- `RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (32) must match the size of tensor b (29) at non-singleton dimension 1` when the columns have different total lengths.
- `ValueError: Target size (torch.Size([1])) must be the same as input size (torch.Size([3]))` when they have the same total length.

### Change

Split flattened `input_ids` at `cu_seq_lens_q` and compare the paired sequences one by one. Padded inputs keep the existing comparison of their unpadded tokens, and explicit labels are unchanged.

### Validation

- The new test builds both columns with `DataCollatorWithFlattening(return_flash_attn_kwargs=True)` and checks that the inferred labels give the same loss and gradients as explicit labels. Both cases fail on `main` with the two errors above. With the fix, `test_contrastive_tension.py` gives 19 passed, also with the minimum supported versions (Python 3.10, torch 2.2.0, transformers 5.0.0).
- `tests/sentence_transformer/losses`: 454 passed, 51 skipped.
- End-to-end on CPU with `sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors`: I enabled the flattening setup in `Transformer` (patching only the two Flash Attention availability checks, since flash-attn isn't installed here) and ran 2 steps with `SentenceTransformerTrainer`. On `main` the first step fails with the size mismatch. With the fix it trains, and the inferred labels match both the pairs and the labels from padded inputs.
- pre-commit passes.

Windows 11, CPU, Python 3.12.14, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.1. I couldn't run real Flash Attention here, so the end-to-end run used eager attention over the packed row. The inferred labels only depend on `input_ids` and `cu_seq_lens_q`, not on the attention kernel.

title: [fix] Upcast int8/uint8 embeddings in the dense similarity functions
body:
`_convert_to_float_tensor` (sentence_transformers/util/tensor.py) only upcasts sub-float32 floats, so int8/uint8 quantized embeddings (from `quantize_embeddings` or `encode(precision="int8")`) reach the dense similarity functions as integers:

- `cos_sim`, `pairwise_cos_sim`: crash, `linalg.vector_norm: Expected a floating point or complex tensor`
- `euclidean_sim`, `manhattan_sim`: crash, `cdist only supports floating-point dtypes`
- `dot_score`, `pairwise_dot_score`, `pairwise_manhattan_sim`, `pairwise_euclidean_sim`: silently wrong, because integer products and differences overflow or wrap around (int8 `dot_score([[100, 100]], [[100, 100]])` returns 32 instead of 20000)

This also affects `model.similarity(...)` on quantized embeddings. `EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator` already works around it by casting to float32 before calling these functions, and MaxSim got the same upcast in 9386f8b.

**Change:** `_convert_to_float_tensor` now also upcasts integer inputs to float32. Floating inputs behave as before. I found this by reading the code, then reproduced it with the test below.

**Test:** `test_quantized_integer_embeddings_match_float32` in tests/util/test_similarity.py runs all 8 functions on random int8 and uint8 embeddings and checks the scores are float32 and equal to scoring the same values as float32. On main all 16 cases fail (crash or wrong values); with the fix they pass.

```
pytest tests/util/test_similarity.py -k quantized_integer   # 16 passed (16 failed before the fix)
pytest tests/util/                                          # 1218 passed; the only errors were model downloads blocked in my environment
ruff check / ruff format --check on the changed files       # clean
```

**AI disclosure:** I used an AI assistant (Claude) to help find the bug, write the fix and test, and draft this description. I reviewed every line and ran the tests myself.

title: [fix] Stack tensor-formatted labels in the CrossEncoder data collator
body:
`CrossEncoderTrainer` fails on the first training step when the label column is formatted as tensors, for example after `dataset.with_format("torch")`, or after `load_from_disk` on a dataset that was saved with that format. #4231 fixed this in `BaseDataCollator`, but `CrossEncoderDataCollator` overrides `__call__` with its own label handling, so CrossEncoder training still has the problem.

A 0-dim tensor counts as a `collections.abc.Collection`, so the collator treats each scalar label as a list of labels and returns a Python list of 0-dim tensors instead of one tensor. The pointwise losses then fail, including both losses that `CrossEncoderTrainer` uses by default:

| Loss | Error on main |
| --- | --- |
| `BinaryCrossEntropyLoss` (default for `num_labels=1`) | `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'numel'` |
| `CrossEntropyLoss` (default for `num_labels>1`) | `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'is_floating_point'` |
| `MSELoss` | `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'numel'` |

Minimal reproducer:

```python
from datasets import Dataset

from sentence_transformers.cross_encoder.data_collator import CrossEncoderDataCollator

dataset = Dataset.from_dict({"query": ["q1", "q2"], "document": ["d1", "d2"], "label": [1.0, 0.0]})
dataset = dataset.with_format("torch", columns=["label"], output_all_columns=True)
collator = CrossEncoderDataCollator(preprocess_fn=None)
print(collator([dataset[0], dataset[1]])["label"])
# main: [tensor(1.), tensor(0.)], plus a UserWarning about copy-constructing from a tensor
# this PR: tensor([1., 0.])
```

I found this through code analysis while checking which collators #4231 covers, not in actual use. I then trained each CrossEncoder loss for two steps on a small local model, with an unformatted and a torch-formatted dataset: the three losses above fail on main and pass with this change. `MarginMSELoss` and the listwise losses already accept a list of labels, so they ran, but every tensor row went through `torch.tensor(tensor)`, which copies it and emits a `UserWarning`.

### Change

When the labels are tensors, stack 0-dim ones into one tensor, and keep larger ones as the per-sample list that the listwise losses expect, without copying them. Python-valued labels take the same path as before.

### Tests

- `tests/cross_encoder/test_data_collator.py` (new): torch-formatted float and integer labels collate to the same tensor as the unformatted dataset, and torch-formatted label lists stay one tensor per sample.
- `tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py::test_trainer_tensor_formatted_labels`: one `CrossEncoderTrainer` step with the default loss for `num_labels=1` and `num_labels=3` on a torch-formatted dataset. The model is a small randomly initialized `BertForSequenceClassification` built in the test, so nothing is downloaded. The step completes, and the weights change and stay finite.

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_data_collator.py tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py::test_trainer_tensor_formatted_labels tests/base/test_data_collator.py -q
```

| Environment: macOS, CPU, Python 3.12, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.2, datasets 5.1.0 | Result |
| --- | --- |
| New tests on main | 4 failed, 1 passed (the label-list test passes, with the warning) |
| Command above with this PR | 37 passed |

`ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` pass on the changed files. I had no Hub access, so the CrossEncoder tests that download models did not run: in `tests/cross_encoder` and `tests/base/test_data_collator.py`, the same tests fail on main and on this branch, all with download errors. GPU training and the minimum-versions setup were not run.

title: Explain batch sizes for cached contrastive losses
body:
The SentenceTransformer training overview lists `per_device_train_batch_size` and `gradient_accumulation_steps`, but it doesn't explain how they relate to the cache `mini_batch_size` of `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss`. In #3134 a user raised the training batch from 512 to 8192 without knowing which setting to tune, and the reply there noted that the documentation should make this distinction clearer.

### Change

This adds a short section under Training Arguments:

- A table of the three settings. The training batch sets the contrastive pool. The cache mini-batch sets how many sequences are embedded, and how many similarity-matrix rows are computed, at once. Gradient accumulation adds batches to one optimizer update without sharing negatives between them.
- A single-device example (128 pairs, `mini_batch_size=16`, two accumulation steps) that explains what each number means.
- Which setting to tune for memory and which one changes the objective. It also explains that `mini_batch_num_tokens` replaces the sequence count only for the embedding mini-batches, while `mini_batch_size` still chunks the similarity rows (`_minibatch_ranges` in `sentence_transformers/base/losses/gradcache.py`, `calculate_loss` in `cached_multiple_negatives_ranking.py`).

The memory note is a little more qualified than the earlier reply in #3134. A smaller `mini_batch_size` lowers activation memory, but the full batch's inputs, embeddings, and cached gradients still grow with `per_device_train_batch_size`.

### Validation

- I ran the added code block verbatim on CPU with a tiny local trainable `WordEmbeddings` model:
  - The cached loss and parameter gradients match uncached `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss` in float64 for `mini_batch_size` 1, 3, and 16, and for `mini_batch_size=1` with `mini_batch_num_tokens=4`.
  - Two accumulated 3-pair batches give a different loss (4.561 vs 6.013) and different gradients from one 6-pair batch.
  - With a token budget, an encoder mini-batch can hold several sequences, and a sequence over the budget is embedded alone.
  - A `SentenceTransformerTrainer` run with the documented settings makes two 128-pair loss calls for one optimizer update.
- `tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_cmnrl.py` and `test_gradcache.py` give 64 passed and 3 skipped (two need MPS; one is the known Windows bfloat16 skip).
- Full docs build with the pinned `docs` group (`sphinx-build -c docs -a -E . <out>`): it gives the same 76 warnings as `main`, none from the changed page. The new heading, table, and link render, and the link opens the existing Speeding up Inference page.
- pre-commit passes.

Windows 11, CPU, Python 3.12.14, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.1. This is a docs-only change. I didn't run a GPU, Flash Attention, or a real fine-tuning job, and the section makes no speed or quality claims.

### AI assistance

AI helped check the cached-loss implementation against the text, write the section and the validation script, and draft this description.

title: Don't share the transformers tokenizer's backend in StaticEmbedding
body:
When `StaticEmbedding` is created with a `PreTrainedTokenizerFast`, it uses that tokenizer's backend `tokenizers.Tokenizer` (`tokenizer._tokenizer`) directly. Calling the transformers tokenizer sets the padding and truncation of this backend tokenizer, so after a call such as `tokenizer(texts, padding=True)`, `StaticEmbedding.preprocess()` pads the texts of a batch to the longest one, and `nn.EmbeddingBag` averages the padding tokens into the embeddings of the shorter texts. After a call with `truncation=True, max_length=...`, it truncates its inputs to that length.

This also happens without any direct tokenizer call when another module uses the same tokenizer, for example in a `Router` that encodes queries with a `StaticEmbedding` and documents with a `Transformer`:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules import Pooling, Router, StaticEmbedding, Transformer

transformer = Transformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
static_embedding = StaticEmbedding(transformer.tokenizer, embedding_dim=128)
router = Router.for_query_document(query_modules=[static_embedding], document_modules=[transformer, Pooling(128)])
model = SentenceTransformer(modules=[router])

queries = ["What is a cat?", "How do cats and dogs get along with other animals at home?"]
before = model.encode_query(queries)
model.encode_document(["Cats are small domesticated felines."])
after = model.encode_query(queries)
print(model.similarity_pairwise(before, after))
```

On `main`, this prints a value well below 1 for the shorter query, for example `tensor([0.2308, 1.0000])` (it depends on the random embedding weights): once documents have been encoded, the query embeddings change. With this change, it prints `tensor([1.0000, 1.0000])`.

This change copies the backend tokenizer, so that `StaticEmbedding` has its own and keeps tokenizing without padding or truncation. A `tokenizers.Tokenizer` that is passed directly is used as before.

I found this through code analysis, not in actual use. I searched the issues and pull requests about `StaticEmbedding` and its tokenizer and didn't find this. The closest is #3925, which fixed a tokenizer that was shared between `WordEmbeddings` instances.

**Tests**

New `test_tokenize_after_transformers_tokenizer_call` in `tests/sentence_transformer/modules/test_static_embedding.py`: it tokenizes two texts with a `StaticEmbedding` created from a `PreTrainedTokenizerFast`, before and after calling that tokenizer with `padding=True`, and with `truncation=True, max_length=4`. Both cases fail on `main` (the inputs have padding tokens, or are truncated) and pass with this change.

- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/modules/test_static_embedding.py` (`HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`): 20 passed, 3 skipped and 1 failed on `main`; 22 passed, 3 skipped and the same 1 failed with this change. The failure is `test_loading_model2vec`, which downloads a model.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/modules tests/base/modules tests/sparse_encoder/modules` (`HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`): 593 passed on `main` and 595 with this change, with the same 19 failures and 2390 errors in both runs, from tests that need models that aren't in my local cache.
- The example above: `tensor([1.0000, 1.0000])` with this change.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` on the changed files: passed.
- Not run: the tests that need models I don't have locally.

Versions: Python 3.12.13, transformers 5.17.0, tokenizers 0.23.2, torch 2.14.0.

AI assistance: Claude Code helped me find this bug and write the fix and the test.

title: [fix] Score SparseRerankingEvaluator with the model's similarity function
body:
`SparseRerankingEvaluator` defaults to `similarity_fct=cos_sim` ([sparse_reranking.py#L116](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/a5f62a56d86990ad490b6eb29439b48487494b65/sentence_transformers/sparse_encoder/evaluation/sparse_reranking.py#L116)), while `SparseEncoder` models score with dot product unless configured otherwise ([model.py#L824-L839](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/a5f62a56d86990ad490b6eb29439b48487494b65/sentence_transformers/sparse_encoder/model.py#L824-L839)), and `SparseInformationRetrievalEvaluator` and `SparseNanoBEIREvaluator` already default to the model's own similarity ([sparse_information_retrieval.py#L49](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/a5f62a56d86990ad490b6eb29439b48487494b65/sentence_transformers/sparse_encoder/evaluation/sparse_information_retrieval.py#L49)). So with default arguments the reranking evaluator scores SPLADE-style models with a function they are not used with, and these are the numbers that reach the trainer's evaluation metrics and the model card. I found this by reading and testing the code.

On the docstring example itself (`naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil`, first 1000 rows of MS MARCO v1.1 validation, 967 evaluated queries), main reproduces the documented MAP 53.41 / MRR@10 54.14 / NDCG@10 65.06 exactly, so those are cosine numbers. Scored with the model's dot product:

| Model | Metric | main (cosine) | this PR (model's dot product) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil` | MAP | 53.41 | 62.28 |
| | MRR@10 | 54.14 | 62.99 |
| | NDCG@10 | 65.06 | 71.84 |
| `opensearch-project/opensearch-neural-sparse-encoding-doc-v2-mini` | MAP | 48.45 | 59.42 |
| | MRR@10 | 49.01 | 60.23 |
| | NDCG@10 | 61.16 | 69.59 |

The change follows `MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator` ([reranking.py#L88-L98](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/a5f62a56d86990ad490b6eb29439b48487494b65/sentence_transformers/multi_vector_encoder/evaluation/reranking.py#L88-L98)): `similarity_fct` now defaults to `None`, and `__call__` uses `model.similarity` unless a function was passed. Passing `similarity_fct=cos_sim` gives the old scores. I also updated the `similarity_fct` argument description and the example output in the docstring and in `examples/sparse_encoder/evaluation/sparse_reranking_evaluator.py` to the values measured above.

Reproducer (CPU; downloads the 91 MB model and the MS MARCO v1.1 parquet files, about 220 MB; each evaluator call took about 5 minutes on 2 threads):

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

from sentence_transformers import SparseEncoder
from sentence_transformers.sparse_encoder.evaluation import SparseRerankingEvaluator

model = SparseEncoder("opensearch-project/opensearch-neural-sparse-encoding-doc-v2-mini")
print(model.similarity_fn_name)

# Same data as the SparseRerankingEvaluator docstring example
eval_dataset = load_dataset("microsoft/ms_marco", "v1.1", split="validation").select(range(1000))
samples = [
    {
        "query": sample["query"],
        "positive": [t for s, t in zip(sample["passages"]["is_selected"], sample["passages"]["passage_text"]) if s],
        "negative": [t for s, t in zip(sample["passages"]["is_selected"], sample["passages"]["passage_text"]) if not s],
    }
    for sample in eval_dataset
]

for label, kwargs in [("default", {}), ("model.similarity", {"similarity_fct": model.similarity})]:
    results = SparseRerankingEvaluator(samples=samples, batch_size=32, write_csv=False, **kwargs)(model)
    print(label, {key: round(float(results[key]), 4) for key in ("map", "mrr@10", "ndcg@10")})
```

| Run | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| default | map 0.4845, mrr@10 0.4901, ndcg@10 0.6116 | map 0.5942, mrr@10 0.6023, ndcg@10 0.6959 |
| `similarity_fct=model.similarity` | map 0.5942, mrr@10 0.6023, ndcg@10 0.6959 | map 0.5942, mrr@10 0.6023, ndcg@10 0.6959 |

`model.similarity_fn_name` is `dot` in both runs.

Tests: the new `tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation/test_reranking_evaluator.py` (batched and per-sample encoding) fails on main with `assert 0.0 == 1.0` and passes with this change. `pytest tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation/` gives 14 passed, 2 skipped (CUDA unavailable). pre-commit (ruff check, ruff format, typos) passes on the changed files. I didn't run the full suite.

I left the dense `RerankingEvaluator`'s `cos_sim` default unchanged. I found no existing issue or PR for this.

Versions: sentence-transformers main (a5f62a56), transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1+cpu, Python 3.12.13.

I made this PR and directed its development, with AI assistance from Claude and GPT-6 Astra.

title: Fix rescoring gate for reused USearch float indexes
body:
Reusing a USearch `f16` index with the default `corpus_precision="float32"` wrongly enters the quantization rescoring path. Fractional stored vectors are then cast to integers: the regression's cosine distances `0.029857` and `0.552786` both become `0`.

Gate rescoring on `corpus_precision`, as documented and as the FAISS helper does. This preserves the supplied float index's native metric and leaves int8/binary rescoring unchanged. No new precision option or index type is introduced.

The four real-index regressions compare IDs and distances with direct USearch search for f16/f32 storage, one/two queries, and rescoring on/off. This was found through source inspection, not a personal production incident.

Validation: baseline 2 failures / 2 passing controls; patched full quantization suite 153 passed. Repository pre-commit hooks (Ruff lint/format and typos) passed for both changed files.

OpenAI Codex assisted with investigation, implementation and local CPU validation. Draft pending human owner review.

title: Allow underscores in the NanoBEIREvaluator aggregate_key
body:
`NanoBEIREvaluator` raises a `KeyError` when its `aggregate_key` contains an underscore, for example `"median_score"`, or `"geometric_mean"` with a matching `aggregate_fn`. `SparseNanoBEIREvaluator` and `MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator` use the same `__call__`, so they're affected too. The data doesn't matter, so this example uses small local datasets in place of the NanoBEIR datasets:

```python
import numpy as np

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.evaluation import NanoBEIREvaluator


class LocalNanoBEIREvaluator(NanoBEIREvaluator):
    # Small local datasets in place of the NanoBEIR datasets
    def _load_dataset_subset_split(self, subset, split, required_columns):
        return {
            "corpus": [
                {"_id": "d0", "text": "Paris is the capital of France."},
                {"_id": "d1", "text": "Berlin is the capital of Germany."},
                {"_id": "d2", "text": "Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa."},
            ],
            "queries": [
                {"_id": "q0", "text": "What is the capital of France?"},
                {"_id": "q1", "text": "Who painted the Mona Lisa?"},
            ],
            "qrels": [{"query-id": "q0", "corpus-id": "d0"}, {"query-id": "q1", "corpus-id": "d2"}],
        }[subset]


model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
evaluator = LocalNanoBEIREvaluator(dataset_names=["msmarco", "nq"], aggregate_fn=np.median, aggregate_key="median_score")
results = evaluator(model)
print(evaluator.primary_metric, results[evaluator.primary_metric])
```

On `main`:

```
  File ".../sentence_transformers/sentence_transformer/evaluation/nano_beir.py", line 399, in __call__
KeyError: 'cosine_ndcg@10'
```

With this change:

```
NanoBEIR_median_score_cosine_ndcg@10 1.0
```

`__call__` finds the metric name in each dataset key, such as `NanoMSMARCO_cosine_ndcg@10`, by splitting off as many underscores as its own name has. Its name is `NanoBEIR_{aggregate_key}`, and with a `truncate_dim` (or a `max_active_dims` for the sparse evaluator) both its name and the dataset names get the same suffix, so this works as long as `aggregate_key` has no underscore. With `"median_score"`, the split also removes the score function: `cosine_ndcg@10` becomes `ndcg@10`, and the lookups of the aggregated `cosine_*` metrics fail. With an `output_path`, it already fails when it writes the CSV (`KeyError: 'cosine_accuracy@1'`).

This change removes the dataset evaluator's own name, which `prefix_name_to_metrics` puts in front of each of its metrics, from the key instead. With the default `"mean"`, the results are the same as before.

I found this through code analysis, not in actual use. I searched the issues and pull requests about `NanoBEIREvaluator`, `aggregate_key` and `aggregate_fn`, and didn't find this.

**Tests**

New `test_nanobeir_evaluator_aggregate_key_with_underscore` in `tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_nanobeir_evaluator.py`, with and without `truncate_dim`. It uses `np.median` with `aggregate_key="median_score"` on small local datasets, and checks the name of the primary metric, that each metric of a dataset has an aggregated metric with the same name, and the aggregated value. On `main`, it fails (`KeyError: 'cosine_ndcg@10'`); with this change, it passes. It doesn't download anything, but this module is skipped on CI, so it won't run there. I can move it to a module that runs on CI if you prefer.

- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation tests/base/test_model_card.py` (default markers, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`): on `main`, 213 passed, 3 failed and 7 skipped; with this change, 215 passed, 3 failed and 7 skipped. The 3 failures are the existing NanoBEIR tests, which download the NanoBEIR datasets.
- With local datasets that differ from each other, `NanoBEIREvaluator` (with and without `truncate_dim`) and `SparseNanoBEIREvaluator` (with and without `max_active_dims`) give the same results, primary metric and CSV on `main` and with this change, with the default `aggregate_key`. With `aggregate_key="median_score"`, they raise a `KeyError` on `main`. With this change, they return the same keys as with `"mean"`, and each aggregated ranking metric is the median over the datasets.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` on the changed files: passed.
- Not run: the existing NanoBEIR tests with the NanoBEIR datasets, and `tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_evaluators.py` (the model of its fixture is not in my local cache).

Versions: Python 3.12.13, transformers 5.17.0, torch 2.14.0, datasets 5.0.1.

AI assistance: Claude Code helped me find this bug and write the fix and the test.

title: Fix max pooling for sequences with no effective tokens
body:
Empty text, stop words, or words outside a `WordEmbeddings` vocabulary leave no unmasked tokens. Max pooling currently returns `-inf` for these rows; normalizing the embeddings then produces `NaN`, which also reaches similarity scores. This was found during code review and reproduced locally, rather than encountered in a production deployment.

For example, this runs on CPU without downloading a model:

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules import Pooling, WordEmbeddings
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules.tokenizer import WhitespaceTokenizer

words = WordEmbeddings(
    tokenizer=WhitespaceTokenizer(vocab=["PADDING_TOKEN", "hello", "world"]),
    embedding_weights=torch.tensor([[0., 0.], [-1., -2.], [-3., -4.]]),
)
model = SentenceTransformer(modules=[words, Pooling(2, "max")], device="cpu")
print(model.encode(["hello world", "", "unknownword", "the"], normalize_embeddings=True))
```

The last three rows contain `NaN` before this change and zero vectors afterward. The known-token row keeps its negative maximum before normalization.

Return zero only when the attention mask or flattened effective sequence length says a row has no remaining tokens. This covers prompt exclusion as well as empty inputs, and leaves genuine non-finite values in valid model output visible. Mean pooling, tokenization, and model weights are unchanged. #4179 added a masked position so empty inputs can pass through CNN/LSTM; this fixes the subsequent max reduction rather than changing that padding.

Validation on Python 3.12.14 / PyTorch 2.14.1, macOS arm64 CPU:

- 22 new regression cases failed before the fix and passed afterward, including normalized public `encode`/similarity, combined max+mean pooling, padded and flattened inputs, prompt exclusion, negative values, and gradients.
- `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/sentence_transformer/modules/test_pooling.py tests/sentence_transformer/modules/test_word_embeddings.py -k 'not respects_include_prompt and not prompt_exclusion_is_idempotent and not hf_tokenizer_preprocess'`: 271 passed, 156 skipped because CUDA is unavailable, 9 deselected because their fixtures download pretrained models. The same result was rechecked against the complete `b83a7f57` source tree in the existing environment. This is not a full model or GPU test run.
- `pre-commit run --all-files`: passed for the fix based on `d75b4f16`. On `b83a7f57`, the same pinned Ruff 0.15.6 lint/format and typos 1.45.0 checks passed across the source tree in read-only mode.
- Separate automated review and CPU checks passed, including a real Normalize-module/retrieval workflow and mask ownership. Eight independent public API groups also passed on the current source tree. CUDA and live Flash Attention were not tested.

OpenAI Codex assisted with investigation, implementation, tests, and this description. Review used separate agents and executed local checks.

title: Correct the DDP evaluator note in the training overviews
body:
The SentenceTransformer, SparseEncoder, MultiVectorEncoder, and CrossEncoder training overviews still warn that with distributed training "the evaluator only runs on the first device". Since #4004, the trainer splits the evaluator's `encode()` and `predict()` calls across the existing DDP processes, process zero computes the metrics and writes the output once, and the metrics are broadcast to every process (`distributed_evaluation` in `sentence_transformers/util/distributed.py`, used by `evaluation_loop` in `sentence_transformers/base/trainer.py`). The distributed training guide already describes this, so the overviews contradict it.

### Change

Replace the warning in all four overviews with a note that matches the guide: evaluator inference is shared across DDP processes, process zero computes and writes the results, the metrics are broadcast, direct evaluator calls outside the trainer keep their single-process behavior, and the FSDP and DeepSpeed limitations are in the guide.

The CrossEncoder overview linked to `training/distributed.html`, which doesn't exist under `docs/cross_encoder/` (https://sbert.net/docs/cross_encoder/training/distributed.html returns 404). It now links to `../sentence_transformer/training/distributed.html`, like the SparseEncoder and MultiVectorEncoder overviews.

### Validation

- Full docs build with the pinned `docs` group (`sphinx-build -c docs -a -E . <out>`, as in `make docs`): it succeeds with the same 76 warnings as `main`, none from the changed pages. In the rendered HTML, all four notes link to the existing distributed training page.
- The existing distributed evaluator tests still pass: `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/base/test_distributed_evaluation.py -k "False or without_process_group" -q` gives 6 passed and 4 deselected (the deselected cases need two GPUs and NCCL). Windows 11, CPU, Python 3.12.14, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.1.

There are no code changes or new tests. I didn't run multi-GPU training.

### AI assistance

Found through an AI-assisted comparison of the docs with #4004, not from a training run. AI helped check the implementation, write the new text, and draft this description.

title: Restore the MLM training example on Transformers v5
body:
The bundled MLM example no longer runs anywhere in the supported `transformers>=5.0.0,<6.0.0` range:

```bash
python examples/sentence_transformer/unsupervised_learning/MLM/train_mlm.py <bert-style-mlm-model> train.txt [dev.txt]
```

- Transformers 5.20.1 fails at import: `ImportError: cannot import name 'DataCollatorForWholeWordMask' from 'transformers'`
- Transformers 5.0.0 still has that class (deprecated), but fails on the training arguments: `TypeError: TrainingArguments.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'overwrite_output_dir'`. `evaluation_strategy` is rejected as well.

### Change

- Use `DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(whole_word_mask=do_whole_word_mask)`, the replacement named in the 5.0.0 deprecation warning, and `eval_strategy`. Drop `overwrite_output_dir`.
- The v5 whole-word masking finds word boundaries from `offset_mapping`, so the dataset requests offsets when whole-word masking is on, and `remove_unused_columns=False` keeps them until the collator, which pops them before the forward pass.
- The collator pads through `tokenizer.pad`, which doesn't pad `offset_mapping`. Sentences of different lengths then fail with `Unable to create tensor ... (offset_mapping in this case)` on both 5.0.0 and 5.20.1, so with whole-word masking on, the dataset pads to the script's `max_length` (100). Without whole-word masking the script keeps dynamic padding and doesn't request offsets.

The new collator also returns `attention_mask` and keeps padding out of the MLM labels. #2971 reports that the old collator dropped the attention mask, which breaks GTE models. I didn't run the GTE checkpoints from that issue, so this is related to #2971 rather than a confirmed fix for it.

The offset padding gap is in the Transformers collator. I didn't find an existing Transformers issue for it and haven't opened one yet.

### Tests

`test_mlm_example_trains_with_transformers_v5` in `tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py` saves a tiny local BERT and tokenizer, runs the actual script with `runpy`, with and without a dev file, and checks that it trains for 3 steps, saves `model.safetensors`, changes the weights while keeping them finite, evaluates the dev file, and collates batches with an attention mask and `-100` labels on padding. It passes the model and corpus as relative paths, because the script builds its output directory name from the model name and an absolute Windows path would put a drive letter in it.

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py -q -k mlm_example
```

| Environment (Windows 11, CPU) | New test on the unchanged example | With the fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python 3.12.14, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.1 | 2 failed (ImportError) | 2 passed |
| Minimum versions resolved as in `min-versions.yml`: Python 3.10.21, torch 2.2.0, transformers 5.0.0, datasets 2.16.0 | 2 failed (TypeError) | 2 passed |

I also ran the script from the command line in both environments with a train and dev file, and with `do_whole_word_mask = False` in a local copy; both trained and saved. title: Handle single-document cross-encoder reranking evaluation
body:
`CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator` raises `ValueError: Computing NDCG is only meaningful when there is more than 1 document` when a query has one relevant candidate. This can occur when the retrieval stage returns one document or a sample has one positive and no negatives. One such query stops the entire evaluation.

The evaluator permits these samples, but passes them to sklearn's NDCG function, which requires at least two documents. Handle singleton NDCG in `compute_metrics`: it is one when the only document is relevant. The helper also returns zero when the only document has no relevance. Both base and reranked metrics use this path. Multi-document NDCG, MRR, average precision and invalid cutoff handling retain their existing behavior.

This was found through code analysis and reproduced using the real `cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce` model. A minimal reproducer is:

```python
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
from sentence_transformers.cross_encoder.evaluation import CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator

model = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce")
evaluator = CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator(
    [{"query": "test", "positive": ["yes"], "negative": []}]
)
print(evaluator(model))
```

Validation on Windows, Python 3.13, PyTorch 2.11, Transformers 5.5.4 and scikit-learn 1.6.1:

- `pytest tests/cross_encoder/evaluation/test_reranking.py -q`: 12 passed. The six new regression cases fail on pristine source and pass with the fix.
- 144 multi-document metric comparisons with tied/untied scores produce identical results on base and patch.
- Eight real-model public comparisons preserve metrics, source samples and CSV bytes across both sample formats and repeated appends.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` and `git diff --check` passed.

Existing models, metric names and CSV formats stay unchanged. The full training suite and other operating systems were not tested locally; this change affects the evaluation helper only.

title: Raise an error in fit() when InputExamples have different numbers of texts
body:
Closes #4238

## What does this PR do?

`fit()` turns the `InputExample`s into a `Dataset` with `zip(*texts)`, so if they don't all have the same number of texts, every example is silently cut down to the shortest one. One `(anchor, positive)` example removes the hard negatives from a whole `(anchor, positive, neg_1, ..., neg_5)` dataset.

With this change, `fit()` raises a `ValueError` in that case, e.g.:

```text
ValueError: All InputExamples for training objective 1 must have the same number of texts, but got examples with [2, 7] texts.
```

I went for an error because I can't think of a case where cutting every example down is what the user wants, and the `SentenceTransformerTrainer` already fails on the same data (the missing columns become `None`). If you'd rather not break scripts that currently run, I'm happy to make it a warning instead.

`CrossEncoder.fit()` builds its dataset the same way. I left it out to keep this small, but I can add the same check there if you'd like.

We hit this in actual use; details and the reproduction are in #4238.

title: Log eval loss components for any metric_key_prefix
body:
Evaluations whose `metric_key_prefix` is not `"eval"` don't log the loss components of losses that return a dict, such as `SpladeLoss` and `CSRLoss`. This includes each dataset of a dict `eval_dataset`, which the trainer evaluates with the prefix `eval_{name}`, and `trainer.evaluate(dataset, metric_key_prefix="test")`. These evaluations also don't reset the accumulated components, so the next evaluation with the `"eval"` prefix logs components averaged over the batches of all of them:

```python
import tempfile

from datasets import Dataset, DatasetDict

from sentence_transformers import SparseEncoder, SparseEncoderTrainer, SparseEncoderTrainingArguments
from sentence_transformers.sparse_encoder.losses import SparseMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, SpladeLoss


def make_dataset(name):
    return Dataset.from_dict(
        {
            "anchor": [f"{name} question number {i}" for i in range(8)],
            "positive": [f"{name} answer text number {i} with some words" for i in range(8)],
        }
    )


model = SparseEncoder("sparse-encoder-testing/splade-bert-tiny-nq")
loss = SpladeLoss(
    model, SparseMultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model), document_regularizer_weight=3e-5, query_regularizer_weight=5e-5
)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as output_dir:
    args = SparseEncoderTrainingArguments(output_dir=output_dir, per_device_eval_batch_size=4, report_to="none")
    eval_dataset = DatasetDict({"a": make_dataset("a"), "b": make_dataset("b")})
    trainer = SparseEncoderTrainer(model=model, args=args, eval_dataset=eval_dataset, loss=loss)

    trainer.evaluate()  # evaluates "a" and "b" as eval_a and eval_b
    trainer.evaluate(make_dataset("a"), metric_key_prefix="test")
    trainer.evaluate(make_dataset("a"))
    for logs in trainer.state.log_history:
        print({key: round(value, 4) for key, value in logs.items() if key.endswith("loss")})
```

On `main`:

```
{'eval_a_loss': 0.6842}
{'eval_b_loss': 0.7565}
{'test_loss': 0.6842}
{'eval_loss': 0.6842, 'eval_base_loss': 0.6918, 'eval_document_regularizer_loss': 0.0049, 'eval_query_regularizer_loss': 0.0056}
```

The last evaluation uses the same data as the first one, but its `eval_base_loss` (0.6918) is the average over the batches of all four evaluations, and the components don't add up to `eval_loss`. With this change:

```
{'eval_a_loss': 0.6842, 'eval_a_base_loss': 0.6738, 'eval_a_document_regularizer_loss': 0.0049, 'eval_a_query_regularizer_loss': 0.0056}
{'eval_b_loss': 0.7565, 'eval_b_base_loss': 0.7458, 'eval_b_document_regularizer_loss': 0.005, 'eval_b_query_regularizer_loss': 0.0058}
{'test_loss': 0.6842, 'test_base_loss': 0.6738, 'test_document_regularizer_loss': 0.0049, 'test_query_regularizer_loss': 0.0056}
{'eval_loss': 0.6842, 'eval_base_loss': 0.6738, 'eval_document_regularizer_loss': 0.0049, 'eval_query_regularizer_loss': 0.0056}
```

The cause is in `BaseTrainer.log()`: it only treats a log as an evaluation log when the log has an `eval_loss` key, and it names the components `eval_{component}`. This change resets the eval accumulators at the start of each `evaluation_loop()` and stores its `metric_key_prefix`. `log()` then uses that prefix to recognize the evaluation log and to name the components, for example `eval_a_base_loss` or `test_base_loss`. Evaluations with the `"eval"` prefix log the same keys as before.

This affects the multi-dataset training in the Sparse Encoder training overview, which allows a dict `eval_dataset`: with `SpladeLoss`, the evaluation logs during training have `eval_{name}_loss`, but none of the base loss and regularizer losses, so the regularization can't be followed on the evaluation data. A later evaluation with the `"eval"` prefix then also reports components that mix in these evaluations.

I found this through code analysis, not in actual use. I searched issues and pull requests about loss components and `metric_key_prefix`: #4181 changed how non-finite components are averaged and doesn't touch this, and #2749 is about `load_best_model_at_end` with multiple evaluation datasets.

**Tests**

New `test_trainer_logs_eval_loss_components_under_the_metric_key_prefix` in `tests/sparse_encoder/test_trainer.py`, with `SpladeLoss`: it evaluates a `DatasetDict` with two datasets, then one of them with `metric_key_prefix="test"`, then the same one with the default prefix, and checks that each evaluation logs the three components under its own prefix and that they add up to its loss. On `main`, it fails (`KeyError: 'eval_a_base_loss'`); with this change, it passes.

- `pytest tests/base/test_trainer.py tests/sparse_encoder/test_trainer.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py` (default markers, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`): on `main`, 108 passed, 1 failed (the new test) and 1 skipped; with this change, 109 passed and 1 skipped. This includes `test_evaluator_runs_once_and_broadcasts_under_ddp`, which runs `evaluation_loop()` in 2 CPU processes.
- The same files with `-m slow`: 300 passed and 180 skipped, on `main` and with this change.
- A training run with `eval_strategy="steps"` and a `DatasetDict` `eval_dataset` logs `eval_a_*` and `eval_b_*` components at each evaluation, and the training logs have the same keys as before.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` on the changed files: passed.
- Not run: `tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_trainer.py` (the model of its fixture is not in my local cache), and loss components with more than one process.

Versions: Python 3.12.13, transformers 5.17.0, torch 2.14.0, datasets 5.0.1.

AI assistance: Claude Code helped me find this bug and write the fix and the test.

title: Filter empty widget texts per column instead of dropping whole rows
body:
# Filter empty widget texts per column instead of dropping whole rows

`BaseModelCardData.set_widget_examples` skipped a sampled row as soon as *any*
of its columns held an empty text:

```python
values = [value for key, value in sample.items() if key != "dataset_name"]
if any(value == "" or (isinstance(value, dict) and "" in value.values()) for value in values):
    continue
```

Only the texts end up in the widget, so that discarded the perfectly good texts
in the row's *other* columns. When the shortest rows happen to be the ones with
an empty field — which is what a dataset looks like when a model is trained on
one side only, e.g. `anchor`-only or `positive`-only data — the whole widget
comes out empty even though the dataset is full of text, and `push_to_hub`
publishes a card with no widget examples at all.

The fix filters the empty texts per column and drops a row only once it has no
text left. No empty value can reach the widget either way, which is the
condition the Hub enforces, so the guard keeps its purpose while the usable
texts survive.

## Testing

Three regression tests cover it (a partly empty `anchor` column, a partly empty
`positive` column, and a row whose other column is still usable), all
parametrized over the dataset shapes that produce the situation:

- `pytest tests/base/test_model_card.py` → `3 failed, 109 passed, 6 skipped` before, `112 passed, 6 skipped` after
- `ruff` at the pinned 0.15.6 (`ruff-check` + `ruff-format`): clean on both changed files

AI assistance: this change was produced with AI assistance (an autonomous coding
agent) from the library's own behaviour rather than an issue report; the
reproduction, the red/green evidence, the test run and the lint run were
executed locally, and a human reviewed the result before submission.

title: Fix float64 sparse similarity conversion
body:
## Problem

Mixed sparse/dense similarity supports float32, but passing the same float64 values fails in cosine, dot and Euclidean similarity: the shared converter downcasts only the sparse operand. Sparse Manhattan similarity also returns float32 for float64 inputs. Lists of sparse rows have the same unconditional cast.

This was found through source analysis and reproduced locally, not a production incident. It affects comparing double-precision embedding arrays while keeping one operand sparse. For example, on the base revision:

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers import util

x = torch.eye(2, dtype=torch.float64)
print(util.cos_sim(x, x))              # works
print(util.cos_sim(x.to_sparse(), x))  # RuntimeError: expected scalar type Float but found Double
```

## Change

Preserve float64 in the common sparse conversion path, including lists of sparse rows, and return sparse Manhattan results in the converted input dtype. Other sparse dtypes retain their existing float32 conversion. Extend the existing mixed-layout regression across float32/float64 and tensor/list inputs, both operand orders, four metrics and their pairwise variants.

This follows the mixed-layout support in #3906 and sparse float64 normalization in #4045; both are already on the base, and this addresses the remaining conversion step.

## Validation

Run from the checkout root with Python 3.10.10, PyTorch 2.12.1 and Transformers 5.13.0:

- Before the fix: `python -m pytest tests/util/test_similarity.py -k test_similarity_mixed_sparse_dense -q` — 16 failed, 16 passed.
- After: `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/util/test_similarity.py tests/util/test_tensor.py -k 'not test_pairwise_angle_sim_even_and_odd_sparse_embeddings' -q` — 206 passed, 17 skipped, 1 deselected. GPU cases require unavailable hardware. The excluded existing angle test requires an uncached model; the initial offline run failed at that fixture. No model/GPU suite claim.
- Scoped repository pre-commit hooks (Ruff check/format and typos) and `git diff --check` passed.
- Independent agent review and public-API check passed 16 float64 layout/metric comparisons against dense outputs at 1e-12 tolerance, verifying the package loaded from the patched checkout.

AI assistance was used for investigation, implementation, tests and independent review. No model downloads or external providers were used.

title: Skip rows with an empty text when building widget examples
body:
Closes #4232

## What does this PR do?

If a training dataset contains an empty text, `set_widget_examples` very likely picks it, because the shortest sampled rows are used first. The Hub rejects a model card whose widget contains an empty text, so `push_to_hub` failed and, since the README is uploaded in the same commit as the weights, nothing was uploaded:
