title: Stack tensor-formatted labels in the data collator
body:
Offline embedding distillation fails before the first training step when the teacher embeddings in the `label` column are formatted as tensors. The [offline distillation design in #3665](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/pull/3665#issuecomment-3966062562) has users compute teacher embeddings before training and store them in the dataset. After `dataset.with_format("torch")`, each label row is a tensor, and `BaseDataCollator` passes the list of rows to `torch.tensor`, which only accepts Python values or one-element tensors:

```
ValueError: only one element tensors can be converted to Python scalars
```

Minimal reproducer:

```python
import torch
from datasets import Dataset

from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.data_collator import SentenceTransformerDataCollator

dataset = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["hello", "world"], "label": torch.randn(2, 8).tolist()})
dataset = dataset.with_format("torch", columns=["label"], output_all_columns=True)
collator = SentenceTransformerDataCollator(preprocess_fn=lambda texts, **kwargs: {})
batch = collator([dataset[0], dataset[1]])  # ValueError before this PR; a (2, 8) label tensor after
```

Leaving the dataset unformatted avoids the error, but the message does not point to the cause.

### Change

Stack the label rows with `torch.stack` when they are tensors, and keep the existing `torch.tensor` conversion otherwise. Python-valued labels, including vector labels for `MSELoss` and probability targets for `SoftmaxLoss`, take the same path as before. The SentenceTransformer, SparseEncoder, and MultiVectorEncoder collators inherit this method. #4098 used the same approach for this error in the similarity utilities.

### Tests

- `tests/base/test_data_collator.py`: tensor-formatted `Dataset` rows with scalar, vector, and matrix labels. The scalar case already passed before the fix.
- `tests/base/test_trainer.py`: one `MSELoss` distillation step on the local `StaticEmbedding` fixture with tensor-formatted targets. The step completes, and the weights change and stay finite.

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/base/test_data_collator.py tests/base/test_trainer.py::test_embedding_distillation_with_tensor_formatted_labels -q
```

| Environment (Windows 11, CPU) | New tests on unchanged source (`-k tensor_formatted`) | Command above with the fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python 3.12.14, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.1, datasets 5.1.0 | 3 failed, 1 passed | 33 passed |
| Minimum versions resolved as in `min-versions.yml` (without the vision, audio, and video extras): Python 3.10.21, torch 2.2.0, transformers 5.0.0, datasets 2.16.0 | 3 failed, 1 passed | 33 passed |

title: [feat] Support opt-in fp32 computation for selected linear layers
body:
Hello!

Heads up, I developed this PR with AI assistance and reviewed the changes before opening it.

## Pull Request overview

* Add opt-in fp32 computation for selected CrossEncoder linear layers via `keep_in_fp32_modules`
* Persist the selection in the CrossEncoder model configuration
* Add tests and documentation for configuration, autocast, and serialization

## Details

Following the discussions in https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb/pull/5666 and https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb/pull/5679, I've added a way to compute selected CrossEncoder linear layers in fp32 while keeping the rest of the model in reduced precision. CrossEncoder rerankers typically produce a single score per query-document pair, where rounding to bf16 can cause distinct scores to tie.

For example, a GPU reranker can use a bf16 backbone with fp32 computation in its final classifier:

```python
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

model = CrossEncoder(
    "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    device="cuda",
    model_kwargs={"dtype": "bfloat16"},
    keep_in_fp32_modules=["0.model.classifier"],
)
```

The paths match `model.named_modules()`. The selection is saved in `config_sentence_transformers.json`, and passing `keep_in_fp32_modules=[]` disables a saved selection. It can also be replaced on an existing model with `model.set_keep_in_fp32_modules(...)`.

I've kept the implementation small: selected plain `nn.Linear` instances use a subclass that disables autocast locally and computes with fp32 inputs and weights, returning fp32 outputs. The existing module and parameter objects are preserved, including tied weights and state-dict keys. Stored weights retain their dtype, so this does not recover precision already lost when loading or casting them.

I compared bf16 with bf16 plus an fp32 final head on 11 NanoBEIR datasets (550 queries), reranking the top 100 BM25 documents plus all positives. The runs used an RTX 3090, batch size 32, and a maximum sequence length of 512. Latency is the mean time to score 100 documents, including tokenization, transfers, and output conversion. Each cell below shows bf16 followed by bf16 plus the fp32 head.

| Model | NDCG@10 (×100) | Latency (ms/100 documents) | Queries with top-10 score ties (out of 550) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-68m-v1` | 70.038 → 70.025 | 139.82 → 139.99 | 316 → 4 |
| `Alibaba-NLP/gte-reranker-modernbert-base` | 70.015 → 70.124 | 234.98 → 234.87 | 282 → 4 |
| `mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-base-v1` | 65.562 → 65.545 | 257.60 → 257.62 | 136 → 1 |

The main benefit here is fewer score ties. NDCG@10 and latency were largely unchanged, so I've kept this opt-in without automatically selecting any heads.

This supports plain linear layers on the torch backend. Selecting an LM head also works, but casting the full vocabulary matrix and producing fp32 logits can require substantial temporary memory.

The 25 targeted tests pass, including CPU/CUDA autocast and gradient checks, selection replacement, CrossEncoder save/load behavior, tied embeddings, pickle/deepcopy, and a basic `torch.compile` check. They also cover Dense behavior and MultiVectorEncoder conversion with an irrelevant saved fp32 selection. Lint and formatting checks also pass.

- Tom Aarsen

title: Fix fit() crash with a DataLoader batch_sampler and warn that it is not used
body:
Closes #4227

## What does this PR do?

`fit()` crashed with `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for //: 'int' and 'NoneType'` when a training `DataLoader` was built with `batch_sampler=...`. PyTorch sets `DataLoader.batch_size` to `None` in that case, and `fit()` read the batch size straight from the loader.

With this change, `fit()`:

- reads the batch size from `data_loader.batch_sampler.batch_size` when the loader's `batch_size` is `None`, keeping the existing default (8) if the sampler doesn't have one;
- logs a warning that the custom batch sampler is not used, since `fit()` re-batches the data with a default batch sampler, and points to `SentenceTransformerTrainer` or `old_fit()`.

`NoDuplicatesDataLoader` and loaders built with `batch_size=...` take the same path as before.

We hit the crash in actual use: we train a bilingual retrieval model with `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss` and a custom batch sampler, and a teammate worked around it by setting `batch_size` on the loader. I found that the sampler wasn't used later, while looking into that workaround. Details and the reproduction are in #4227.

I kept the scope to the crash and the warning. Making `fit()` honor custom batch samplers seemed out of scope for a deprecated method, but I'm happy to change the approach.

## Validation

```bash
pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py -k custom_batch_sampler   # 1 passed
pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py                          # 45 passed, 320 deselected (default markers)
pre-commit run --files sentence_transformers/sentence_transformer/fit_mixin.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py   # ruff check, ruff format, typos passed
```

- The new test `test_fit_with_custom_batch_sampler` fails on `main` with the `TypeError` above, and passes with this change. It checks that the batch size comes from the sampler (`per_device_train_batch_size == 4`) and that the warning is logged.
- The reproduction from #4227 now trains and logs the warning instead of crashing.
- Ran on macOS 14.5 arm64, CPU, Python 3.12, torch 2.14.1. I didn't run the slow tests or the full suite.

## AI disclosure

I used Claude Code to help trace the code path, write the fix, the test and the reproductions, and draft this description. I reviewed the changes.

cc @tomaarsen, since this touches `fit()` like #4066 did.

title: [fix] Share quantization ranges in similarity evaluation
body:
`EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator(precision="int8")` (and `"uint8"`) calibrates the two sentence columns separately, so the same sentence can get different quantized embeddings depending on which column it is in. Reversing one pair then changes the reported correlations, even though every similarity function is symmetric. I found this by reading the code, not in a training run.

For int8/uint8 I now encode both columns in one call, so they share the calibration ranges, and split the result back into the two columns. The float32, binary and ubinary paths are unchanged. I noted the shared ranges in the `precision` docstring and added a regression test covering cosine, dot, Euclidean and Manhattan.

Reproducer (CPU, no downloads):

```python
import logging
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.evaluation import EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules import BoW

logging.getLogger("sentence_transformers.util.quantization").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
model = SentenceTransformer(modules=[BoW(["apple", "banana", "orange"])], device="cpu")
a = ["apple", "banana", "apple banana", "orange"]
b = ["apple orange", "banana orange", "apple banana", "apple banana orange"]

for precision in ("int8", "uint8"):
    for reverse in (False, True):
        left, right = a.copy(), b.copy()
        if reverse:
            left[0], right[0] = right[0], left[0]
        result = EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator(
            left, right, [0.7, 0.7, 1.0, 0.6],
            precision=precision, similarity_fn_names=["cosine"], write_csv=False,
        )(model)
        print(precision, reverse, round(result["pearson_cosine"], 6))
```

Pearson correlation, original pairs / first pair reversed:

| Precision | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| int8 | 0.923638 / 0.839687 | 0.869056 / 0.869056 |
| uint8 | 0.997308 / 0.919484 | 0.997308 / 0.997308 |

Tests: the new test fails on main for both precisions and passes with the fix. The dense and sparse embedding-similarity evaluator test files pass (11 tests), and pre-commit (ruff check, ruff format, typos) passes on the changed files. I didn't run the full suite.

Related: #3948 (binary unpacking) and #4058 (search rescoring) don't touch this calibration, and the open QAT draft #3655 keeps the two separate calibration calls.

AI assistance helped with the investigation, the patch, the test and this write-up.

I made this PR and directed its development, with AI assistance from Claude and GPT-6 Astra.

title: Span every objective's steps in the fit() learning rate schedule
body:
With `k` objectives, `fit()` trains everything after the first `1/k` of the run at a learning rate of 0 (the second half for two objectives).

**Cause:** `fit()` builds one optimizer and one scheduler for all objectives, but sizes the schedule as `steps_per_epoch * epochs`. The round-robin sampler gives every objective a batch per iteration, so the optimizer takes `k` times that many steps. The linear/cosine schedule hits zero after `1/k` of training. `old_fit` did not have this, it built one scheduler per objective.

**Fix:** size the schedule as `max_steps` when set, otherwise `steps_per_epoch * epochs * len(objectives)`.

**Reproducer** (CPU, stsb-bert-tiny, 2 objectives of 4 batches each, `warmup_steps=1`, `optimizer_class` records `lr` per step):

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, InputExample, losses

lrs = []
class Rec(torch.optim.AdamW):
    def step(self, *a, **k):
        lrs.append(self.param_groups[0]["lr"]); return super().step(*a, **k)

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
def objective(k):
    ex = [InputExample(texts=[f"a {i} {k}", f"b {i}"], label=0.5) for i in range(16)]
    return DataLoader(ex, batch_size=4), losses.CosineSimilarityLoss(model)
model.fit([objective(0), objective(1)], epochs=1, warmup_steps=1, optimizer_class=Rec, show_progress_bar=False)
print(lrs)  # before: steps 5 to 8 have lr 0.0 (9 of 12 with 3 objectives); after: only step 1 (warmup start) is 0.0
```

**Tests:** `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py -k "fit_scheduler or training_updates_loss_weights"` on CPU. Before the fix 2 failed (2 and 3 objectives), after 5 passed. `ruff check` and `ruff format` clean. I did not run the rest of the suite.

**How found:** code reading, comparing `fit()` with `old_fit`. Not hit in real use. Versions: sentence-transformers main (1fa45b4), transformers 5.5.0, torch 2.11.0.

AI disclosure: Claude Code helped find the bug and write the patch and test.

title: Gather anchors for GISTEmbedLoss's anchor-anchor term across devices
body:
With `gather_across_devices=True`, `GISTEmbedLoss` and `CachedGISTEmbedLoss` gather the positives and negatives from every rank, but the anchor-anchor term (`contrast_anchors=True`, the default) still compares each anchor only against the anchors on its own rank. So a multi-GPU run trains on a different objective than the same global batch on one device: every row is missing `(world_size - 1) * batch_size` in-batch negatives in that term, and the loss and gradients don't match. Anyone training GIST with DDP and `gather_across_devices=True` hits this, since `contrast_anchors` is on by default.

I found this through code analysis while comparing the gather logic with `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss`, whose `query_to_query` term already uses the gathered queries, and then reproduced it with a real 2-process run.

Repro: 2 CPU ranks (gloo), each with half of an 8-pair batch, against the same loss on the full batch in one process (`sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors`, eval mode, guide = perturbed copy):

```
                      gathered 2x4                  single process 1x8
main      GIST        loss=0.310586 logits/row=20   loss=0.315287 logits/row=24
this PR   GIST        loss=0.315287 logits/row=24   loss=0.315287 logits/row=24
this PR   CachedGIST  loss=0.315287 logits/row=24   loss=0.315287 logits/row=24
```

The fix gathers the anchors (and their guide embeddings) as candidates for the anchor-anchor term, the same way the positive-positive term already uses the gathered positives. The rows are still only this rank's anchors, so the backward pass and labels are unchanged, and the self-similarity is masked by `mask_false_negatives` as in the single-process case (it now sits at column `offset + i`). The extra all_gathers only happen when `contrast_anchors=True`. Without a process group `all_gather_with_grad` returns its input, so single-device training is unchanged.

Note for the release notes: multi-GPU runs with `gather_across_devices=True` and `contrast_anchors=True` will see different loss values after this, since they now follow the global-batch objective, and each step does two extra `(batch_size, dim)` all_gathers.

This comes from #3442, which added `gather_across_devices` and switched the positive-positive term to the gathered positives but left the anchor-anchor term local; #3453 and #3817 didn't touch it. I searched open and closed issues and PRs and didn't find a report or fix for this.

Validation (Python 3.12.12, torch 2.14.1+cpu, transformers 5.20.1, base 1fa45b42):
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gist_embed.py tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_cached_gist_embed.py -q`: the new `test_gather_rank1_matches_global_batch` tests (3) fail on main and pass with the fix; 29 passed. They reuse the existing `simulate_rank1_world2` fixture.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses -q`: 455 passed, 51 skipped.
- Real 2-rank gloo run above, plus a gradient check over 12 configs (GIST and CachedGIST with `mini_batch_size=3`, contrast_anchors/contrast_positives on and off, with and without negatives): distributed loss equals the single-process loss, max relative gradient difference 1.1e-6.
- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>`: ruff check, ruff format and typos pass.

Not run: multi-GPU NCCL.

title: Keep new sparse search corpora from sharing an index name

head: 998d29a3078bcdebef9015325f331a642d773a47

title: Fix FAISS hard-negative mining with distance similarities
body:
FAISS always uses an inner-product index while positive scores use the model's selected similarity. Euclidean/Manhattan models therefore compare candidate and positive scores on different scales, corrupting margin filtering and output scores.

Select FAISS L2 or L1 for the corresponding model metric. L2 returns squared distance, so clamp round-off below zero, take its square root and negate; L1 only needs negation. Cosine and dot retain the inner-product path. A unit-vector conversion is insufficient because normalized zero vectors remain zero.

Found through code inspection. Compare actual CPU FAISS mining against non-FAISS mining for all four similarities, with and without an absolute margin. Assert both selected negatives and numerical output scores match, including a zero vector in the corpus.

title: [fix] Pass 1-based ranks to the custom rank_discount_fn in PListMLELambdaWeight
body:
`PListMLELambdaWeight(rank_discount_fn=...)` is documented as receiving rank positions (the `PListMLELoss` docstring and `training_ms_marco_plistmle.py` both show `def custom_discount(ranks): return 1.0 / torch.log1p(ranks)  # ranks: [1, 2, 3, ...]`), but `forward` calls it with the boolean validity mask.

title: Pool the first token when cls_token_embeddings is None
body:
`Pooling("cls")` crashes on top of `WordEmbeddings`. `WordEmbeddings.forward` always writes `cls_token_embeddings=None` into the features, and `Pooling` only checks that the key exists, so it appends `None` and `torch.cat` fails. words = WordEmbeddings(WhitespaceTokenizer(["PAD", "alpha", "beta"]), torch.randn(3, 4))
```python
SentenceTransformer(modules=[words, Pooling(4, "cls")]).encode(["alpha beta"])
# TypeError: expected Tensor as element 0 in argument 0, but got NoneType
```

title: Apply per-dataset prompts and losses to a reused DatasetDict
body:
When the same `DatasetDict` is passed to a second trainer, the second trainer does not add the `dataset_name` column, even when it needs the column for per-dataset prompts or a loss dict. With per-dataset prompts, the prompts are dropped without an error or a warning. With a loss dict, training fails with `TypeError: 'dict' object is not callable`.

```python
import tempfile

from datasets import Dataset, DatasetDict

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer, SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import MultipleNegativesRankingLoss

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
loss = MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)
train_dataset = DatasetDict(
    {
        "ds1": Dataset.from_dict({"anchor": ["hello world"], "positive": ["hi there"]}),
        "ds2": Dataset.from_dict({"anchor": ["good night"], "positive": ["sleep well"]}),
    }
)
output_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()

# A trainer without per-dataset prompts or losses, e.g. for a baseline run
args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(output_dir, per_device_train_batch_size=1, max_steps=2)
SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_dataset, loss=loss)

# A later trainer with per-dataset prompts on the same DatasetDict
args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(
    output_dir, prompts={"ds1": "query: ", "ds2": "passage: "}, per_device_train_batch_size=1, max_steps=2
)
trainer = SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_dataset, loss=loss)
dataloader = trainer.get_train_dataloader()
print(sorted(model.tokenizer.decode(batch["anchor_input_ids"][0], skip_special_tokens=True) for batch in dataloader))

# A later trainer with a loss dict on the same DatasetDict
trainer = SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_dataset, loss={"ds1": loss, "ds2": loss})
trainer.train()
print("trained")
```

On `main`:

```
['good night', 'hello world']
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "transformers/trainer.py", line 2014, in training_step
    loss = self.compute_loss(model, inputs, num_items_in_batch=num_items_in_batch)
  File "sentence_transformers/base/trainer.py", line 510, in compute_loss
    loss = loss_fn(features, labels)
TypeError: 'dict' object is not callable
```

With this change (or with a new `DatasetDict` for each trainer), it prints `['passage : good night', 'query : hello world']` and `trained`.

Versions: sentence-transformers `main` (1fa45b42), transformers 5.17.0, datasets 5.0.1, torch 2.14.0, Python 3.12.

**Cause**

`preprocess_dataset` tags the dataset with `_sentence_transformers_preprocessed`, so that a later call does not apply the `dataset_name` map or transform again (added in #2964). But it also sets the tag when `should_dataset_name_column_be_added` is false and it adds no column. A later trainer then returns the tagged `DatasetDict` early, before it checks whether it needs the column. A plain `dict` is not affected, because each trainer wraps it in a new `DatasetDict`.

This change sets the tag only after the column is added. A `DatasetDict` without the column is not tagged, so a later trainer runs `validate_column_names` and `should_dataset_name_column_be_added` on it again. A `DatasetDict` that already has the column is still skipped, as before. The cross-encoder, sparse encoder and multi-vector trainers use the same `preprocess_dataset`, so they get the fix too. A per-dataset `router_mapping` goes through the same check, but I did not run that case.

**Affected workflow**

The prompts guide (`examples/sentence_transformer/training/prompts/README.md`) compares models trained with and without prompts. If you do both runs in one session with the same `DatasetDict`, for example in a notebook or in a loop over training configurations, and the baseline runs first, the run with per-dataset prompts trains without them. Nothing warns, so the comparison can suggest that the prompts do not help. In the same way, if you change a single loss to a loss dict and create a new trainer in a notebook, you get a `TypeError` that does not point to the cause.

I found this through code analysis, not in actual use. I did not find an issue or pull request about it.

**Tests**

New `test_trainer_prompts_with_a_dataset_dict_from_another_trainer` in `tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py`: a first trainer uses the `DatasetDict` without per-dataset prompts or losses. Then a second trainer with per-dataset prompts trains on it, with a single loss and with a loss dict, and the test checks that the model gets the texts with the prompts. On `main`, both cases fail (the prompts are missing, or the `TypeError` above); with this change, they pass.

- `pytest tests/base/test_trainer.py tests/cross_encoder/test_trainer.py tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_trainer.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py tests/sparse_encoder/test_trainer.py` (default markers, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`): on `main`, 105 passed and 1 skipped; with this change, 107 passed (the 2 new tests) and 1 skipped. In both runs, the 10 tests in `tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_trainer.py` error because the model for their fixture is not in my local cache.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_trainer.py -m slow -k test_trainer_prompts`: 200 passed and 120 skipped, on `main` and with this change.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` on the changed files: passed.

AI assistance: Claude Code helped me find this bug and write the fix and the test.

title: fix: handle empty queries in FAISS rescoring
body:
## Summary

- avoid reconstructing and rescoring nonexistent FAISS candidates for an empty query batch
- add regression coverage for ubinary rescoring and uint8 rescoring with explicit ranges or representative calibration
- preserve caller-supplied index identity and the optional returned-index contract

## Why

FAISS accepts a valid zero-row query matrix and returns zero result rows. The rescoring path then builds `np.array([])` from the empty reconstruction loop, losing the candidate rank and expected byte dtype. Binary rescoring consequently fails in `np.unpackbits`, while calibrated uint8 rescoring fails when dequantizing the rank-lost array.

There are no candidates to reconstruct or rescore for an empty query batch. Guarding that post-search work preserves the existing backend search, timing, validation, and result construction, which naturally returns one result list per query: zero lists for zero queries.

Uint8 zero-query rescoring still requires explicit ranges or representative calibration. Inferring calibration from an empty query batch remains unsupported. This was identified through code analysis and reproduced through the public `semantic_search_faiss` API with a populated FAISS index and a zero-row query array.

## Tests

- regression before fix: 3 failed with the expected ubinary dtype and uint8 broadcasting errors
- regression after fix: 3 passed
- full quantization module: 152 passed
- semantic-search retrieval selection: 28 passed, 134 deselected
- local adjacent zero-query matrix: 15 passed
- Ruff check, Ruff format, typos, and `git diff --check`: passed

Commands used for the core runs (inside the Linux test environment):

```sh
/usr/local/bin/python -m pytest -p pytest_env.plugin tests/util/test_quantization.py -k semantic_search_faiss_empty_queries -vv --tb=long -o cache_dir=/tmp/pytest-cache --basetemp=/tmp/pytest-green --junitxml=/results/green.xml
/usr/local/bin/python -m pytest -p pytest_env.plugin tests/util/test_quantization.py -q -ra -o cache_dir=/tmp/pytest-cache --basetemp=/tmp/pytest-quantization --junitxml=/results/quantization.xml
/usr/local/bin/python -m pytest -p pytest_env.plugin tests/util/test_retrieval.py -k semantic_search -q -ra -o cache_dir=/tmp/pytest-cache --basetemp=/tmp/pytest-retrieval --junitxml=/results/retrieval.xml
```

The tests ran on Linux arm64 with Python 3.12.15, FAISS 1.15.1, NumPy 2.5.4, and CPU-only Torch 2.14.1. Full-suite, x86_64, and hosted-CI equivalence are not claimed.

title: Speed up semantic_search up to 1.46x on CPU by normalizing each corpus chunk once
body:
`semantic_search` calls `cos_sim` once per (query chunk, corpus chunk) pair, and `cos_sim` normalizes both inputs on every call. With the default `query_chunk_size=100`, the same corpus chunk is renormalized once per 100 queries, which was about 30% of the runtime on large corpora.

This swaps the loops so the corpus chunk is the outer loop. When `score_function` is `cos_sim`, each corpus chunk is normalized once and every query chunk is normalized and scored with `dot_score`. Those are the same operations `cos_sim` runs on the same slices, so scores are bit-identical. Each query still receives the corpus chunks in the same order, so the heap sees the same pushes and ties keep their order. Other score functions are called exactly as before, and peak memory is unchanged. I also trimmed the per-hit heap loop a little.

CPU (Apple M5, 4 threads, 384 dims, median of 7 alternating fresh processes):

| queries x corpus, top_k | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1k x 1M, 10 | 1.522 s | 1.150 s | 1.32x |
| 10k x 100k, 10 | 1.413 s | 0.968 s | 1.46x |
| 10k x 10k, 100 | 0.510 s | 0.379 s | 1.35x |
| 20k x 5k, 10 | 0.206 s | 0.155 s | 1.33x |

At 10k x 100k the new time is within about 6% of the bare `mm` + `topk` cost, so there isn't much left to take here.

I compared old and new outputs on about 5,000 configurations (float32/float16/bfloat16, heavy ties, chunk sizes from 1 to 1M, top_k larger than the corpus, `dot_score` and custom functions, numpy, lists, 1-D queries, sparse COO, empty corpus) and all results were identical, including float bits and tie order. The new test checks that the `cos_sim` path matches calling `cos_sim` through a lambda, with ties. `tests/util/test_retrieval.py` (174 passed, 5 skipped) and `test_quantization.py` / `test_import.py` (97 passed) pass; ruff and typos are clean.

I used an AI assistant to help profile and write the comparison script, and reviewed the change and numbers myself.

title: Rewrite pairwise_angle_sim as clearer cos+sin form
body:
## Problem

Addresses [#3223](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/issues/3223).

`pairwise_angle_sim` currently expresses AnglE similarity via complex-number chunking. That is correct but harder to read than the equivalent cosine + sine form discussed in the issue (and matching @user799595's sketch).

@ssivitskii — you had offered to take this forward. This PR is meant as a concrete draft of that scope (clearer form + parity tests + microbenchmark). Happy to co-author, adjust, or hand it over if you already have a branch — no pressure either way.

## Change

- Rewrite `pairwise_angle_sim` in `sentence_transformers/util/similarity.py` as an L2-normalized cosine + sine form over **paired half-dimensions** (`torch.chunk(..., 2)` → first half / second half, i.e. dimension `i` paired with `i + D/2`). This matches the AnglE pairing described in the issue thread; it is **not** even/odd index interleaving.
- Keep sparse densification and odd-dimension zero-padding for compatibility with the previous behavior.
- Add numerical and gradient parity tests against the previous complex-chunk implementation.
- Add a soft CPU microbenchmark (`test_pairwise_angle_sim_not_slower_than_legacy`) so the rewrite does not regress speed on a representative `1024×768` batch.

No intentional change to public API or expected outputs for even-dimensional embeddings.

## Validation

```bash
pytest tests/util/test_similarity.py -q
# focused parity + bench:
pytest tests/util/test_similarity.py -k pairwise_angle_sim -q
```

Local result: parity/gradient checks pass; microbenchmark (CPU, 1 thread, median of 50 timed calls after warmup):

| batch | dim | legacy | new | speedup |
|------:|----:|-------:|----:|--------:|
| 256 | 768 | 1.12 ms | 0.90 ms | ~1.24× |
| 1024 | 768 | 6.20 ms | 3.85 ms | ~1.61× |
| 256 | 1024 | 0.92 ms | 0.50 ms | ~1.87× |
| 64 | 4096 | 0.90 ms | 0.51 ms | ~1.77× |

Readability is the primary goal; the speedup is a bonus when it holds. The CI soft bound is `new ≤ 1.5 × legacy` to avoid flake.

## Notes for reviewers

- Intent: readability + maintainability, with numerical/gradient parity as the acceptance bar (per #3223).
- Pairing convention is **first-half / second-half** (`i` ↔ `i + D/2`), matching the issue write-up and @user799595's snippet — not even/odd indices.

title: [fix] Run the SoftmaxLoss classifier in float32 for low-precision models
body:
`SoftmaxLoss` creates its classifier in float32, but a model loaded or converted to bfloat16, float16 or float64 produces embeddings in that dtype, so the first forward pass fails:

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import SoftmaxLoss

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors", model_kwargs={"torch_dtype": torch.bfloat16})
loss = SoftmaxLoss(model, model.get_embedding_dimension(), num_labels=3)
features = [model.preprocess(["The cat sits outside."]), model.preprocess(["The cat is outdoors."])]
loss(features, torch.tensor([0]))
# RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 must have the same dtype, but got BFloat16 and Float
```

Training such a model with `SentenceTransformerTrainer` and `SoftmaxLoss` fails on the first step the same way.

I cast the concatenated features to the classifier's dtype before the classifier. The classifier and the cross-entropy then stay in float32 whatever the model's dtype, as the cross-encoder ranking losses do for low-precision models (#3800), and gradients still flow back into the model in its own dtype. Float32 models are unaffected.

| Model dtype | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bfloat16, single forward/backward | `RuntimeError` | loss 1.1043 (float32) |
| bfloat16, 3 training steps with `SentenceTransformerTrainer` | `RuntimeError` | losses 1.3137, 1.2408, 1.1295 |

Validation:

- The new `test_model_dtype_matches_float32_reference` in `tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_softmax.py` runs the loss with the model in float32, float16, bfloat16 and float64, compares the logits and the loss with the classifier applied to the model's embeddings cast to float32, and checks that the classifier and the model's embedding weights get finite, nonzero gradients. The float16, bfloat16 and float64 cases fail on main; all pass with this change.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_softmax.py -q`: 10 passed.
- `pre-commit run --files sentence_transformers/sentence_transformer/losses/softmax.py tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_softmax.py`: ruff check, ruff format and typos passed.

I used AI assistance to find, fix, and test this bug.

title: [fix] Use router_mapping for model card dataset statistics
body:
The model card callback computes token statistics for every text column with `task="document"` and ignores the trainer's `router_mapping`. For a `Router` without a `"document"` route (and without a default route), creating the trainer fails, even though `router_mapping` maps every column to an existing route:

```python
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import torch
from datasets import Dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer, SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments
from sentence_transformers.base.modules import Router
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import MultipleNegativesRankingLoss
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules import Pooling, WordEmbeddings
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules.tokenizer import WhitespaceTokenizer

embedding = WordEmbeddings(WhitespaceTokenizer(["hello", "world"]), torch.ones(2, 4))
router = Router({"left": [embedding, Pooling(4)], "right": [embedding, Pooling(4)]}, allow_empty_key=False)
model = SentenceTransformer(modules=[router])
dataset = Dataset.from_dict({"anchor": ["hello", "hello world"], "positive": ["world", "world hello"]})

with TemporaryDirectory() as output_dir:
    args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(
        output_dir=output_dir, router_mapping={"anchor": "left", "positive": "right"}, report_to="none", use_cpu=True
    )
    SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=dataset, loss=MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model))
# main: ValueError: No route found for task type 'document'. Available routes: task='left' and task='right'
```

I pass `router_mapping` from `on_init_end` to the dataset metadata extraction, resolve per-dataset mappings for a `DatasetDict` the same way the trainer does, and compute each column's statistics with its mapped route. Columns without a mapping, and models without a `Router`, use the same task as before. title: [fix] Exclude self-matches before taking paraphrase mining's top_k
body:
`paraphrase_mining_embeddings` takes `top_k + 1` candidates per sentence, assuming the sentence itself is its best match, and drops the self-match afterwards. That holds for cosine similarity, but not for `dot_score` on unnormalized embeddings: a sentence can score higher with a longer vector than with itself. Then the self-match isn't among the candidates, and the sentence keeps `top_k + 1` neighbours.

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers.util import dot_score, paraphrase_mining_embeddings

paraphrase_mining_embeddings(torch.tensor([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]), top_k=1, score_function=dot_score)
# main:    [[6.0, 1, 2], [3.0, 0, 2], [2.0, 0, 1]]
# this PR: [[6.0, 1, 2], [3.0, 0, 2]]
```

Sentence 0's nearest neighbour is sentence 2, but `(0, 1)` is returned too.

I now set the self-similarity scores to `-inf` before taking the top `k` in each corpus chunk, so every sentence keeps exactly `top_k` other sentences, and the `top_k` docstrings say that the sentence itself is excluded.

With `sentence-transformers/multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-dot-v1` (a dot-product model) on the first 1000 unique `sentence1` values of `sentence-transformers/stsb`, 18 sentences score higher with another sentence than with themselves. `paraphrase_mining(model, sentences, top_k=k, score_function=dot_score)` compared with each sentence's top `k` neighbours computed directly:

| `top_k` | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 778 pairs, 2 not among either sentence's top 1, 1 top-1 pair missing | 777 pairs, exactly the top-1 pairs |
| 5 | 3656 pairs, 2 not among either sentence's top 5, 1 missing | 3655 pairs, exactly the top-5 pairs |

Validation:

- The new `test_paraphrase_mining_embeddings_dot_product_excludes_self` compares against a NumPy float64 nearest-neighbour reference for query and corpus chunk sizes 1-3 and `top_k` 0, 1, 2 and 5. 18 of the 36 cases fail on main and all pass with this change.

Source-code analysis found that unequal source/target sentence counts can silently produce an MSE through broadcasting when either side has a single sentence. title: [fix] Preserve valid sparse tokens when padding shares their ID
body:
When a tokenizer uses the same ID for padding and unknown tokens, SparseStaticEmbedding can drop valid unknown tokens depending on batch_size. A shorter query keeps its unknown token when encoded alone, but loses it when right padded beside a longer query.

The token presence scatter writes both 1 and 0 to the same vocabulary position. The masked occurrence can overwrite the valid one. Use an amax reduction so any unmasked occurrence preserves the token. Weighting and output shape stay the same.

Discovered through code analysis and reproduced on main with a local tokenizer, without model or dataset downloads.

Reproducer:
```python
import torch
from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, pre_tokenizers
from transformers import PreTrainedTokenizerFast
from sentence_transformers import SparseEncoder
from sentence_transformers.sparse_encoder.modules import SparseStaticEmbedding

backend = Tokenizer(models.WordLevel(
    {"[UNK]": 0, "known": 1, "longer": 2}, unk_token="[UNK]"
))
backend.pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.Whitespace()
tokenizer = PreTrainedTokenizerFast(
    tokenizer_object=backend, unk_token="[UNK]",
    pad_token="[UNK]", model_max_length=32
)
model = SparseEncoder(modules=[SparseStaticEmbedding(tokenizer)], device="cpu")
texts = ["unseen", "known longer"]
single = model.encode(texts, batch_size=1, convert_to_sparse_tensor=False)
batch = model.encode(texts, batch_size=2, convert_to_sparse_tensor=False)
assert torch.equal(single, batch)
```
Before the fix, the first embedding changes from [1, 0, 0] to [0, 0, 0]. After the fix they match.

Validation:
* `python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/modules/test_sparse_static_embedding.py -q --tb=short`: 7 passed. The new regression failed before the fix and covers both padding sides and shared/separate padding IDs.
* `python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/modules -q --tb=short`: 29 passed.
* `python -m pre_commit run --all-files`: Ruff check, Ruff format and typos passed.
* `git diff --check`: passed.
* Python 3.14.0, PyTorch 2.14.1+cpu, Transformers 5.18.0, Sentence Transformers 6.2.0.dev0.

title: fix: honor WordEmbeddings sequence length limit
body:
`WordEmbeddings` stores and saves `max_seq_length`, but its preprocessing never uses it. Consequently, setting the limit on this module (or through `SentenceTransformer.max_seq_length`) does not truncate inputs, contrary to that property's documented behavior. A word-embedding pipeline configured to process only a document's first N known tokens instead embeds all of them, changing the pooled result and leaving the embedding tensor's sequence dimension unbounded by the configured limit.

Discovered through code analysis and reproduced through the public API, not a production incident. This example needs no model download:

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules import Pooling, WordEmbeddings
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules.tokenizer import WhitespaceTokenizer

words = WordEmbeddings(
    tokenizer=WhitespaceTokenizer(vocab=["PADDING_TOKEN", "alpha", "beta", "gamma"]),
    embedding_weights=torch.tensor([[0., 0.], [1., 0.], [0., 1.], [9., 9.]]),
    max_seq_length=2,
)
model = SentenceTransformer(modules=[words, Pooling(2, "mean")])
print(model.max_seq_length)  # 2
print(model.preprocess(["alpha beta gamma"])["input_ids"])
print(model.encode("alpha beta gamma"))
```

On main `d8a4090d`, this prints `[[1, 2, 3]]` and `[3.3333333, 3.3333333]`. With the fix it prints `[[1, 2]]` and `[0.5, 0.5]`, the same result as encoding `"alpha beta"`.

The one-line fix truncates token IDs before calculating lengths and padding. Inputs within the limit retain their original behavior. No API or dependency changes.

Tom Aarsen simplified the regression to two prompt/no-prompt cases and explicitly pinned the model to CPU in `39f4ba2`. The original test incorrectly compared a potentially CUDA-selected model's output with CPU tensors; my original CPU-only validation missed this. The current test checks token IDs, padding masks, lengths and pooled embeddings. His subsequent merge `fb72251` incorporates the upstream empty-batch fix from #4179.

Related #4179 fixes zero-width batches with no known tokens; this PR's length-limit fix does not duplicate that behavior.

title: Average filtered loss components over the logged calls
body:
With `logging_nan_inf_filter=True` (the default), a nan or inf loss component (e.g. from `SpladeLoss`) is replaced by `accum / (1 + global_step - _globalstep_last_logged)`. That formula comes from the Trainer's main loss, where each optimizer step adds one value. Here the accumulator gets one value per loss call, and `log()` divides by that call count (`steps`). So under gradient accumulation, or during evaluation where `global_step` does not move, the replacement sits far above the running mean and shifts the logged component.

I found this by reading the code, not in a training run. Only the logged components are affected, not the loss or the gradients.

Fix: divide by `steps`.

Test: `pytest tests/base/test_trainer.py` (10 passed). The new test fails on main (logged mean 1.20 after 4 accumulated calls and 1.98 over 99 eval batches, expected 1.0) and passes here. Ruff check and format pass. CPU only, torch 2.11.0, transformers 5.5.0.

AI disclosure: Claude Code helped find the bug and write the patch and test.

title: [fix] Keep modules shared between Router routes shared after loading
body:
`Router.save` writes a separate copy of a module for every route that uses it. A module shared between routes, as in `Router.for_query_document([shared], [shared])`, comes back from `Router.load` as two independent modules: its files are written twice, and a training step on one route no longer updates the other, so training resumed from a checkpoint behaves differently from the original model.

`Router.load` already maps a repeated id in `structure` to the same module, so I only changed `save` to write each module instance once and reuse its id. `Asym`, which `Router` replaced, saved shared modules once because its ids were based on `id(model)`. Separate modules with identical weights stay separate.

With a `Dense` module shared by the query and document routes, after saving and loading:

| | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same module in both routes | `False` | `True` |
| Document output after one SGD step on the query route (original model: `[[0.8, 0.8]]`) | `[[1.0, 1.0]]` | `[[0.8, 0.8]]` |

Two existing tests used the same `StaticEmbedding` in both routes. `test_router_load_with_config` now uses a copy for the document route, so it still covers two separately saved modules, and `test_router_load_forwards_trust_remote_code` now expects one resolution for the shared child instead of two.

Validation:

- The new `test_router_save_load_preserves_shared_modules` covers shared and separate modules with both safetensors and pickle. It reloads the router, takes an SGD step on the query route, and checks both routes' outputs and whether the module is shared. The shared cases fail on main and pass with this change.

title: [fix] Pad WordEmbeddings batches that have no known tokens
body:
`WordEmbeddings.preprocess()` pads each batch to its longest tokenized input. When no input in a batch has a token from the vocabulary (empty strings, whitespace, or only unknown words), the tensors have zero width. Mean pooling handles that, but `LSTM` fails with `RuntimeError: Cannot pack empty tensors.` and `CNN` with `RuntimeError: Calculated padded input size per channel: (0). Kernel size: (1). ...`. The same inputs encode fine when they share a batch with a known sentence, so whether `encode()` crashes depends on the batch size and on how the inputs get sorted into batches.

I now keep one masked position when that happens. The attention mask and sentence lengths stay zero, so those inputs embed to zeros, which is what they already get in mixed batches. `LSTM` already clamps zero lengths to one; it just needed a position to pack.

`model.encode(["hello world", "", "unknownword"], batch_size=1)` with the vocabulary `["PADDING_TOKEN", "hello", "world"]`:

| Model | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WordEmbeddings` + mean `Pooling` | works | unchanged |
| `WordEmbeddings` + `LSTM` + `Pooling` | `RuntimeError: Cannot pack empty tensors.` | zeros for the two inputs without known tokens |
| `WordEmbeddings` + `CNN` + `Pooling` | `RuntimeError: Calculated padded input size per channel: (0). ...` | zeros for the two inputs without known tokens |

Validation:

- The new `test_word_embeddings_encode_batch_without_known_tokens` covers `LSTM` and `CNN`, empty and unknown-word inputs, and batch sizes 1 and 2, and checks that the known sentence's embedding doesn't change. All 8 cases fail on main and pass with this change.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/modules/test_word_embeddings.py -q`: 13 passed.
- `pre-commit run --files` on the changed files: ruff check, ruff format, and typos passed.

title: Export whole model with transformers.exporters
body:
Export and load the whole model (transformer, pooling, normalization,...) as a single graph with                                     
  `transformers.exporters`,  instead of exporting only the Transformer module. Current support include `backend="onnx"` and `backend="openvino"` but more could be added in the future. 

 Models exported by earlier versions of sentence-transformers only contain the Transformer module, in an `onnx/` or `openvino/` subfolder. They still load, through Optimum as before, with a deprecation warning asking to re-export (asking to loading them with `model_kwargs={"export": True}` to export the whole model instead). If no legacy file is found, `load_onnx_model` / `load_openvino_model` now raise instead of exporting a Transformer-only model.


  ```python
  from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

  # Exports the whole model the first time it is loaded
  model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", backend="onnx")
  model.save("all-MiniLM-L6-v2-onnx")

  # The saved export (export.json + the graph) is loaded as is, nothing is exported again
  model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2-onnx", backend="onnx")
  ```

Quantize while exporting, by passing an export config with a quantizer (ONNX Runtime or NNCF officially supported). The backend will be inferred from the `export_config` when provided.

  ```python
  from transformers.exporters import OnnxConfig, OnnxRuntimeDynamicConfig, OnnxRuntimeQuantizer

  export_config = OnnxConfig(dynamic=True, quantizer=OnnxRuntimeQuantizer(OnnxRuntimeDynamicConfig()))
  model = SentenceTransformer(
      "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
      model_kwargs={"export_config": export_config},  # backend="onnx" is inferred
  )
  model.save("all-MiniLM-L6-v2-onnx-int8")
  ```
 
  ## Changes
  
- `sentence_transformers/backend/export.py`: export the model as one graph (`export`), the runtime wrapper that runs it and saves it (`ExportedModule`), detecting and loading a saved export (`has_export_config`, `load_exported_model`, tracked by an `export.json` manifest that also stores the export format)
- `BaseModel`: loads an ONNX or OpenVINO model if exists or exports the model if there is none.
- `Transformer`: the PyTorch model is not loaded when a converted model is loaded (`_skip_torch_model`), and the export-only `model_kwargs` (`export`, `export_config`)
- `backend` can be inferred by the `export_config`if provided


merging blockers : requires https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/48986

title: Optional probability-target validation for SoftmaxLoss
body:
Floating-point class probabilities passed to SoftmaxLoss can have the right shape and still be an invalid distribution. Negative values, non-finite values, and rows that do not sum to 1 still produce a finite loss, so training continues on bad soft labels.

## Pull Request overview

SoftmaxLoss accepts validate_probability_targets, default False, and stores it in get_config_dict. When the flag is on, num_labels is greater than 1, and labels is a floating-point tensor shaped like the logits, the detached targets are checked and left unchanged: every value must be finite and non-negative, and each row sum in float64 must pass torch.isclose against 1 at rtol 0, with atol 1e-4 for dtypes at least as precise as float32 and eps/4 for float16 and bfloat16. The lowest failing row raises ValueError naming that constraint. Integer class labels, scalar labels, shape mismatches, and the default flag still follow the previous path into the loss function.

## Validation

The SoftmaxLoss test module completed with 11 passed tests and 1 skipped test.

Fixes #4125

body:
`MatryoshkaLoss` truncates the token embeddings to each Matryoshka dimension along with the sentence embeddings. The Matryoshka dimensions are sentence embedding dimensions (they're checked against `model.get_embedding_dimension()`), but the token embeddings can be narrower than the sentence embedding, for example with concatenated pooling modes like `Pooling(dim, ("mean", "max"))` or a `Dense` layer that projects up. Training such a model fails on the first step:

```
ValueError: Dimension 256 in matryoshka_dims cannot be greater than the model's embedding dimension: 128
```

even though the model's embedding dimension is 256. The same model and dimensions already train with gradient caching losses such as `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss`, because that path only truncates the sentence embeddings.

I removed the token embedding truncation. None of the Sentence Transformer losses read token embeddings, so models that already worked get the same loss values.

Validation:

- `sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors` with an added `Dense(128, 256)`, trained for 3 steps on CPU with `MatryoshkaLoss(model, MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model), [256, 128, 64])`: main raises the error above on the first step. With this change the training loss goes 3.296, 2.974, 2.711.
- On small `WordEmbeddings` models with mean + max pooling and with an up-projecting `Dense` layer, `MatryoshkaLoss` with `[16, 8]` raises the same `ValueError` on main for `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss`. With this change it gives the same loss as with `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss` (2.18635 and 2.558578).
- The new `test_matryoshka_dims_can_exceed_token_embedding_dimension` covers both model shapes and compares the loss and its gradients with in-batch cross-entropy on the truncated sentence embeddings. Both cases fail on main and pass with this change.
- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses -q`: 446 passed, 52 skipped (they need CUDA, MPS, or Pillow and torchvision).
- `pre-commit run --files` on the changed files: Ruff check, Ruff format, and typos passed.

I used AI assistance to find, fix, and test this bug.

title: [fix] Keep LambdaLoss pairs that cross the top-k cutoff
body:
With `k` set, `LambdaLoss` and `RankNetLoss` only use document pairs where both documents are in the model's top `k`. A relevant document ranked below the cutoff loses all of its pairs, so nothing pushes it up. If it's the only relevant document for the query, the loss and its gradients are exactly zero. `k=1` never trains, because the only pair left is the top document with itself.

The [LambdaLoss paper](https://marc.najork.org/papers/cikm2018.pdf) truncates the loss for NDCG@k with the indicator `I(i <= k or j <= k)` (Section 6.2, Eq. 18), so a pair counts when at least one of its documents is in the top k. TF-Ranking, from the same authors, does the same: its [LambdaLoss pair mask](https://github.com/tensorflow/ranking/blob/5b1d1338c1cb76507466d062e2d48bae57b17ac4/tensorflow_ranking/python/losses_impl.py#L339-L344) is `logical_or(ranks <= topn)` and cites Eq. 18. The `[:k, :k]` mask here is the same as in allRank's `lambdaLoss`, which this implementation follows. I changed the mask to the paper's rule and described it in the `k` docstrings of both losses. `k=None` is unchanged.

With `cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce` on CPU, one query with five documents, and the model's lowest-ranked document labeled as the only relevant one:

| Loss | `k` | main: loss / grad norm | this PR: loss / grad norm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `LambdaLoss` | None | 3.7415 / 71.63 | 3.7415 / 71.63 |
| `LambdaLoss` | 1 | 0 / 0 | 4.8833 / 93.83 |
| `LambdaLoss` | 3 | 0 / 0 | 3.0231 / 56.59 |
| `RankNetLoss` | None | 2.4611 / 44.91 | 2.4611 / 44.91 |
| `RankNetLoss` | 1 | 0 / 0 | 4.6446 / 89.24 |
| `RankNetLoss` | 3 | 0 / 0 | 2.7551 / 51.16 |

The loss with `k` can be higher than with `k=None` because it averages over fewer pairs, and the pairs it keeps include the one with the top-ranked document.

Validation:

- Three new tests in `tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_misc.py` compare the loss and its gradients with float64 references. With `k=1`, a relevant third document is still paired with the first document but not with the second. With `k=2` on four documents, `RankNetLoss` keeps every ordered pair except the one ranked entirely below the cutoff. All three fail on main and pass with this change.
- `pytest tests/cross_encoder/losses -q`: 122 passed, 7 skipped (the skipped tests need CUDA).
- `pre-commit run --files` on the changed files: Ruff check, Ruff format, and typos passed.

I used AI assistance to find, fix, and test this bug.

title: [fix] Keep string features whole in encode(output_value=None)
body:
I fixed `SentenceTransformer.encode(output_value=None)` returning a wrong `"modality"` value and crashing on larger batches. When it splits the batch's features into one dict per input, it indexed every value with `value[idx]` and only kept values whole when that raised `TypeError`. The `Transformer` module's `"modality": "text"` is a string, so indexing it returned one character per input: `"t"` for the first text, `"e"` for the second, and so on, and a batch of five or more texts raised `IndexError: string index out of range`.

I now carry string values into each dict unchanged; everything else is split as before. `MultiVectorEncoder.encode(output_value=None)` already carries strings as-is.

On CPU with `sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors`, `model.encode(["hello"] * n, batch_size=n, output_value=None)` gives:

| `n` | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `["t"]` | `["text"]` |
| 2 | `["t", "e"]` | `["text", "text"]` |
| 5 | `IndexError: string index out of range` | `["text"] * 5` |

title: Stabilize PListMLE position weights for long ranking lists
body:
### Summary

Keep the default PListMLE position weights finite for long ranking lists.

### Problem

A query with 129 or more documents produces NaN loss and gradients, even for scores between -1 and 1. This affects training on long lists; the original PListMLE paper evaluates datasets averaging about 700 and 1,000 documents per query. #4165 contains a runnable reproducer and a real-model check.

### Root Cause

The default `2 ** (num_docs - rank) - 1` weights overflow float32 before the loss normalizes each row. The resulting `inf / inf` is NaN. This remains after #4012 (score normalization) and #4051 (one-based ranks).

### Solution

For long lists, remove a shared power of two before exponentiation:

```text
scale = max(num_docs - 127, 0)
weight = 2 ** (num_docs - rank - scale) - 2 ** (-scale)
```

This preserves relative weights and keeps the float32 row sum finite. Lists of up to 127 documents retain their exact previous weights. The public helper starts returning rescaled absolute weights at 128 documents; its return documentation now explains this. Custom weight functions are unchanged.

### Validation

- New regression cases on unmodified main: **6 failed, 7 passed**. Failures cover lengths 129, 200, and 1,000 in both ordering modes.
- Complete `tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_misc.py`: **109 passed, 6 skipped**. CUDA float16 model tests are skipped on this machine.
- Regression tests compare loss and parameter gradients against independent float64 suffix cross-entropies with Python integer weights. They include long/short mixed batches and the 127/128/129 boundary.
- Real CPU CrossEncoder, 200+3 document batch: NaN loss and gradients before; loss `2.822076`, all 41 parameter gradients finite, and a finite optimizer step after.
- MPS forward/backward checks at lengths 128, 129, 200, and 1,000: finite weights, losses, and gradients.
- Changed-file pre-commit: Ruff, formatting, and typos all pass. Separate automated numerical review found no blocking issue.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_misc.py -q -rs --tb=short
pre-commit run --files sentence_transformers/cross_encoder/losses/plist_mle.py tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_misc.py
```

### Related Issues

Fixes #4165.

### Additional Notes

Discovered through code analysis and verified using the native package. Tested on macOS arm64, Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.10.0, and Transformers 5.19.0. The full repository suite and CUDA were not run. This addresses the standard float32 weight path; the existing limitation with a global `torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float16)` is outside this change.

Codex assisted with investigation, implementation, tests, and a separate automated review.

title: Treat a string positive or negative as one document in RerankingEvaluator
body:
`RerankingEvaluator` expects `positive` and `negative` to be lists. When a sample gives a single document as a string, the evaluator extends `all_docs` with it character by character and counts it with `len()`. So it embeds single characters as documents, and the scores are wrong without an error or a warning. This also happens when you pass a (query, positive, negative) triplet dataset, the most common training format, directly as `samples`:

```python
from datasets import Dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.evaluation import RerankingEvaluator

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
rows = [
    {"query": "What sound does a cat make?", "positive": "Cats meow.", "negative": "Dogs bark loudly at night."},
    {"query": "What is the capital of France?", "positive": "Paris is the capital of France.", "negative": "Berlin is in Germany."},
]
as_lists = [{"query": r["query"], "positive": [r["positive"]], "negative": [r["negative"]]} for r in rows]

RerankingEvaluator(as_lists, name="dev")(model)              # dev_map 0.750, dev_mrr@10 0.750, dev_ndcg@10 0.815
RerankingEvaluator(Dataset.from_list(rows), name="dev")(model)  # dev_map 0.428, dev_ndcg@10 0.363
```

The wrong scores depend on how the model embeds single characters, so they can differ between devices. With only `positive` as a string, the scores are also wrong. Both `use_batched_encoding=True` and `False` are affected.

This wraps a string `positive` or `negative` in a list in `__init__`, the same way `CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator` already handles a string positive (covered by `test_string_positive`). List inputs are unchanged. `SparseRerankingEvaluator` and `MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator` call this `__init__`, so they get the fix too. I updated the docstrings of `RerankingEvaluator` and `SparseRerankingEvaluator`.

I found this through code analysis, not in actual use. I did not find an issue or pull request about it. The open PRs on reranking evaluators (#4054, #4077) change `CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator` only.

**Tests**

New `tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_reranking_evaluator.py`: for both `use_batched_encoding` values, string documents (a list of dicts and a `Dataset`) give the same scores as the same documents in lists.

- `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_evaluators.py tests/cross_encoder/evaluation -m "not slow"` (with `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`): on `main`, the 2 new tests fail; with this change they pass, and the other results are the same (103 passed, 1 skipped). In both runs, the 2 NanoBEIR tests fail because they need to download datasets.
- I also checked `SparseRerankingEvaluator` with string documents against the same documents in lists.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` on the changed files: passed.

AI assistance: Claude Code helped me find this bug and write the fix and the test.

title: Restore autocast state during GradCache embedding replay
body:
GradCache saves embeddings inside autocast, but its backward hook can recompute them in FP32 after the caller leaves that context. Restoring dropout RNG alone then fails to reproduce the embeddings or their parameter Jacobians. This affects custom PyTorch AMP loops and the public `old_fit(use_amp=True)` path; modern Trainer/Accelerate normally wraps `model.forward` in its own autocast context.

Capture autocast enabled/dtype/weight-cache state alongside each mini-batch's RNG snapshot, and restore CPU and supported accelerator contexts during recomputation. Reuse PyTorch checkpoint's compatibility helper and preserve the existing surrogate precision and backward scaling code.

Found through source analysis and reproduced with the real tiny BERT fixture plus a Dense layer. Validation:

- CPU related suites (`test_gradcache.py`, `test_cached_gist_embed.py`, `test_cached_splade.py`, and CrossEncoder `test_cached_multiple_negatives_ranking.py`): 86 passed, 3 CUDA-only cases skipped. Three new CPU regressions fail on unchanged upstream.
- RTX 5090, PyTorch 2.12.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0: `python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gradcache.py -q` reports 46 passed, no skips. Both new CUDA FP16/BF16 cases fail on upstream and pass with the patch.
- Real CUDA and MPS FP16/BF16 replay, with weight caching enabled/disabled: identical dtype and bitwise-identical embeddings after the fix; CPU/device RNG state is preserved. Exception restoration is covered too.
- With weight caching disabled, unscaled CUDA FP16/BF16 gradients exactly match ordinary MNRL. An eight-step real AMP/GradScaler loop starting at scale 128 completes all eight updates in both arms: BF16 updates match exactly; FP16 relative update difference is 0.0155%.
- Repository-pinned Ruff check/format, typos, and `git diff --check`: passed.

Numerical limits: cached and ordinary backward retain different low-precision accumulation/scaling orders. Default weight caching still produces rounding differences; in the native eight-step BF16 fixture the relative update difference is 1.75% after this change versus 1.05% before. Native FP16 GradScaler also skips different numbers of steps at its default initial scale. These results establish correct embedding replay, not general multi-step training equivalence or improved convergence/performance.

PyTorch 2.2 helper compatibility was source-reviewed, not runtime-tested. An existing CrossEncoder prompt-replay exact-equality test fails on MPS identically on upstream and patched source and passes on CPU. The full repository and multi-GPU suites were not run.

OpenAI Codex assisted with investigation, implementation, regression tests, independent review, and this description.

title: Fix mean pooling precision and flattened CLS prompt exclusion
body:
Hello!

Heads up, this PR was AI-generated and human-reviewed.

## Pull Request overview

* Fix half-precision accumulation in padded mean pooling
* Respect prompt exclusion in flattened CLS pooling

## Details

While reviewing #4104, I found two more differences between padded and flattened pooling. Padded `mean` and `mean_sqrt_len_tokens` can overflow their FP16 sums even when the final result is representable. Flattened `cls` also ignores prompt exclusion, selecting the original first token instead of the first token after the prompt.

I've kept mean-pooling masking in the input dtype and accumulated the sums and denominators in FP32 for FP16/BF16 inputs. This avoids a full FP32 token-embedding intermediate and preserves output dtypes, including fractional results for integer inputs. I've also applied the prompt offset to flattened CLS selection and removed the batch-wide prompt-length clamp and its CPU/GPU synchronization.

The pooling tests pass locally with 393 passed on CPU and CUDA. Six live Flash Attention integration tests were excluded because FlashAttention2 isn't installed. The tests cover values, gradients, precision, dtype promotion, and left/right padding.

I benchmarked isolated padded mean pooling against main on an RTX 3090 with Torch 2.10, FP16 inputs, dimension 768, and eager execution. These are medians of three timed runs in microseconds. Sequence lengths vary between half the listed maximum and that maximum.

| Batch size | Maximum length | Forward, before to after | Forward + backward, before to after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 256 | 87 to 96 | 335 to 383 |
| 32 | 256 | 125 to 88 | 340 to 396 |
| 32 | 1024 | 434 to 224 | 578 to 470 |

CPU FP32 improved across these shapes. Short-sequence CUDA training still has about 15 to 16% pooling overhead, roughly 50 microseconds per batch. These are pooling-only measurements, not end-to-end model timings.

- Tom Aarsen

title: Fix CI NumPy conflict by excluding pyctcdecode
body:
﻿Hello!

Heads up, this PR was AI-generated and human-reviewed.

* Exclude `pyctcdecode` from CI on all Python versions

Python 3.11 and 3.12 CI jobs fail during test collection because `transformers[audio]` pulls in `pyctcdecode`, which pins `numpy<2`, while PyArrow 26 requires NumPy 2 at runtime. I've checked the exclusion script for all four Python versions and verified dependency resolution with PyArrow 26 and NumPy 2 for Python 3.11 and 3.12 on Linux. The full test suite still needs to run in CI. This change only affects CI, leaving package dependencies unchanged.

title: Add per-batch CPU tensor offloading to MultiVectorEncoder
body:
Closes #4152.

`MultiVectorEncoder` currently keeps tensor outputs on the model device, while its CPU-output option converts them to NumPy and upcasts bfloat16. The reported long-document retrieval workflow needs CPU tensors with their original dtype.

Add opt-in `save_to_cpu=True` to `encode`, `encode_query`, and `encode_document`, reusing the existing per-batch transfer. Defaults and existing positional arguments are unchanged. NumPy output still forces CPU transfer. Raw feature dictionaries also move their tensors to CPU, after any token pooling. The option is forwarded through the existing multi-process and distributed inference paths.

A minimal example (the new argument raises `ValueError` on the current main):

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder

model = MultiVectorEncoder("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors").to(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
embeddings = model.encode_document(["short", "a longer document"], batch_size=1, save_to_cpu=True)
assert all(emb.device.type == "cpu" and emb.dtype == torch.bfloat16 for emb in embeddings)
```

## Validation

Validated commit `140eb37034d1cbfb4140e8fcef8c385213688d69` on both macOS/MPS and an RTX 5090. The GPU checkout's 813 files were checked against the submitted source hashes.

```bash
  tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_multi_process.py \
  tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_token_pooling.py -q -rs
python -m pre_commit run --all-files
git diff --check
```

- **Default related suite: 177 passed, 3 skipped** on each platform after installing `fastcluster`. On macOS the skips are two CUDA cases and the existing PEFT test; on Linux they are two MPS cases and that PEFT test. The new CUDA transfer tests both passed on the RTX 5090, and the corresponding MPS cases passed locally. Repository-pinned lint, formatting and typo checks passed.
- **Expanded Linux validation: 181 passed, 2 MPS skips**, including all three marked-slow tests (Qwen2-VL preprocessing, PaliGemma image-document encoding, and mixed CPU/CUDA multiprocessing). Its original two save/reload checks passed with PEFT 0.21.2. The same unchanged test also passed on both upstream and this PR locally with PEFT 0.21.1. The repository's PEFT skip marker is unchanged.

title: Fix backward for sparse pairwise Euclidean similarity
body:
Discovered through code analysis and reproduced on current main (`ff694867`, 6.2.0.dev0), with Python 3.13.16 and PyTorch 2.14.1 on macOS arm64 CPU.

`pairwise_euclidean_sim` computes correct forward scores for sparse COO embeddings, but backward fails. This also breaks `TripletLoss.compute_loss_from_embeddings` when supplied sparse embeddings, even when the hinge loss is zero:

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers.util import pairwise_euclidean_sim

a = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [4., 6.]], requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [1., 2.]], requires_grad=True)
scores = pairwise_euclidean_sim(a.to_sparse(), b.to_sparse())  # [0, -5]
scores.sum().backward()
# RuntimeError: Sparse division requires a scalar or zero-dim dense tensor divisor
```

The sparse path now uses the autograd-supported `torch.sparse.sum`, converts only the reduced norms to dense, and masks zero norms before taking the square root. This avoids unsupported sparse backward operations and gives identical embeddings a finite zero subgradient. Dense floating-point and integer paths are unchanged. Related to #4033, which explicitly left sparse backward outside its scope.

### Validation

The new regressions cover batched and single embeddings, both mixed layouts, empty rows, duplicate COO entries that cancel, analytical nonzero gradients, and active/inactive triplet losses. The regression-and-control selection gave **9 failed, 16 passed before** the fix.

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 python -m pytest \
  tests/util/test_similarity.py tests/util/test_tensor.py \
  tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_triplet.py -q \
  -k 'not test_pairwise_angle_sim_even_and_odd_sparse_embeddings'
```

Result: **158 passed, 5 CUDA-only skips, 1 model-dependent test deselected**. Pinned Ruff 0.15.6 lint/format checks, typos 1.45.0, and `git diff --check` passed on the changed files. The source distribution and wheel built successfully.

title: Fix MaxSim memory use for long query batches
body:
Fixes #4151.

A long query could push late-interaction retrieval batches over `chunk_elements`. MaxSim padded every query to the longest one and always scored at least one document, leaving the scoring intermediate unbounded.

This chunks queries and documents separately, counting both padded inputs and the 4D intermediate against the budget. Query chunks are sized against the widest document. Documents are processed again for each query chunk, and a single pair can still exceed the budget. With 200 16-token queries, one 2,000-token query and four 1,000-token documents (dim 128, fp16, budget 10M), extra peak allocated CUDA memory fell from 869.7 MiB to 18.3 MiB, with identical scores.

Shared masks and padding dtypes behave as before.

Added budget, gradient, mask and dtype regressions. `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/util/test_similarity.py` passes. The offline full-suite run had existing failures and missing model fixtures.

Assisted by Claude/Codex.

title: [fix] Raise a clear error when int8/uint8 ranges come from a single embedding
body:
## Description

Follows up on @tomaarsen's closing comment on #4128 (https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/pull/4128#issuecomment-6036891401), which suggested a clear diagnostic instead of silently quantizing a single embedding into one bucket. This is also the behavior reported in #2837.

When `quantize_embeddings` has to compute int8 or uint8 ranges from the embeddings themselves and only one embedding is given, every dimension gets the same minimum and maximum. All values then land in a single bucket, so the output is all `-128` (int8) or all `0` (uint8) and carries no information. Today this only logs the generic "more stable with more embeddings" warning.

The most common way to hit this is encoding a single text with a scalar precision:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors")
print(model.encode("A man is eating food.", precision="int8"))
# main: [-128 -128 -128 ... -128]
```

This PR raises a `ValueError` in that case instead:

```
ValueError: Cannot compute int8 quantization ranges from a single embedding, as every dimension would collapse
into a single bucket. Call `quantize_embeddings` with `ranges` or `calibration_embeddings` computed from a
representative set of embeddings instead.
```

I found this while testing single input paths across the encode APIs, and confirmed it with the snippet above.

## Change

* `quantize_embeddings` raises when ranges would be computed from a 1D embedding or a single row, and neither `ranges` nor `calibration_embeddings` is given. The message points to `quantize_embeddings` since `encode` does not accept calibration arguments.
* With `ranges` or `calibration_embeddings`, a single embedding quantizes exactly as before. Two or more embeddings without calibration also behave as before (including the existing warning below 100 embeddings).
* Documented the new `ValueError` under `Raises`.

**Behavior change:** calls that previously returned a constant all `-128` / all `0` array now raise. I believe this is acceptable because that output could not be used for search, but I am happy to downgrade it to a warning if you prefer.

The documented workflows in `examples/sentence_transformer/applications/embedding-quantization/` all pass `calibration_embeddings`, so they are unaffected.

## Tests

Added `test_scalar_quantize_single_embedding_without_calibration_raises` (1D and `(1, dim)` inputs, int8 and uint8; fails on `main`) and `test_scalar_quantize_single_embedding_with_calibration` (guards the valid single embedding path via `ranges` and `calibration_embeddings`).

```
pytest tests/util/test_quantization.py tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py
638 passed, 9 skipped

pytest tests/sentence_transformer/test_multi_process.py tests/multi_vector_encoder -k "int8 or uint8 or quantiz or precision"
3 passed, 2 skipped

ruff check / ruff format --check on the changed files: passed
```

Environment: Windows 11, Python 3.14.0, torch 2.14.1 (CPU), transformers 5.18.0. GPU and multi process tests that are skipped on this machine were not run.

## AI disclosure

I used Claude Code to help search the codebase, write the tests and draft this description. I reviewed every changed line and verified the results above myself.

title: [fix] Normalize a single sparse embedding as one vector in normalize_embeddings
body:
## Description

`SparseEncoder.encode()` returns a 1D sparse tensor for a single input. `normalize_embeddings` treats the only axis of such a tensor as the row axis, so every value gets its own "row norm" and is divided by its own magnitude. The result is a vector of signs instead of a unit vector.

This makes `pairwise_cos_sim`, and therefore `SparseEncoder.similarity_pairwise` with `similarity_fn_name = "cosine"`, silently return wrong scores for single embeddings. Both methods document `[embedding_dim]` shaped inputs as supported. `cos_sim` is not affected because it adds a batch axis first.

## Reproducer

```python
from sentence_transformers import SparseEncoder

model = SparseEncoder("sparse-encoder-testing/splade-bert-tiny-nq")
model.similarity_fn_name = "cosine"
query = model.encode("What is the capital of France?")
doc = model.encode("Paris is the capital of France.")

print(model.similarity_pairwise(query, doc))  # tensor(64.) on main
print(model.similarity(query, doc))           # tensor([[0.9705]])
```

After this change both calls return `0.9705`.

I found this through code analysis while reading `util/tensor.py`, then confirmed it with the snippet above.

## Change

For a 1D sparse input, all stored values are assigned to a single row, so they share one norm. The 2D path is unchanged.

Related work:
* #4076 fixed the dense 1D case and deliberately left the sparse path as it was. This PR covers that remaining case.
* #4045 (open) fixes the dtype of the same accumulator. The two changes touch neighbouring lines but are independent; whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase.

## Tests

Added `test_normalize_embeddings_single_sparse_vector` and `test_pairwise_cos_sim_single_sparse_vectors`. Both fail on `main` and pass with the fix.

```
pytest tests/util/test_tensor.py tests/util/test_similarity.py
122 passed, 8 skipped

pytest tests/sparse_encoder/test_model.py tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation
369 passed

ruff check / ruff format --check on the changed files: passed
```

Environment: Windows 11, Python 3.14.0, torch 2.14.1 (CPU), transformers 5.18.0. GPU tests were not run.
