title: Detect IR evaluator cutoff ties without full-size temporaries
body:
### Problem

Since ties are broken by `corpus_id` (110bb37e, first released in v5.7.0), `InformationRetrievalEvaluator` uses about 4x the peak memory it used before when the corpus contains exact duplicates. Per corpus chunk it now:

1. counts `(pair_scores >= thresholds).sum(dim=1)`, which materialises a `(queries x chunk)` integer temporary, and
2. if any query has a tie at the top-k cutoff, builds two more `(queries x chunk)` int64 key matrices for **every** query, not only the tied ones.

With Q = C = 32,000 that is ~4 GB of scores plus ~16 GB of temporaries. On a 16 GB laptop the evaluation starts swapping; on smaller machines it can be killed. Exact duplicates are common in real corpora (Natural Questions below: 3,897 duplicate answers in the first 32k rows), so the tie path triggers in practice.

How it was found: through automated scaling tests (time and peak memory per doubling of input size), not in actual use. I then measured it on real data, below.

Reproducer (CPU, ~1 min; prints the peak memory added during the evaluation):

```python
import threading, time

import psutil
from datasets import load_dataset

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.evaluation import InformationRetrievalEvaluator

n = 32_000
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1", device="cpu")
nq = load_dataset("sentence-transformers/natural-questions", split=f"train[:{n}]")
queries = {f"q{i}": text for i, text in enumerate(nq["query"])}
corpus = {f"d{i}": text for i, text in enumerate(nq["answer"])}  # contains exact duplicates
relevant_docs = {f"q{i}": {f"d{i}"} for i in range(n)}
evaluator = InformationRetrievalEvaluator(queries, corpus, relevant_docs, batch_size=512, write_csv=False)

process = psutil.Process()
start, peak, running = process.memory_info().rss, [0], [True]

def watch():
    while running[0]:
        peak[0] = max(peak[0], process.memory_info().rss)
        time.sleep(0.01)

thread = threading.Thread(target=watch)
thread.start()
evaluator(model)
running[0] = False
thread.join()
print(f"peak +{(peak[0] - start) / 2**30:.2f} GB")  # main: ~20.5 GB, v5.6.1 and this PR: ~5.1-5.5 GB
```

### Change

- Ask `topk` for one extra candidate. More than `top_k` scores reach the cutoff exactly when that candidate equals the `top_k`-th score, so no full-size comparison or count is needed.
- Reselect only the tied rows, in blocks of 1024, so the int64 keys stay small next to the score matrix.

The tie-break order is unchanged: the same `(-score, corpus_id)` keys, applied to the same rows.

### Measurements

Kaggle CPU (4 cores), `sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1`, `sentence-transformers/natural-questions` (first N queries and their answers), Q = C = N, default settings, one fresh process per point, peak RSS above the start of the evaluation:

| N | v5.6.1 (before tie-break) | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8,000 | 0.67 GB, 5.2 s | 1.49 GB, 6.1 s | 0.72 GB, 5.1 s |
| 16,000 | 1.69 GB, 12.1 s | 5.35 GB, 16.1 s | 1.77 GB, 12.1 s |
| 32,000 | 5.12 GB, 32.0 s | **20.55 GB**, 48.0 s | **5.48 GB**, 37.0 s |
| 50,000 | n/a | not run (would exceed the machine's RAM) | 11.84 GB, 73.3 s |

Metrics of main and this PR are identical at every N (the v5.6.1 metrics differ slightly, as expected, because v5.6.1 did not break ties by corpus id).

### Validation

- **Equivalence with main:** 40 random tie-heavy setups on Kaggle (exact duplicate documents, queries equal to documents, mixed id formats, `corpus_chunk_size` in {7, 50, 333, 50000}, k values up to 100 including chunks smaller than k) plus 120 more locally: metrics **and** the per-query `write_predictions` files are byte-identical to main in all 160.
- **Tests:** `tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_information_retrieval_evaluator.py` passes on Linux (Kaggle) for main and this PR. Two tests added:
  - `test_tie_reselection_only_builds_keys_for_tied_queries`: one tied query among nine; the reselection keys must cover only that row. Fails on main (54 key entries instead of at most 6), passes here.
  - `test_ranking_follows_score_then_corpus_id`: mixed tied/untied queries, `corpus_chunk_size` 1 to 100 (including chunks smaller than `top_k`); predictions must follow `(-score, corpus_id)`. Passes on main and here (pins the behaviour this PR must keep).
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on the changed files.

Command used for the tests:
```
pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_information_retrieval_evaluator.py
```

Not run: the full test suite, and GPU. The change is device-agnostic (row indices are created on `pair_scores.device`).

### Limitations

- The score matrix itself is still `(queries x corpus_chunk_size)`; this PR only removes the extra temporaries added with the tie-break. Users with many queries can still lower `corpus_chunk_size`.
- If a score is NaN, `torch.topk` ranks it differently from the previous `>=` comparison, so tie detection could differ for NaN rows. I did not find a way NaN scores arise from the built-in score functions.

Related: #4147 changes three other lines in the same file (corpus model handling); there is no overlap with this change.

### AI disclosure

Claude (Anthropic) wrote the scaling and equivalence harness, this change and the tests. I reviewed every line, checked the equivalence argument, and ran the measurements above on Kaggle.

title: Fix sparse IR evaluation ignoring corpus model and embeddings
body:
`SparseInformationRetrievalEvaluator` accepts `corpus_model` and `corpus_embeddings` through its inherited call interface, but drops the arguments before delegating to the base evaluator. Evaluating a query encoder against a separate document encoder or a precomputed document index therefore silently uses the query encoder for the corpus instead, which can report the wrong retrieval metrics.

This was discovered through source review. The regression test builds real `SparseEncoder` models with a local tokenizer and static token weights. For the query `alpha beta`, the query encoder ranks the irrelevant `alpha` document first (scores 4 and 1), while the supplied corpus encoder or its cached embeddings rank the relevant `beta` document first (scores 0 and 2). Before the fix, NDCG@1 is 0.0 instead of 1.0 for both positional and keyword corpus overrides. This represents evaluating a changing query encoder against a fixed document encoder/index; the test uses no downloaded models or datasets.

Forward the call arguments, collect corpus sparsity/FLOPS statistics when embeddings are supplied, and select sparse COO corpus chunks with `index_select` instead of unsupported tensor slicing. The tests cover separate encoders, precomputed COO/dense embeddings, both argument styles, two chunk sizes, and evaluator reuse without an override.

Validation on Python 3.13.15, PyTorch 2.14.0 and Transformers 5.17.0, against main `ff69486771998c07008ebd3c7e05e827f03df46f`:

- `python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation/test_information_retrieval_evaluator.py -q`: all 12 new cases fail on the unmodified source and pass with the fix.
- `python -m pytest tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation/test_information_retrieval_evaluator.py tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_information_retrieval_evaluator.py -q`: 17 passed.
- `pre-commit run --files sentence_transformers/sentence_transformer/evaluation/information_retrieval.py sentence_transformers/sparse_encoder/evaluation/sparse_information_retrieval.py tests/sparse_encoder/evaluation/test_information_retrieval_evaluator.py`: Ruff check, Ruff format, and typos passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

Validation was CPU-only; the full repository and GPU suites were not run. AI assistance was used to investigate the cause, implement the fix and regression tests, and draft this description.

title: Fail fast when a multi-process pool worker dies
body:
`encode(..., pool=pool)` hangs forever if a pool worker dies without raising, e.g. when it is killed by a signal. Workers that raise are already reported through the results queue (#3920), but a dead worker reports nothing, so `_multi_process` waits on `output_queue.get()` for a chunk that never arrives.

I found this while debugging a job that hung after a worker hit a CUDA OOM (was fixed in #3920).

### Changes
`BaseModel._get_worker_result` replaces the bare `output_queue.get()`. It polls the queue and raises `RuntimeError: N multi-process pool worker(s) died unexpectedly ...` if a worker has died.

title: Flatten (n, 1) labels in losses that take one label per row
body:
While messing around with the proposed loss update in #4030, I noticed that `CoSENTLoss` doesn't handle labels of shape `(n, 1)`, which is what a score column of one-element lists gets collated to. `labels[:, None] < labels[None, :]` broadcasts the mask to `(n, n, n)`, and the loss ends up pushing the scores of the higher-labelled pairs down. There's no error thrown meaning that it can silently corrupt training. Checking the other losses that take one label per row indicated there's the same problem in a few more places.

I compared each loss on the same batch with labels of shape `(n,)` and `(n, 1)`:

| Loss | Impact |
|---|---|
| `CoSENTLoss`, `AnglELoss`, `SparseCoSENTLoss`, `SparseAnglELoss` | Gradient points the wrong way |
| `ContrastiveLoss` |  `(n, 1) * (n,)` broadcasts to n×n, so every pair trains towards the batch's mean label |
| `BatchHardTripletLoss`, `BatchHardSoftMarginTripletLoss`, `BatchAllTripletLoss` | The label masks are built at the wrong shape |
| CrossEncoder `MSELoss` | Only a broadcast warning from torch |
| `OnlineContrastiveLoss`, `BatchSemiHardTripletLoss`, n-tuple `AnglELoss`, CrossEncoder `BinaryCrossEntropyLoss` | Shape error |

Realistically, this mostly affects `ContrastiveLoss` and the CrossEncoder `MSELoss`, since pair and score datasets are where `(n, 1)` labels tend to show up. Class labels for triplet losses stored as one-element lists seem far less likely.

`CosineSimilarityLoss` and `SoftmaxLoss` already handle this by calling `labels.view(-1)` inside the loss, with no validation. This PR does the same at the top of each loss in the table. Any other label count still raises a shape error.

## Testing

`tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_label_shapes.py` and `tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_label_shapes.py` check that `(n, 1)` labels give the same loss and gradients as `(n,)` for every loss above, and that `(n, 2)` labels still raise. The 13 equivalence tests fail on main as expected.

title: Fix half-precision overflow in padded mean pooling
body:
Padded `mean` and `mean_sqrt_len_tokens` pooling can return infinity even when the final embedding is representable. For 1,024 float16 token embeddings equal to 100, their expected outputs are 100 and 3,200; both currently return infinity. Excluding every token can also return NaN when the denominator guard underflows.

Accumulate and divide half/bfloat16 inputs in float32, then restore the expected output dtype. Preserve external normalizer dtype promotion and perform its clamp/square root in the accumulation dtype. This extends the approach in #4106 to the remaining padded mean variants; weighted and flattened pooling are unchanged.

Discovered through code analysis and reproduced on CPU using the public module, without a model download:

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.modules import Pooling

for mode in ("mean", "mean_sqrt_len_tokens"):
    features = {"token_embeddings": torch.full((1, 1024, 1), 100, dtype=torch.float16)}
    print(mode, Pooling(1, pooling_mode=mode)(features)["sentence_embedding"])
# Before: inf, inf. After: 100, 3200 (both float16).
```

title: Fix community_detection to drop communities whose centre was already claimed
body:
## Problem

`community_detection` can emit an invalid residual community when a high-scoring candidate centre has already been claimed by an earlier community. The current loop removes already-extracted members but continues processing the remaining tail, even though that candidate is no longer a valid centre.

For the reproducer in #4140, this produces an extra community whose internal minimum cosine similarity is `0.766`, below the requested threshold of `0.9`.

## Root cause

Communities are processed greedily by candidate score. Once a candidate's centre has been assigned to an earlier community, the entire candidate must be discarded. Filtering only claimed members changes the candidate's centre and violates the threshold guarantee used when the candidate was formed.

## Fix

Before removing claimed members, skip a candidate if its centre has already been claimed. This preserves the greedy centre assignment and prevents a residual tail from being returned as a separate community.

## Tests

Added a deterministic regression test covering the overlapping-candidate case:

- before the fix, the test fails because an extra below-threshold community is returned;
- after the fix, the claimed-centre candidate is dropped and only valid communities remain.

Verification:

- related test suite: 109 passed;
- 1 GPU-only test skipped because CUDA was unavailable;
- `ruff check` passes;
- `ruff format --check` passes;
- remote compare contains only the implementation and regression-test files;
- secret scan found no credentials.

Fixes #4140

title: Size SparseStaticEmbedding.from_json weights by the vocabulary size
body:
`SparseStaticEmbedding.from_json` sizes its weight vector by the largest token id in the IDF file (`max(token_ids) + 1`), not by the vocabulary size. This works when the IDF file has a weight for the last token in the vocabulary. An IDF file that does not contain the highest token ids, for example one computed on your own corpus to build an inference-free SPLADE model, gives a query module with fewer dimensions than the document encoder. Then `similarity()` fails, and `encode_query()` fails for any query with a token id above the maximum in the file:

```python
import json, os, tempfile
from sentence_transformers import SparseEncoder
from sentence_transformers.sparse_encoder.modules import Router, SparseStaticEmbedding, SpladePooling, Transformer

doc_encoder = Transformer("sparse-encoder-testing/splade-bert-tiny-nq", transformer_task="fill-mask")
idf = {"paris": 3.1, "capital": 2.4, "france": 2.9, "spiders": 4.0}
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "idf.json")
with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(idf, f)

query_module = SparseStaticEmbedding.from_json(path, tokenizer=doc_encoder.tokenizer, frozen=True)
print(query_module.get_embedding_dimension())  # 14161, but the vocabulary has 30522 tokens

model = SparseEncoder(modules=[Router.for_query_document([query_module], [doc_encoder, SpladePooling("max")])], device="cpu")
q = model.encode_query("capital of france")
d = model.encode_document("Paris is the capital of France.")
model.similarity(q, d)
# RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (1x14161 and 30522x1)
model.encode_query("zebra")
# RuntimeError: index 29145 is out of bounds for dimension 1 with size 14161
```

This sizes the weights by the tokenizer vocabulary, which is the same size `__init__` uses when no weights are given. Tokens that are not in the IDF file get a weight of 0, as before. The size is never smaller than before, so an IDF file that has a weight for the last token in the vocabulary gives the same weights as before.

I found this through code analysis, not in actual use. I searched the open and closed issues and pull requests and did not find a report or a fix. #4057 changed the same function (the JSON encoding), but not the weight size.

**Tests**

`test_sparse_static_embedding_from_json_partial_vocabulary` in `tests/sparse_encoder/modules/test_sparse_static_embedding.py` loads an IDF file with 3 tokens. It checks that the query module has the vocabulary size, that `similarity()` works with the document embeddings, and that a query with only unknown tokens gives an all-zero embedding.

- `pytest tests/sparse_encoder -m "not slow"` (with `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`): on `main`, the new test fails and 442 tests pass. With this change, 443 tests pass. In both runs, `test_train_stsb` errors because it needs to download a dataset.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `typos` on the changed files: passed.
- I did not run the slow OpenSearch tests in `tests/sparse_encoder/test_opensearch_models.py`, because they download the full models.

AI usage: I used Claude Code to find this bug and write the fix and the test. I reviewed the change and ran the tests locally.

title: Fix TSDAE reconstruction with left padding and shared EOS/PAD
body:
# Fix TSDAE reconstruction with left padding and shared EOS/PAD

## Summary

Discovered through code analysis and reproduced in native TSDAE reconstruction training with variable-length inputs, left padding and shared EOS/PAD tokens. The public Trainer regression covers the affected training workflow.

Use target attention masks to supervise real next-token pairs in `DenoisingAutoEncoderLoss`, and keep its single pooled source representation visible to decoder cross-attention.

A left-padded source can receive zero reconstruction gradient when its first token is padding. Ignoring all labels equal to `pad_token_id` also drops real EOS targets when PAD aliases EOS. For an attended BOS-to-EOS-only target, that produces a NaN loss.

The change selects attended adjacent target pairs with `-100` masking. Eager execution retains the existing unmasked decoder fast path for ordinary right padding, and passes a decoder mask when the actual target mask has a masked position before a real token. This also covers public per-call left-padding overrides when tokenizer defaults still say right. When a target mask is present, compiled execution always passes it to the decoder to avoid a tensor-valued Python branch.

Target preprocessing with `processing_kwargs={"text":{"return_attention_mask":False}}` remains supported and keeps the legacy padding-ID label masking. That route cannot distinguish real EOS from padding when their IDs alias; the docstring makes this limit explicit. Caller tensors, preprocessing options and tokenizer defaults stay unchanged.

The ordinary right-padding rationale in #3268 is preserved. Historical retokenization and tying fixes in #1467 and #3781 are separate changes.

## Validation

Minimal runnable SDPA reproducer: `python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_denoising_auto_encoder_masks.py -k left_padded_source_receives_reconstruction_gradients -q`.

Commands run:
- `python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_denoising_auto_encoder_masks.py -q`
- `python -m pytest tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_denoising_auto_encoder.py tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_denoising_auto_encoder_masks.py -q`
- `make check`
- `git diff --check HEAD`

Results and scope:

- Twenty new native cases on pristine main `d16320793e41be84d4904a92f08e04bb2b8c907f`: 13 failures and 7 passing controls in each tested environment. All 20 pass with the change.
- The complete existing TSDAE test module plus new cases: 27 passed, no skips, on Python 3.12.14 / Transformers 5.19.0, Python 3.13.5 / 5.19.0, and Python 3.12.14 / 5.0.0. All use Torch 2.14.1+cpu.
- Locally saved random BERT and GPT-2 checkpoints load through production constructors. The custom GPT-2 ByteLevel-BPE tokenizer round-trips nonempty text and inserts BOS/text/EOS. This demonstrates a supported checkpoint route with active EOS targets; it does not imply stock GPT-2 tokenization inserts EOS automatically.
- Independent valid-pair cross-entropy and output-gradient references, target immutability, optional target masks, per-call overrides, internal mask gaps, masked-token changes and a public Trainer step are covered.
- CPU `torch.compile(..., backend="eager", fullgraph=True)` preserves values and finite gradients for left/right masked-input loss calls in the three environments. This does not test Inductor or accelerator kernels.
- Pinned repository `make check` and `git diff --check` pass.

A small CPU experiment uses two-layer BERT, hidden size 48, batch size 16, target lengths up to 16/64/120 words, one thread, 15 warmups and 50 forward/backward iterations. Three fresh-process pairs alternate order. Median candidate/baseline ratios are 1.056/1.060/0.919 for SDPA and 1.034/1.043/0.972 for eager attention. All ordinary losses are identical. Individual ratios span 0.668–1.546, so shared-CPU variance prevents a throughput claim. The eager tensor decision can synchronize accelerator data; GPU latency remains unmeasured.

The full repository suite, minimum Torch, Python 3.10/3.11, Windows, accelerators and pretrained-model training quality were not tested. Completely invalid target masks still have no supervised pairs and retain the inherited NaN boundary. EOS-only claims require an attended BOS-to-EOS pair.

title: Shuffle equal-size datasets independently in multi-dataset samplers
body:
With a `DatasetDict` and `NO_DUPLICATES`, two datasets of the same size are shuffled with the same permutation, so batch k of each dataset always holds the same row indices. For parallel datasets (same rows, different languages or negatives) this couples their order every epoch.

Cause: the trainer builds every per-dataset sampler with the same generator and seed, and `NoDuplicatesBatchSampler.__iter__` reseeds the generator with `seed + epoch` before drawing its permutation, so each child draws the same one.

Fix: `MultiDatasetDefaultBatchSampler` offsets each child sampler's seed by its dataset index. This is independent of #4109, which passes `args.seed` to these samplers.

Test: the new test checks that two equal-size datasets get different orders under both `RoundRobinBatchSampler` and `ProportionalBatchSampler`. It fails on main and passes here. Sampler tests: 63 passed; the 3 failures are torchcodec audio loading in my env and also fail on main.

title: [fix] Restore checkpoints into compiled models

title: [fix] Clear ValueError instead of bare IndexError in mine_hard_negatives column resolution
body:
## Summary

`mine_hard_negatives` with a one-column dataset and no explicit column names crashes with a bare `IndexError: list index out of range` — the positional fallback reads `columns[1]`, which doesn't exist, and the error says nothing about the actual problem (no second column for the positive entries).

The guard that was supposed to catch this —

```python
if not anchor_column_name and not positive_column_name and len(columns) != 2:
    raise ValueError("Dataset must contain exactly two columns.")
```

— is unreachable: after the two fallback assignments, both names are always non-empty strings, so the `and` chain can never be true. Datasets with more than two columns also pass through silently (first two columns used, as before — that behavior is kept).

## Changes

- Raise a descriptive `ValueError` when a positional default is impossible: no columns at all (anchor fallback), or fewer than two columns (positive fallback) — with the actual column list included in the message.
- Remove the dead check (its intent is now enforced by the guards above it).
- Explicitly named, existing columns are unaffected; datasets with >2 columns keep working.

## Tests

`tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py::test_one_column_dataset_raises_value_error` and `::test_missing_named_column_raises_value_error` — both raise `ValueError` with the fix and a bare `IndexError` without it (verified via `git stash` of the source change only).

title: [fix] Support 1D embeddings in quantize_embeddings for every precision
body:
## Summary

`quantize_embeddings` assumed 2D input, but `model.encode("one sentence")` returns a **1D** array — and the five precisions behaved inconsistently on it (measured on `main`, torch 2.14.1+cpu):

| precision | 1D input before this PR | after |
|---|---|---|
| float32 | works, returns `(dim,)` | unchanged |
| int8 | **no crash, but silently wrong**: ranges computed as a single global min/max instead of per-dimension, so the bucket mapping differs from the equivalent 2D row | identical to the 2D row |
| uint8 | same silent mismatch | identical to the 2D row |
| binary | `ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 2 into shape (9,newaxis)` | returns `(ceil(dim/8),)` int8 |
| ubinary | same crash | returns `(ceil(dim/8),)` uint8 |

The int8/uint8 case is the nastiest one: no error, just a quietly different quantization than the same embedding quantized as `(1, dim)`.

## Changes

- If the input is 1D, promote it to `(1, dim)` up front, run the existing quantization unchanged, and squeeze the result back — so every precision returns a 1D array whose values match the equivalent 2D row exactly.
- No behavior change for 2D inputs, lists of matrices, or the empty-matrix early returns.

## Tests

`tests/util/test_quantization.py::test_quantize_embeddings_1d_matches_first_row_of_2d` parametrizes all five precisions and asserts the 1D result is 1D and element-identical to the first row of the 2D result. int8, uint8, binary and ubinary fail on unmodified `main` (binary/ubinary with the reshape `ValueError`, int8/uint8 with mismatched buckets); float32 passes both sides.

Local verification: `pytest tests/util/ --ignore=tests/util/test_dataset.py --ignore=tests/util/test_backend.py` — 674 passed with the fix; checking out the old `quantization.py` produces exactly the 4 failures above (the `test_backend.py` module downloads third-party backend models and `test_dataset.py` needs the `datasets` package, so both are outside this change's scope). `ruff check` clean.

title: Fix dense FP16 embedding normalization
body:
## Summary

Normalize dense FP16 embeddings with FP32 arithmetic, then restore their original dtype.

The existing normalization stores the epsilon and L2 norm from [Torch's normalization contract](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.normalize.html) in FP16. FP16 rounds the default epsilon to zero, and the norm of finite values can exceed 65504. On current main:

- `[0, 0]` becomes `[NaN, NaN]`
- `[60000, 60000]` becomes `[0, 0]`
- Stored equal coordinates near `1e-7` normalize to about `[0.6665, 0.6665]`

After this change, zero vectors stay zero and both nonzero equal-coordinate rows become `[0.70703125, 0.70703125]`. Empty text through a real FP16 `StaticEmbedding` model also returns a finite zero embedding.

A private helper is used by the existing dense utility, `Normalize` module, dense/multi-vector encode normalization, and Matryoshka prefix normalization. Public signatures, epsilon, axes, feature keys, dtype/device, and flags remain unchanged. Other dtypes and sparse normalization keep their existing behavior.

## Verification

- Native regression baseline at `4a3b5cd6ec718e421f57e824a41ed3fd99595df6`: 24 failed, 14 passed with unchanged production code
- Fixed regressions: 38 passed on Python 3.12.14 and 3.13.5 with Torch 2.14.1+cpu
- Tests use real, locally constructed StaticEmbedding and WordEmbeddings pipelines; tensor/NumPy/list outputs, zero/tiny/large/ordinary values, input preservation and representable backward gradients are covered
- Audited native CPU checks, serialized in fresh per-file processes: 351 passed, 13 repository-standard skips and 1 default slow-test deselection on each interpreter; the 38 regressions are included in those totals
- The sole default slow deselection, `tests/util/test_retrieval.py::test_paraphrase_mining`, was explicitly enabled unchanged with `-m slow`: 1 passed on each interpreter using the exact public MiniLM checkpoint offline under the same guard
- `make check`: pinned Ruff lint/format and typos passed

The default epsilon remains `1e-12`, so zero/tiny FP16 leaf gradients can still exceed the representable range. This fix establishes normalization output correctness. CUDA, ONNX/OpenVINO, the minimum-version matrix and the complete repository suite remain unverified.

The initial offline broad run had a public Model2vec fixture-cache failure. Completing that exact snapshot resolved it. A combined Python 3.13 run reached 2.29 GiB RSS; final checks use the same files, inputs and assertions in sequential processes with a 2 GiB resident-memory guard.

## Validation scope and disposition

The reported local validation was CPU-only; CUDA autocast and loss scaling were not tested.

[Tom Aarsen closed this PR](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/pull/4126#issuecomment-6059486616) after reproducing the edge cases and reporting a CUDA-autocast output-dtype change and NaN gradients with loss scaling, including ordinary inputs such as `[3, 4]`. That GPU finding is his validation, not a result of the CPU checks above. The proposal remains closed and unmerged.

title: Support probability targets in SoftmaxLoss
body:
Fixes #3228.

`SoftmaxLoss` currently flattens every target before passing it to the loss function. For probability targets shaped `(batch_size, num_labels)`, this turns a two-example, three-class batch into six targets and raises:

The docs show probability targets and explain how hard labels can be represented as one-hot vectors in the same dataset.

title: Skip softmax over single-label CrossEncoder scores
body:
`predict(apply_softmax=True)` is documented to apply softmax only when
`model.num_labels > 1`, but single-label scores are still `[batch, 1]`
when the softmax check runs, so it softmaxes over one column and every
score becomes 1.0. `rank()` only accepts single-label models and passes
`apply_softmax` through, so `rank(..., apply_softmax=True)` returns all
1.0 scores in input order.

```python
model = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder-testing/reranker-bert-tiny-gooaq-bce")
model.predict(pairs)                      # [0.859 0.0697 0.0824]
model.predict(pairs, apply_softmax=True)  # [1. 1. 1.]
model.rank(query, docs, apply_softmax=True)
# [{'corpus_id': 0, 'score': 1.0}, {'corpus_id': 1, 'score': 1.0}, {'corpus_id': 2, 'score': 1.0}]
```

This squeezes single-label scores before the softmax check, so
`apply_softmax` is a no-op for them as documented. Multi-label models
are unchanged.

Added `test_predict_softmax_single_label` next to `test_predict_softmax`;
it fails on main and passes here. `pytest tests/cross_encoder/test_model.py
-k "softmax or rank or predict"` passes (bar one test that needs
`datasets`, not installed locally), ruff is clean.

title: fix: make saved weight files as readable as other saved files
body:
## Summary

`SentenceTransformer.save()` left `model.safetensors` with mode `0o600` while every other file in the saved directory is group/world-readable (`0o666 & ~umask`). The restrictive mode comes from `safetensors`, which creates the file with `0o600` regardless of the umask — so a model saved by root during a Docker build, for example, fails to load for non-root users with `FileNotFoundError`.

The fix adds a `_relax_weight_file_permissions()` step at the end of `BaseModel.save()` that resets `model.safetensors` / `pytorch_model.bin` (including sharded `model-*-of-*.safetensors` / `pytorch_model-*.bin` variants) to `0o666 & ~umask`, matching the other saved files. This covers all model classes (`SentenceTransformer`, `SparseEncoder`, `MultiVectorEncoder`, `CrossEncoder`) and both the safetensors and legacy torch save paths.

Fixes #4010.

## Changes

| File | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `sentence_transformers/base/model.py` | New `_relax_weight_file_permissions()` helper, called at the end of `BaseModel.save()` so saved weight files get `0o666 & ~umask` like their siblings |
| `tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py` | New `test_saved_weight_files_are_readable` regression test (parametrized over `safe_serialization` True/False): asserts each saved weight file mode equals the sibling files mode |

- Reproduced pre-fix: saved `sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors` via `model.save()` → `model.safetensors` was `0o600` while all other files were `0o660`; post-fix it is `0o660`.

title: [fix] Use the auto-detected device in StaticEmbedding.from_distillation
body:
Closes #4055

## What

`StaticEmbedding.from_distillation` documents that `device=None` selects the strongest available device, but the detected value was computed **after** the `kwargs` dict was built and never written back — `model2vec.distill()` therefore always received `device=None`:

```python
kwargs = {..., "device": device, ...}  # still None
device = get_device_name()             # computed but unused
static_model = distill(model_name, **kwargs)
```

The fix writes the detected device into `kwargs` only when the caller did not supply one, and only when the installed `model2vec` version actually supports the `device` parameter (older signatures lack it — the existing leftover-argument filtering already drops it in that case, and the fix must not re-add it).

## Tests

Three mocked regression tests were added to `tests/sentence_transformer/modules/test_static_embedding.py` (no Hub download, no real `model2vec` install — the `model2vec.distill` module is faked via `sys.modules`, `get_device_name` is stubbed, and `StaticEmbedding.__init__` is stubbed so only the kwargs plumbing is exercised):

1. `test_from_distillation_uses_detected_device` — no explicit device → `distill` receives the detected device (fails without the fix).
2. `test_from_distillation_respects_explicit_device` — an explicit device is passed through untouched.
3. `test_from_distillation_does_not_inject_device_when_unsupported` — an older `model2vec` signature without `device` must not receive one.

`ruff check` / `ruff format` are clean for both touched files.

*Disclosure: prepared with the help of an AI coding agent; the kwargs plumbing is verified by the mocked tests above.*

title: Follow only duplicate pairs in the paraphrase mining transitive closure
body:
`ParaphraseMiningEvaluator(add_transitive_closure=True)` treats pairs marked `False` in `duplicates_dict` as duplicates.

The closure walks every key of `graph[node]` and ignores the value, while the rest of the evaluator reads the value. With labeled pairs like Quora's (`a-b: 1, b-c: 0, c-d: 1`), the gold set grows from 2 pairs to 6, so recall and AP are scored against pairs the data says are not duplicates. The fix follows only the pairs marked `True`.

Test: `pytest tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_paraphrase_mining_evaluator.py`. The new case fails before (3 gold pairs instead of 1) and passes after; 9 pass. Ruff 0.15.6 check and format pass. Run on CPU.

title: fix(gradcache): preserve fp64 precision in the backward hook's surrogate dot product
body:
## Summary

`_backward_hook` in `sentence_transformers/base/losses/gradcache.py` computes a surrogate dot product to replay cached gradients through the re-embedded mini-batch. It always casts both operands to fp32 via `.float()`. That's correct under autocast (cached gradients are reduced-precision, the re-embedding runs outside autocast in fp32), but it also silently downcasts a fp64 model/cache to fp32, so a fp64 training run's cached loss no longer matches its non-cached counterpart to fp64 accuracy.

## Problem

Reported in #4081: with a fp64 encoder and `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss`, the cached gradient/SGD update differs from the non-cached fp64 computation by ~1.16e-7 (fp32 machine epsilon), while keeping the surrogate in fp64 brings that down to ~2.6e-15 (fp64 machine epsilon).

## Root cause

`surrogate = torch.dot(reps_mb.flatten().float(), grad_mb.flatten().float()) * grad_output` hardcodes the target dtype to fp32 regardless of what precision the model/cache actually hold.

## Implementation

Replaced the hardcoded `.float()` with `torch.promote_types(reps_mb.dtype, grad_mb.dtype)`, flooring the result up to fp32 only when it resolves to fp16/bf16 (the autocast case the original comment was written for). fp32 inputs stay fp32, fp64 inputs now stay fp64.

```python
surrogate_dtype = torch.promote_types(reps_mb.dtype, grad_mb.dtype)
if surrogate_dtype in (torch.float16, torch.bfloat16):
    surrogate_dtype = torch.float32
surrogate = (
    torch.dot(reps_mb.flatten().to(surrogate_dtype), grad_mb.flatten().to(surrogate_dtype))
    * grad_output
)
```

No behavior change for fp16/bf16/fp32 models (the common cases); only fp64 models are affected, and only in the direction of becoming more precise.

## Testing

- Added `test_gradcache_surrogate_keeps_fp64_precision` in `tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gradcache.py`, following the existing `test_cached_mnrl_matches_mnrl` pattern but casting the test model to fp64 and asserting the cached vs. non-cached loss/gradients match to `rtol=1e-10` (fp64-appropriate) rather than the `1e-4`/`1e-5` tolerance used for the default-precision test.
- Verified the new test **fails** against the pre-fix code (via `git stash` on just `gradcache.py`) with an `AssertionError` on the embedding gradient, and **passes** with the fix restored.
- Full `tests/sentence_transformer/losses/test_gradcache.py`: 38 passed, 1 skipped (pre-existing, unrelated bf16-on-CPU-crash guard).
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on both changed files.

## Validation

Reproduced the issue's own comparison (cached fp64 loss vs. direct fp64 loss) through the project's existing tiny test fixture rather than the issue's standalone `nn.Module` repro, so the regression test exercises the real `SentenceTransformer` + `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss` path end to end.

Closes #4081.

title: Compare CSR reconstructions with the raw input when normalize=True
body:
With `SparseAutoEncoder(normalize=True)`, a perfect reconstruction gets a nonzero CSR loss.

`forward()` stores the layer-normalized input as `sentence_embedding_backbone`, while `decode()` maps reconstructions back to the raw space. `CSRReconstructionLoss` then compares the two.

Derivation: `decode(z) = (Wz + b)σ + μ`, so `L_k = 0` needs `Wz + b = (LN(x) - μ)/σ`, a target about `1/σ ≈ √d` times the right one. For unit-norm d=384 inputs that makes `L_k` about 500x too large at init (0.98 vs 0.002).

The CSR reference code (`train_CSR_models.py`, `model_zoo.py`) returns the raw `x` from `forward()` and compares it with the de-normalized reconstruction. This keeps the raw input as the target.

Test: a hand-built exact autoencoder now has `L_k` near 0 (1.41 before). `test_csr.py`: 9 passed.

title: Preserve ranking-loss gradients with weighted log-sigmoid
body:
LambdaLoss computes a weighted sigmoid in probability space, then clamps it before taking the logarithm. For strongly misordered documents, this caps the loss at `-log(eps)` and gives the model zero ranking gradients. RankNetLoss inherits the same behavior. With scores `[0, 1000]` and relevance `[1, 0]`, the natural-log RankNet loss is about 23 instead of 1000.

Compute the weighted log-probability directly with `logsigmoid`, and convert to binary logarithms afterward. This preserves the pair selection, ranking weights, and mean reduction while retaining gradients for badly misranked documents.

Validation: CPU tests import the complete native source package and run the production losses with a deterministic trainable score model at the model-input boundary. The 50 new cases compare losses and gradients against independent float64 binary cross-entropy references, covering both losses, both logarithm bases, multiple sigma values, large positive/negative score gaps, and variable-length padded batches. Before the change: 16 failed, 34 passed. After: 50 passed. The final targeted run included the existing ListMLE numerical regression cases: 62 passed, 16 deselected. Ruff lint and formatting checks pass for both changed files. No pretrained-model or CUDA training run was performed.

title: Compute large-batch orthogonal regularization with the feature Gram matrix
body:
The default cosine GOR loss materializes a B-by-B similarity matrix, even when the embedding dimension d is much smaller than the batch. The two statistics can instead be computed exactly from the feature Gram matrix of normalized embeddings X:

`sum(i != j, cosine(i,j)) = ||sum_i X_i||^2 - sum_i ||X_i||^2`
`sum(i != j, cosine(i,j)^2) = ||X.T @ X||_F^2 - sum_i ||X_i||^4`

This reduces the principal dense matrix from O(B^2) to O(d^2) and the matrix multiplication from O(B^2 d) to O(B d^2). The loss definition and weights are unchanged. The feature path is used when B >= 2d, with a conservative fallback for custom similarities, sparse tensors, autocast, and norms below normalization's epsilon. The squared-similarity sum is clamped to zero to guard cancellation roundoff. Actual squared row norms are subtracted rather than assuming an exact unit diagonal.

Validation: 54 focused cases plus 10 existing GOR cases pass against the complete current-main package. Coverage includes loss and gradient parity in float64/float32/float16/bfloat16, B=0/1, B=2d-1/2d/2d+1, zero and near-zero vectors, degenerate geometries, custom and sparse similarities, CPU autocast, weighted multi-column aggregation, and the old torch autocast query signature.

On this Windows Intel CPU with torch 2.14.1, float32, one thread, three warmups and nine measurements, median forward-plus-backward time was 70.02 -> 5.45 ms for B=2048,d=128 (12.85x), and 661.82 -> 65.74 ms for B=4096,d=384 (10.07x). The main matrix sizes are 16 MiB -> 64 KiB and 64 MiB -> 576 KiB respectively; these are tensor sizes, not measured process peak memory.

GPU performance has not been measured. The near-zero norm guard converts a tensor predicate to a Python bool, which may synchronize accelerators; GPU throughput needs separate measurement. The old torch API compatibility path was checked using its legacy signature, rather than installing another torch runtime.

title: Exclude unretrieved positives from observed RRF ranking metrics
body:
Top-k retrieval can omit some known relevant documents. The evaluator currently appends those positives to the retrieved relevance vector and assigns them ordinary descending scores. That gives unretrieved documents a rank and positive gain, inflating both average precision and nDCG for dense, sparse, and fused rankings.

For example, with positives `[p, missing]` and retrieved documents `[irrelevant, p]`, AP is currently 7/12 instead of 1/4. At k=10, nDCG is about 0.6934 instead of 0.3869: the missing document incorrectly contributes DCG at rank 3. This is observable without loading a model.

The change evaluates only actual retrieved documents, counts every known positive in the AP denominator and ideal DCG, and keeps existing sklearn score-tie behavior. MRR and fusion ordering remain unchanged. A single retrieved positive is handled directly because sklearn nDCG requires at least two candidates. At a zero cutoff, MRR and nDCG are zero while AP still uses the full ranking.

Validation: 14 focused regression cases plus the 3 existing RRF cases pass against the complete current-main package. The regressions cover omitted positives at several cutoffs, empty and singleton rankings, zero cutoff, score ties, query averaging, prediction output, and complementary retrievers. Before adding the two zero-cutoff cases, pristine main yielded 9 failures and 6 passes.

title: Fix scalar quantization arithmetic for float16 embeddings
body:
Scalar quantization currently evaluates the calibration range and bucket width in the input dtype. For float16 embeddings, a narrow, nonconstant range can underflow when divided by 255. The constant-dimension fallback then replaces the bucket width with 1, collapsing distinct inputs to identical codes. Finite opposite-signed endpoints can also overflow during subtraction.

For example, `quantize_embeddings(np.array([[-1e-6], [0], [1e-6]], dtype=np.float16), "uint8")` returns three zero codes. Quantizing the same stored values after conversion to float32 returns three distinct codes.

Compute scalar calibration arithmetic in `np.result_type(embeddings.dtype, ranges.dtype, np.float32)`. This promotes half precision while preserving float64 inputs. Output dtypes, clipping, constant dimensions and binary quantization retain their existing behavior.

Regression cases cover both integer precisions, narrow and large ranges, each calibration mode, shared ranges for variable-length multi-vector inputs, and real float16 tensor inputs.

Validation:

- Added regression cases: 18 fail on the unchanged upstream module and 18 pass with this patch, using PyTorch 2.14.1+cpu, NumPy 2.5.3 and pytest 9.1.1.
- `python -m pytest tests/util/test_quantization.py -q` — 99 passed, including the existing FAISS and USearch regressions and all 18 new cases.
- Repository pre-commit hooks pass: Ruff check, Ruff format and typos, using the pinned hook versions.
- `git diff --check` passes.

The full affected test file ran from the native checkout with normal package initialization, FAISS 1.15.1 and USearch 2.26.2. Model inference and accelerator backends were not exercised.

title: Keep the CSR 4k latents off the dead-latent mask
body:
`SparseAutoEncoder.top_k` masks the pre-activations for the auxiliary loss in place (`x.data *= dead_mask`), and `forward()` then takes the 4k latents from that same tensor.

With no dead latents the mask is all zeros, so z_4k = relu(topk(0)) = 0, x̂_4k = b_pre, and ∂L(4k)/∂W = 0. Once latents die, z_4k only covers dead latents and no longer contains the top-k latents. The CSR reference code runs a fresh forward pass for 4k, so it never sees the mask.

Fix: mask a copy (`x * dead_mask`).

Test: a new `test_csr.py` case checks that the 4k latents keep the top-k values and the pre-activations stay unchanged. It fails on main and passes with the fix; `test_csr.py` has 9 passed.

title: [docs] Explain that an empty query prompt blocks the default_prompt_name fallback in encode_query
body:
## What

After review, this PR no longer changes behaviour. It documents how `encode_query()` picks its prompt.

- **`encode_query` docstrings** in `SentenceTransformer`, `SparseEncoder` and `MultiVectorEncoder` now say three things. The "query" prompt is empty unless one is configured. An empty "query" prompt still counts as the selected prompt, so no prompt is applied and `default_prompt_name` is not used as a fallback. Models should configure a "query" prompt explicitly to prompt queries. The old "if available" wording suggested the default prompt could take over when no query prompt was configured.
- **Default-prompt warning** in `BaseModel._validate_prompts`: it used to say the default prompt "will be applied to all inference calls" unless `prompt` or `prompt_name` is passed. It now also covers methods that select their own prompt:

  > Default prompt name is set to 'retrieval'. This prompt will be applied to all inference calls, except if a `prompt` or `prompt_name` parameter is provided, or if the method selects its own prompt (e.g. `encode_query` selects the 'query' prompt even when it is empty, so the default prompt is not applied).

The only runtime change is the warning text.

## Why

All three classes put an empty `"query"` entry in `prompts`, and `encode_query()` selects it. A model created with `prompts={"retrieval": "Retrieve: "}, default_prompt_name="retrieval"` therefore prepends `"Retrieve: "` in `encode(x)` but not in `encode_query(x)`. This is deliberate. `None` means no override was given and `""` is an explicit empty prompt (#3554, kept in #3968), so a caller-supplied `prompts={"query": ""}` keeps query encoding unprompted even when another prompt is the default. The docstrings and the warning didn't say this, which is how I misread it as a bug. I found it through code analysis, not in a real workflow.

`encode_document` follows the same rule (the prompt it selects is used even when empty), but #4095 is reworking how it picks between `"document"`, `"passage"` and `"corpus"`. I left its docstring alone so the two PRs don't edit the same docstrings.

## Tests

- New `test_encode_query_empty_query_prompt_skips_default_prompt_name` in `tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py`. It is parametrized over an unconfigured and an explicitly empty `"query"` prompt, both with `default_prompt_name="retrieval"`. It checks that `encode_query(x)` equals the unprompted embedding, while `encode(x, task="query")` does apply the default prompt. It passes on this branch, and both cases fail if `encode_query` is changed to skip empty query prompts (the change this PR first proposed).
- The three tests from the first version, which pinned the behaviour change, are removed.
- `pytest tests/{sentence_transformer,sparse_encoder,multi_vector_encoder,base}/test_model.py -k "encode_query or encode_document or prompt"`: 556 passed.
- The full `tests/{sentence_transformer,sparse_encoder,multi_vector_encoder,base,cross_encoder}/test_model.py`: 1255 passed, 72 skipped. `tests/base/test_model.py::test_device_property` was deselected because it also fails on main on an Apple Silicon machine (it expects `cpu`/`cuda` and gets `mps`).
- `pre-commit run -a` (ruff check, ruff format, typos at the pinned revisions): passed.
- Not run: the documentation build (this change only edits docstring text) and the tests that need CUDA, which are skipped on this machine.

The branch is rebased onto main at 7f36a35 as a single commit.

AI assistance: the docstring and warning wording, the test and this description were drafted with an AI coding assistant (Claude) and checked locally with the commands above.

title: Pass args.seed to the per-dataset batch samplers
body:
`NO_DUPLICATES` and `GROUP_BY_LABEL` produce the same batch order for every `args.seed`, so a multi-seed run trains on identical batches each time. The default batch sampler does respect the seed.

`_build_dataloader` seeds the generator with `args.seed` but calls `get_batch_sampler` without `seed`, so it defaults to 0. Both samplers reseed the generator with `seed + epoch` in `__iter__`, which throws `args.seed` away. The multi-dataset sampler already gets `seed=self.args.seed`.

Fix: pass `seed=self.args.seed` to both `get_batch_sampler` calls.

Test: `test_trainer_batch_sampler_uses_args_seed` checks that seeds 1 and 2 give different batches for both samplers, single and multi-dataset. It fails on main and passes with the fix. The trainer and sampler suites pass (138 passed, 3 skipped).

title: Apply model2vec token mapping and weights when loading StaticEmbedding
body:
Fixes #4107

**What:** `StaticEmbedding.load`, `from_model2vec` and `from_distillation` now fold model2vec's optional `mapping` and per-token `weights` into the embedding matrix: `embedding[id] = embeddings[mapping[id]] * weights[id]`.

**Why:** model2vec averages `embeddings[mapping[id]] * weights[id]`, and these three methods only read `embeddings`. Models that ship the extra tensors, e.g. `minishlab/potion-code-16M`, produce different embeddings than in model2vec (cosine 0.64 / 0.93 on the repro in the issue). Vocabulary-quantized models fail with an out-of-range index. Folding at load time keeps `StaticEmbedding` a plain `EmbeddingBag`, so `save()` and later loads need no format change.

**Test:**
- `tests/sentence_transformer/modules/test_static_embedding.py`: two new tests. One writes a model2vec-format safetensors locally with no model2vec dependency. The other builds a `StaticModel` with `token_mapping` and `weights` and compares against `StaticModel.encode`. Both fail before this change and pass after it; the file gives 10 passed, 1 skipped (the existing distillation test, skipped on transformers v5).
- `potion-code-16M` repro: max abs diff goes from 0.17 to 4e-8.
- ruff, ruff-format and typos pass.

Disclosure: found, reproduced and the draft fix tested locally with the help of an AI coding agent (Claude Code); reviewed before filing.

title: Fix low precision overflow and accumulation errors in pooling
body:
Fixes #4105.

## Changes

Weightedmean pooling over 512 float16 tokens can produce NaN even when all embeddings are one: the positional-weight sum is 131328, beyond the finite float16 range. Weighted products can also overflow for shorter inputs although the final mean is representable. The denominator guard underflows when a prompt excludes every token.

Compute weighted products/reductions in float32 for float16/bfloat16 inputs on both padded and flattened paths. Restore the embedding dtype after division, while preserving the existing dtype promotion when the padded path receives an external token_weights_sum. This preserves the Dense-head compatibility established by #3751. Float32/float64 arithmetic and other pooling modes are unchanged.

## Validation

- 40 new regression cases, untouched base **12 failed / 28 passing controls** on both PyTorch 2.10 and 2.13.
- Full pooling test file **115 passed / 6 existing CUDA-only skips** on both environments (Python 3.12/Transformers 5.0 and Python 3.14/Transformers 5.14).
- Float16/bfloat16/float32/float64, padded and flattened inputs, 512-token constants/varying values, short inputs with large weighted products, fully excluded prompts, external float32/float64 normalizers, independent float64 value/gradient reference, and input/mask immutability.
- **8 padded fullgraph torch.compile(backend='eager') value/gradient cases** per environment, including external normalizer dtype promotion.
- All repository pre-commit hooks (Ruff check/format and typos) passed with --all-files; git diff --check passed.

title: Count weightedmean positions from the first non-padding token
body:
## Summary

Fixes #4103.

Weighted mean pooling currently counts positions in the padded batch tensor. Identical real token embeddings `[1, 3]` pool to `7/3` without padding but `11/5` with one leading pad. The flattened path already counts sequence-relative positions, so those paths disagree too.

Subtract each row's leading-padding count from the position weights. Use the caller's original attention mask to preserve the original sequence positions when excluding prompt tokens. The caller's features remain unmodified; missing/stale mask fallback, output dtype, other pooling modes and the flattened implementation are preserved. The public Pooling docstring explains the convention. Left-padded weightedmean outputs intentionally change to match the sequence-relative reference; no public API changes are introduced.

title: Schedule the regularizer weights of every SpladeLoss
body:
With one `SpladeLoss` per dataset, only the first loss gets the regularizer warmup. The rest train at full FLOPS weight from step 0, silently.

`SparseEncoderTrainer.prepare_loss` runs once per loss and adds a `SpladeRegularizerWeightSchedulerCallback` only if none exists, so the second loss finds the first loss's scheduler and skips.

Fix: only reuse a scheduler whose `.loss` is this loss.

Document weight with two losses, `max_steps=6`:

| step | first | second, main | second, fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 3e-5 | 0 |
| 1 | 7.5e-6 | 3e-5 | 7.5e-6 |

Test: both losses must sit at max * (1/2)^2 at step 1 of the quadratic warmup; fails on main. Sparse trainer and loss tests: 30 passed. ruff 0.15.6 clean.

title: [`fix`] similarity functions crashing or overflowing on quantized (int8/uint8/binary) embeddings
body:
## Summary
Embeddings from `model.encode(..., precision="int8" | "uint8" | "binary" | "ubinary")` break the similarity utilities. Some calls crash; others silently return wrong scores.

**Crashes** (`linalg.vector_norm: Expected a floating point...` / `cdist only supports floating-point dtypes`):
- `model.similarity` with `cosine` (the default), `euclidean` or `manhattan`
- `model.similarity_pairwise` with `cosine`
- `util.semantic_search`, `util.paraphrase_mining_embeddings`, `util.community_detection`

**Silently wrong** (arithmetic wraps around in the input dtype):
- `dot_score` on int8 `[[100, 100, 100, 100]]` with itself returns `64` instead of `40000`
- `pairwise_dot_score` has the same int8 overflow
- `pairwise_manhattan_sim` on uint8 `[[0, 10]]` vs `[[10, 0]]` returns `-256` instead of `-20`

`pairwise_angle_sim` also crashed on numpy input (`'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'is_sparse'`), unlike its sibling functions.

## Reproduction
```python
emb = model.encode(sentences, precision="int8")
model.similarity(emb, emb)  # RuntimeError
```

## Fix
- `_convert_to_float_tensor` already upcasts sub-float32 floats. It now also upcasts integer inputs to float32, which fixes every dense similarity function at once. float32 represents all int8/uint8 values exactly.
- `pairwise_angle_sim` converts its inputs before checking for sparsity.
- `community_detection` casts integer input to float. Float inputs are left unchanged, so there is no extra memory for fp16/bf16 corpora.
- Removed the now-redundant `astype(np.float32)` workaround in `EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator`.

## Tests
Added to `tests/util/test_similarity.py`:
- all 9 dense similarity functions with int8/uint8, as numpy and torch input, compared against a float32 reference
- the int8 dot-product overflow and uint8 Manhattan underflow cases above
- `semantic_search`, `paraphrase_mining_embeddings` and `community_detection` on int8 embeddings

### Test run
New tests with the fix (previously 21 failed, 1 passed):
```
$ pytest tests/util/test_similarity.py -k "integer or int8 or underflow"
22 passed
``` 

Offline util suites with the fix, excluding one test that needs a Hub model download:
```
$ pytest tests/util/test_similarity.py tests/util/test_tensor.py tests/util/test_retrieval.py
145 passed, 9 skipped
```

### Evaluator check
`EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator` gives identical results before and after this change. I checked this offline with a static-embedding model for `precision` = None, float32, int8, uint8, binary and ubinary, with the cosine, dot, euclidean and manhattan similarity functions, so removing the evaluator workaround does not change any results.

## Notes
Packed `binary`/`ubinary` embeddings passed straight to `model.similarity` now return scores instead of raising. As with `dot_score` today, those scores are computed on the packed bytes. Unpacking them, as `EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator` does, is left to the caller.

title: [`fix`] Respect `verbose=False` for the average-positives message in `mine_hard_negatives`
body:
## Summary
`mine_hard_negatives(..., verbose=False)` still prints `Found an average of X positives per query.`
whenever a query in the dataset has more than one positive. Every other message in the function
only prints when `verbose` is on, including the neighbouring `Found N unique queries out of M total queries.`
line. This message was the one left out.

## Reproduction
```python
from datasets import Dataset
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.util import mine_hard_negatives

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1")
dataset = Dataset.from_dict({
    "query": ["What is the capital of France?"] * 2,
    "answer": ["Paris is the capital of France.", "France's capital city is Paris."],
})
mine_hard_negatives(dataset, model, corpus=["Madrid is the capital of Spain."], num_negatives=1, verbose=False)
# Found an average of 2.000 positives per query.
```

## Fix
Only print the message when `verbose` is on, the same as the neighbouring messages.

## Tests
Added `test_verbose_false_prints_nothing_with_multiple_positives`. It mines with a deterministic mock
model on a query with two positives and `verbose=False`, then checks that nothing is printed to stdout.
It fails before the fix and passes after.

title: [`fix`] Accept a string `main_score_function` in `NanoBEIREvaluator`
body:
## Summary
`NanoBEIREvaluator` documents `main_score_function` as `str | SimilarityFunction`, but stores it as given and later reads `self.main_score_function.value`. Passing a string (e.g. `main_score_function="cosine"`) therefore crashes at the end of every evaluation, after all datasets have been encoded:

```
AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'value'
```

This also affects the subclasses that inherit the constructor, e.g. `MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator` (`main_score_function="maxsim"`).

## Fix
Normalize the argument with `SimilarityFunction(...)`, mirroring `InformationRetrievalEvaluator.__init__`.

## Tests
Added `test_nanobeir_evaluator_main_score_function`, parametrized over a string and a `SimilarityFunction`, which mocks the per-dataset evaluators (no network) and checks that the primary metric follows `main_score_function` rather than the best-scoring function. It fails with the `AttributeError` above before this change.

title: Fix uint64 precision loss in resolve_ids
body:
`resolve_ids` can resolve distinct `uint64` document IDs to the wrong text. With lookup IDs `[1, 2**63 + 1, 2**63 + 2]`, NumPy infers `float64` from the decoded Python integers and rounds the two large IDs to the same key. Batched resolution returns the last document twice, individual row reads raise `KeyError`, and nearby missing IDs can incorrectly resolve to a real document.

Preserve the lookup column's `uint64` dtype, and convert integer query IDs from their original values after checking the destination dtype's bounds. This also allows a small valid ID to resolve against an unsigned index without letting negative or oversized IDs wrap. Nullable ID columns retain the existing dictionary path.

Regression tests cover adjacent large IDs, the `uint64` maximum, agreement between batch and single-row reads, missing IDs, and nullable lookups. The six non-null regression cases fail on the unchanged implementation.

Validation:
- `python -m pytest tests/util/test_dataset.py -q --tb=short`: **84 passed** (CPU, Python 3.14).
- `python -m pre_commit run --all-files`: Ruff check, Ruff format, and typos passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

Minimal reproduction:
```python
import pyarrow as pa
from datasets import Dataset
from sentence_transformers.util import resolve_ids

ids = [1, 2**63 + 1, 2**63 + 2]
lookup = Dataset(pa.table({"document_id": pa.array(ids, type=pa.uint64()), "text": ["A", "B", "C"]}))
transform = resolve_ids({"document_id": lookup})
print(transform({"document_id": ids}))
# Before: {"document": ["A", "C", "C"]}
# After:  {"document": ["A", "B", "C"]}
```

title: Fix encode_document() alias selection while preserving explicit empty prompts
body:
## Summary

Fixes #4090. `encode_document()` seeds the `prompts` dictionary with a `"document"` placeholder, but `_validate_prompts()` converted that unfilled placeholder to `""`. Because `"document"` is the first candidate, `encode_document()` always selected it and never used a configured `"passage"` or `"corpus"` prompt.

This change keeps the unfilled `"document"` placeholder as `None` and adds `BaseModel._resolve_document_prompt_name()`, which returns the first **configured** (non-`None`) of `"document"`, `"passage"`, `"corpus"`, falling back to the first **present** candidate (normally `"document"`). `None` means no override was provided; `""` is an explicit empty override and stays authoritative.

All three `encode_document()` implementations (`SentenceTransformer`, `SparseEncoder`, `MultiVectorEncoder`) call this helper behind a `prompt_name is None and prompt is None` guard, so an explicit `prompt=""` is forwarded unchanged.

## Public prompt dictionary change

An unconfigured document prompt is now `None` in `model.prompts` (it was previously `""`) and saves as JSON `null`. Explicit empty prompts remain `""`. The default-value assertions in the three per-encoder `test_model.py` files and `tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py` are updated accordingly.

## Behaviours preserved (Tom Aarsen, Oct 7)

1. **`encode_document(inputs, prompt="")` encodes without a prompt, even when a document prompt is configured.** The caller-side check stays `prompt is None`, and `""` is passed through to `encode()` unchanged.
   - Tested by `tests/base/test_document_prompt_aliases.py::test_empty_argument_forwarded_unchanged`, and by the `{"prompt": ""}` and `{"prompt": "", "prompt_name": "document"}` cases in `test_selection`.

2. **If all document candidates are empty, the empty `"document"` prompt is still selected, so `default_prompt_name` cannot apply a query prompt to documents.**
   - Tested by the `({"query": "q "}, default_prompt_name="query")` case in `test_selection`, and by `test_no_prompts_model_card_and_fallback`.

3. **An explicitly configured `prompts={"document": ""}` stays authoritative, even when a `"passage"` or `"corpus"` prompt exists.**
   - Tested by the `{"document": "", ...}` and `{"passage": "", "corpus": "c "}` cases in `test_selection`, plus `test_runtime_explicit_empty`, `test_old_saved_empty_document_stays_authoritative`, `test_constructor_empty_document_overrides_saved_nonempty`, and `test_save_load_and_alias_override`.

## Other changes

- `BaseModelCardData.register_model()` now uses `model.prompts.get(...)` instead of `len(model.prompts[...])`, since an unfilled document prompt is `None`.
- `MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator` resolves the corpus role with `_resolve_document_prompt_name()`, so its registered-prompt warning matches the alias `encode_document()` actually uses. Covered by `test_ir_warning_matches_selected_alias`.

## Compatibility note

Models saved before this change with `"document": ""` keep that value as authoritative; the original intent (unfilled placeholder vs. explicit empty override) cannot be recovered. Such a model needs to be re-saved without the empty document entry, or loaded with an explicit prompt override, to pick up a `"passage"`/`"corpus"` prompt.

## Tests

- `tests/base/test_document_prompt_aliases.py`: 59 offline checks across all three encoders — alias selection, explicit empty overrides, save/load, constructor overrides, runtime prompt updates, model-card/fallback, and the IR warning.
- Updated `test_prompts`, `test_save_load_prompts`, and conversion assertions in the three per-encoder `test_model.py` files, plus `tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py`, for the retained `None` placeholder.
- Local runs: base model/alias/model-card tests (354 passed, 57 skipped), `tests/multi_vector_encoder/test_evaluators.py` + model-card tests (75 passed), `tests/sentence_transformer/evaluation/test_information_retrieval_evaluator.py` (5 passed), and the prompt-focused per-encoder runs (137 / 133 / 13 passed). `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean.

## Credits

Based on Amisha Gupta's candidate fix in https://github.com/amishaguptaberk/sentence-transformers/commit/9e2b9de5d410521f83d6ceef0ab362dd497081c9.

title: [fix] Keep paraphrase mining top_k per sentence across corpus chunks
body:
`paraphrase_mining_embeddings` took the top `top_k` scores inside each (query chunk, corpus chunk) block, so every sentence kept up to `top_k` candidates per corpus chunk. The result then depends on `corpus_chunk_size`, which is documented as a memory setting only. With the defaults this shows up on corpora above 100k sentences. A small example, `top_k=1` on 12 random embeddings:

| corpus_chunk_size | 100 | 6 | 4 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pairs returned | 9 | 26 | 37 | 48 |

This keeps a running top-k per query across corpus chunks (the same merge `semantic_search` does) and emits pairs once per query chunk, so memory stays bounded by `query_chunk_size * top_k` extra entries.

Checks: against a brute-force reference over 200 random cases with random chunk sizes, 130 differed before and 0 of 1200 (three chunkings each) after. New test `test_paraphrase_mining_embeddings_does_not_depend_on_chunk_sizes` (3 of 4 cases fail before). `pytest tests/util`: 883 passed. ruff clean.

title: Add opt-in lazy preprocessing for cached multimodal training
body:
This PR keeps raw text and image references through the Trainer and collator, then preprocesses and transfers inputs only when each GradCache mini-batch executes. It also supports the existing token budget for Qwen-VL inputs by calculating image-token counts from dimensions, without decoding pixels or expanding image-token sequences during length counting.

Refs #3991.

## Changes

- Add `lazy_preprocessing=True` to `SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments`, disabled by default. In `sentence_transformers/base/data_collator.py` and `sentence_transformers/base/trainer.py`, carry raw inputs with their prompt/task/max-length settings, preserve partial-batch size accounting, and check loss/collator compatibility.
- In `sentence_transformers/base/losses/gradcache.py`, preprocess each raw slice and transfer only that mini-batch to the model device. Reuse the existing gradient cache and RNG replay, including the same mini-batch boundaries in both passes.
- In `sentence_transformers/base/processing.py`, adapt supported Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and Qwen3-VL processors to compute visual token counts from their resize/patch/merge rules. Keep one placeholder per image while tokenizing the template and account for the remaining positions arithmetically, including truncation. `sentence_transformers/base/modules/transformer.py` connects this to the existing input preparation.
- Add a standard-Trainer example and usage/scope documentation under `examples/sentence_transformer/training/multimodal/`, with regression coverage in `test_lazy_image_example.py` and `test_lazy_token_budget.py`.

## Tests and results

Local validation on September 26, 2026: **85 passed, 1 deselected** across the lazy preprocessing/token-budget tests, data collator tests, and existing GradCache range/flattened-slicing tests. The excluded existing constructor test requires a model unavailable in the local offline cache. Coverage includes loss/gradient agreement, dropout replay, CPU/CUDA execution, partial evaluation batches, and processor state preservation.

- Real Qwen processor outputs agree with the calculated lengths for tested image sizes, multiple images, prompts, and truncation. A synthetic million-token image count still sends only one image placeholder to the tokenizer and creates fewer than 20 token IDs.
- An offline FP32 CUDA run used a locally initialized tiny Qwen2-VL on an RTX 4060 Laptop GPU: 32 samples, 36 images, and `mini_batch_num_tokens=512`. Lengths and mini-batch boundaries matched eager preprocessing; loss, all 33 parameter-gradient tensors, and one SGD update matched exactly. Dropout and TF32 were disabled for this numerical comparison.
- The same tiny-model setup completed three Trainer steps, evaluation, and save/reload. The maximum embedding difference after reload was `5.96e-7`. These checks validate execution and numerical agreement, not retrieval quality or production performance.
- Ruff lint/format checks and `git diff --check` passed. This is local validation, not a full-suite or CI result.

## Scope and feedback

- Initial support is for `CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss` with deterministic preprocessing. Other losses and loss wrappers are not enabled. Single-device FP32 training/evaluation is validated; distributed and mixed-precision training are not.
- Image token-budget support requires compatible Qwen-VL processors, local still-image paths or PIL images, and supported resize options. The budget follows the existing non-padding-token rule; it is not a strict GPU-memory limit.
- Images are decoded again during GradCache replay. Dynamic padding can differ from whole-batch preprocessing, and whole-batch embeddings/cached gradients still grow with the outer batch size. Asynchronous prefetching is left for a follow-up.

I would appreciate feedback on the integration point and initial support boundary before expanding the scope, especially which compatibility checks you would prioritize for merging.

title: Fix encode(precision=...) and quantize_embeddings crashing on bfloat16 embeddings
body:
`quantize_embeddings` converts tensors with `.cpu().numpy()`, which raises `TypeError: Got unsupported ScalarType BFloat16` because numpy has no bfloat16 dtype. `encode()` already upcasts bfloat16 before its own numpy conversion, but quantization happens before that step, so `model.encode(..., precision=...)` crashes for bfloat16 models with every non-float32 precision, on CPU and MPS. The docs recommend both bfloat16 inference and `precision="binary"`, so the combination is easy to hit:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers-testing/stsb-bert-tiny-safetensors", model_kwargs={"torch_dtype": "bfloat16"})
model.encode(["The weather is lovely today.", "It's so sunny outside!"], precision="binary")
# TypeError: Got unsupported ScalarType BFloat16
```

This upcasts bfloat16 tensors to float32 before the numpy conversion in `quantize_embeddings`, for both the single-tensor and the list-of-tensors inputs. The results match quantizing the (already upcast) numpy output of `encode()` afterwards.

**Tests**
- `test_quantize_bfloat16_tensors` in `tests/util/test_quantization.py`: all four precisions, tensor and list-of-tensors inputs.
- `test_encode_precision_with_bfloat16_model` in `tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py`: the user-facing `encode(precision=...)` path.

The new tests fail on `main` (12 failures) and pass with this change. `tests/util` and `tests/sentence_transformer/test_model.py` pass locally (1434 passed), and I also checked the four precisions with a bfloat16 model on MPS.

AI usage: I used Claude Code to find this bug and write the fix and tests. I reviewed the change and ran the tests locally.

title: Evaluate the main similarity function in TripletEvaluator
body:
`TripletEvaluator(..., main_similarity_function="euclidean")` on a cosine model only computes `cosine_accuracy`, but still sets `primary_metric` to `euclidean_accuracy`, so `results[evaluator.primary_metric]` raises a `KeyError`.

When `similarity_fn_names` is empty, this now falls back to the main similarity function, the same way `EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator` already does. The sparse and multi-vector triplet evaluators inherit the fix.

title: Include a model identity in the hard negatives embedding cache key
body:
## Problem

The embedding cache in `mine_hard_negatives(cache_folder=...)` keys its files on a hash of `(model.model_card_data.base_model, prompts, texts)`. For models **loaded from a local directory**, `base_model` is `None`, so the hash collapses to only the prompts and texts — and two different models sharing one `cache_folder` silently reuse each other's cached embeddings:

```python
model_a = SentenceTransformer("path/to/model-a")   # base_model: None
model_b = SentenceTransformer("path/to/model-b")   # base_model: None, different weights
util.mine_hard_negatives(ds, model_a, cache_folder=cache)
util.mine_hard_negatives(ds, model_b, cache_folder=cache)  # model_b.encode_query never called:
                                                           # it loads model_a's cached embeddings
```

Hard negatives computed from another model's embeddings silently train on wrong data. Reproduced with two locally loaded models with different weights: the second call performed **zero** encodes (red repro below).

## Fix

Fall back to a short fingerprint of the first module's state dict when no `base_model` is recorded. It distinguishes different weights, while two copies of the same weights correctly keep sharing the cache. Hub-loaded models keep their existing cache keys (`base_model`), so existing caches stay valid.

```python
model_name = model.model_card_data.base_model or _model_fingerprint(model._first_module())
```

## Verification

Two local loads of the same directory, second copy with perturbed weights:

- unfixed `main`: `encode calls: ['a']` → model_b loaded model_a's cached embeddings (bug; verified by temporarily reverting the fix);
- with the fix: `encode calls: ['a', 'b']` → model_b encoded its own embeddings.

Added `test_cache_is_per_model` (mirroring the existing `test_cache_respects_prompt` pattern); it fails on unfixed `main` and passes with the fix.

- `tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py`: 106 passed, 8 skipped.
- `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean with the repo-pinned ruff 0.15.6.

title: Stop the multi-process pool when hard negative mining fails
body:
## Problem

`mine_hard_negatives` with `use_multi_process` leaks the worker pool if encoding (or CrossEncoder rescoring) raises. `stop_multi_process_pool` was only reached after the encodes **finished successfully**:

```python
pool = model.start_multi_process_pool(...)
corpus_embeddings = model.encode_document(...)   # raises? -> pool never stopped
query_embeddings = model.encode_query(...)
if use_multi_process:
    model.stop_multi_process_pool(pool)          # only on success
```

When `encode_document`/`encode_query`/`CrossEncoder.predict` throws (CUDA OOM, corrupt input, disk error...), the spawned workers stay alive for the remainder of the process, each holding its own copy of the model and any GPU memory it claimed.

## Fix

Wrap both pool-using blocks (model embedding and CrossEncoder rescoring) in `try/finally` so the pool is stopped on the failure path. The success path is unchanged.

## Verification

Repro (latest `main`, CPU, `use_multi_process=True`): monkeypatch `encode_document` to raise `RuntimeError`, catch the propagated exception, and probe the pool workers:

```
exception propagated: simulated encode failure
worker processes alive after failure: [True, True, True, True]
LEAK
```

After the fix, the same repro:

```
exception propagated: simulated encode failure
worker processes alive after failure: [False, False, False, False]
NO-LEAK (all workers stopped)
```

- Added a regression test (`test_multi_process_pool_stopped_on_encode_failure`) that asserts the workers are no longer alive after an encode failure; it fails on unfixed `main` (verified by temporarily reverting the fix) and passes with it.
- `tests/util/test_hard_negatives.py`: 105 passed, 8 skipped.
- `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean with the repo-pinned ruff 0.15.6.
